versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Woman: Last week, we talked about realism, in which artists aimed to depict the world as it really exists. Today, we'll explore surrealism. Starting in France in the 1920s, surrealist artists focused on inner realities, concepts such as fantasy and the nature of dreams. Their works reflected a combination of these inner realities as well as outer realities, that is, things we physically experience. Their paintings often depicted a familiar scene, but in a dreamlike manner. Spaniard Joan Miró was especially adept at surrealism. Interestingly though, Miró never wanted to be associated with any artistic movement, and he never called himself a surrealist. But his contemporaries did, and we can see why they did when we look at Miró's work. Miró typically painted in two stages. The latter stage was carefully calculated. It was meticulous and precise. Miró knew exactly what he was doing in this stage. But in the initial stage, Miró didn't plan what he was going to paint. He just started painting. The form, whatever it was—a bird, a building, whatever appeared on the canvas—the form suggested itself under his brush. That's how Miró described it. This method of creating art without conscious control is called automatism. Automatism is quite noticeable in a work of Miró's that is titled simply "Painting". Even Miró couldn't fully explain the meaning of this work. Presumably, the images that appeared came from things deep inside him, things he may not have even known were there.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课的讲座。

女：上周我们谈了现实主义，其中艺术家旨在描绘世界真实存在的样子。今天我们探讨超现实主义。始于一九二〇年代的法国，超现实主义艺术家聚焦内在现实，如幻想与梦的本质等概念。他们的作品反映这些内在现实与外在现实——即我们身体体验的事物——的结合。他们的画常以梦幻方式描绘熟悉场景。西班牙人胡安·米罗尤其擅长超现实主义。有趣的是，米罗从不想与任何艺术运动挂钩，也从不自称超现实主义者。但他的同时代人这样称呼他，看米罗的作品我们就能明白为何。米罗通常分两阶段作画。后一阶段精心计算。细致而精确。米罗在这一阶段确切知道自己在做什么。但在初始阶段，米罗不计划要画什么。他只是开始画。形式，无论是什么——鸟、建筑，无论画布上出现什么——形式在他笔下自行显现。米罗就是这样描述的。这种在无意识控制下创作艺术的方法称为自动主义。自动主义在米罗一幅仅题为《绘画》的作品中相当明显。即便米罗也无法完全解释这件作品的含义。据推测，出现的图像来自他内心深处的东西，甚至他可能并不知道它们在那里。

versions.transcript: Last week, we talked about realism, in which artists aimed to depict the world as it really exists. Today, we'll explore surrealism. Starting in France in the 1920s, surrealist artists focused on inner realities, concepts such as fantasy and the nature of dreams. Their works reflected a combination of these inner realities as well as outer realities, that is, things we physically experience. Their paintings often depicted a familiar scene, but in a dreamlike manner. Spaniard Joan Miro was especially adept at surrealism. Interestingly, though, Miro never wanted to be associated with any artistic movement, and he never called himself a surrealist. But his contemporaries did, and we can see why they did when we look at Miro's work. Miro typically painted in two stages. The latter stage was carefully calculated. It was meticulous and precise. Miro knew exactly what he was doing in this stage. But in the initial stage, Miro didn't plan what he was going to paint. He just started painting. The form, whatever it was, a bird, a building, whatever appeared on the canvas, the form suggested itself under his brush. That's how Miro described it. This method of creating art without conscious control is called automatism. Automatism is quite noticeable in a work of Miro's that is titled, simply, Painting. Even Miro couldn't fully explain the meaning of this work. Miro's painting was a form of self reflection. Presumably, the images that appeared came from things deep inside him. Things he may not have even known were there.
versions.transcriptZh: 上周，我们讨论了现实主义，即艺术家们旨在描绘世界真实存在的面貌。 今天，我们将探讨超现实主义。 超现实主义艺术家于 20 世纪 20 年代诞生于法国，他们专注于内在现实，例如幻想和梦境的本质等概念。 他们的作品反映了这些内在现实与外在现实（即我们身体所经历的事物）的结合。 他们的画作通常描绘熟悉的场景，但却以一种梦幻般的方式呈现。 西班牙人 Joan Miro 特别擅长超现实主义。 但有趣的是，Miro 从不希望与任何艺术运动联系在一起，也从不称自己为超现实主义者。 但他的同时代人却这么认为，当我们看到 Miro 的作品时，就能明白他们为什么这么说了。 Miro 通常分两个阶段作画。 后期阶段是经过仔细计算的。 它细致且精确。 Miro 清楚地知道他在这个阶段在做什么。 但在最初阶段，Miro 并不计划他要画什么。 他只是开始动笔画。 那种形式，无论是一只鸟、一座建筑，还是画布上出现的任何东西，都是在他的画笔下自然形成的。 这就是 Miro 对此的描述。 这种没有意识控制的艺术创作方法被称为“自动主义”。 自动主义在 Miro 的一部名为《绘画》（Painting）的作品中非常明显。 甚至连 Miro 自己也无法完全解释这幅作品的含义。 Miro 的绘画是一种自我反思的形式。 想必，出现的图像源于他内心深处的东西。 那些他可能甚至不知道存在于那里的东西。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
When we think about paintings, we often focus on their subject, their style, or even the type of paint used. What we often overlook is the material underneath the paint, what we call its support, or sometimes, the substrate. This is the surface on which the paint is applied. The support is more important than you might think. Before the 14th century, most paintings were created on wooden panels. Wood was strong and durable, but it posed serious challenges. Large panels were extremely heavy, making transport difficult. Because of this, artists were limited in how big their works could be. Typical subjects for panel paintings were small devotional images, altarpieces, and portraits, works intended for private chapels or fixed locations rather than large public spaces. In the early 14th century, artists in Italy, especially in Venice, began turning to canvas as a support for their paintings. And by the late 15th century, its use had spread widely. Canvas was light and flexible, so paintings could be moved easily and made much larger. This portability meant that monumental works could be displayed in civic buildings, palaces, and even transported for festivals. This brought art beyond the confines of churches and into broader public life. This new use of canvas wasn't just a technical change. It transformed art because it enabled ambitious subjects like vast historical scenes and mythological narratives. For example, Paolo Veronese's The Wedding at Cana, which is a massive banquet scene filled with dozens of figures and rich architectural detail.

请听一段艺术史课的讲座。
想到绘画时，我们常关注题材、风格，甚至颜料种类。常被忽略的是颜料下面的材料，我们称为支撑体，有时也称基底。这就是涂颜料的表面。支撑体比你想的更重要。十四世纪之前，多数画作画在木板上。木材结实耐用，但带来严重挑战。大块木板极重，运输困难。因此艺术家作品尺寸受限。木板画典型题材是小型宗教图像、祭坛画与肖像，供私人礼拜堂或固定场所，而非大型公共空间。十四世纪初，意大利艺术家尤其威尼斯开始改用画布作支撑。到十五世纪末，用法已广泛传播。画布轻而柔韧，画作可轻易移动、也可做得更大。这种可搬运性意味着巨作可在市政建筑、宫殿展出，甚至运去节庆。艺术由此走出教堂局限，进入更广阔的公共生活。画布的新用法不只是技术变化。它改变了艺术，因为它使宏大历史场景与神话叙事这类雄心题材成为可能。例如保罗·委罗内塞的《迦拿的婚礼》，是满是数十人物与丰富建筑细节的巨型宴会场景。

versions.label: Wofo M21
versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
In the early 1900s, sea otters, marine mammals that feed on invertebrates including sea urchins, were nearly wiped out along the United States Pacific coast by fur hunters. With otters gone, urchin numbers exploded, destroying kelp forests. Now kelp is a type of seaweed, and it's sea urchins' favorite food. This left countless marine species without the protective habitat that kelp forests provided to them. In 1972, hunting sea otters was banned. As otters made a comeback, urchin numbers dropped, kelp forests grew back, and biodiversity flourished. Scientists realized otters were a keystone species, organisms whose impact on ecosystems is far greater than their numbers suggest. A similar case occurred in Yellowstone National Park. Wolves, the park's top predator, had been eradicated. Populations of elk, a deer-like animal and a favorite prey for wolves, soared, and their huge populations damaged local vegetation, including the willow and aspen trees for which the park had been famous. In the 1990s, wolves were reintroduced to the park to get the elk population under control. But the wolves didn't just cut elk numbers. They changed elk behavior. Afraid of being eaten by wolves, the elk avoided streamside areas where they're especially vulnerable. This helped willow and aspen trees reestablish themselves there. And the trees brought back beavers, animals that live in streams and build dams to create ponds for themselves. The beaver dams created habitats for fish, birds, and amphibians, a huge cascading effect because of this other keystone species.

请听一段生物学课的讲座。
二十世纪初，海獭——以包括海胆在内的无脊椎动物为食的海洋哺乳动物——在美国太平洋沿岸被毛皮猎人几乎杀光。海獭消失后，海胆数量爆炸，摧毁了海带林。海带是一种海藻，也是海胆最爱的食物。这让无数海洋物种失去了海带林提供的保护性栖息地。一九七二年，猎杀海獭被禁止。随着海獭回归，海胆数量下降，海带林恢复，生物多样性兴旺。科学家认识到海獭是关键种：对生态系统的影响远大于其数量所暗示的生物。类似情况发生在黄石国家公园。公园顶级捕食者狼曾被灭绝。麋鹿——一种似鹿、也是狼最爱猎物的动物——种群飙升，其庞大数量破坏了当地植被，包括公园曾以之闻名的柳树与白杨。一九九〇年代，狼被重新引入公园以控制麋鹿数量。但狼不只减少了麋鹿数量。它们改变了麋鹿行为。因怕被狼吃掉，麋鹿避开它们特别脆弱的溪边地带。这帮助柳树与白杨在那里重新立足。树木又带回了河狸——住在溪流中、筑坝为自己造池塘的动物。河狸坝为鱼、鸟与两栖动物创造了栖息地，因这一关键种而产生巨大级联效应。

questions.promptText: What was the cause for the near disappearance of sea otters from waters along the United States Pacific coast?
questions.promptTextZh: 海獭几乎从美国太平洋沿岸水域消失的原因是什么？

choices.label: Disease
choices.labelZh: 疾病
choices.explanationZh: near disappearance 的原因是 fur hunters 捕猎，不是疾病。

choices.label: Overhunting by humans
choices.labelZh: 人类的过度捕猎
choices.explanationZh: 原文说 sea otters were nearly wiped out by fur hunters，fur hunters 对应人类过度捕猎。

choices.label: Competition from other species
choices.labelZh: 与其他物种的竞争
choices.explanationZh: 原文没有说其他物种竞争导致 sea otters 减少。

choices.label: Habitat destruction
choices.labelZh: 栖息地破坏
choices.explanationZh: 栖息地破坏不是这里给出的原因。

questions.promptText: According to the speaker, what happened to kelp forests when sea otters almost disappeared?
questions.promptTextZh: 根据演讲者的说法，当海獭几乎消失后，海藻森林发生了什么？

choices.label: They became overgrown and crowded out other marine life.
choices.labelZh: 它们过度生长，挤走了其他海洋生物。
choices.explanationZh: kelp forests 不是过度生长，而是因为 sea urchins 增多被吃掉、被破坏。

choices.label: They returned to their original size.
choices.labelZh: 它们恢复到了原来的规模。
choices.explanationZh: sea otters 几乎消失时 kelp 没有恢复原状，反而衰退。

choices.label: They were destroyed by expanding populations of sea urchins.
choices.labelZh: 它们被不断增多的海胆种群破坏。
choices.explanationZh: 海獭消失后 sea urchin numbers exploded，而海胆以 kelp 为食，所以 kelp forests 被大量海胆破坏。

choices.label: They began to attract species that the otters had previously preyed on.
choices.labelZh: 它们开始吸引海獭此前捕食的物种。
choices.explanationZh: 原文强调 sea urchins 破坏 kelp，不是 kelp 吸引 otters 的猎物。

questions.promptText: How did elk behavior change after wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park?
questions.promptTextZh: 在黄石国家公园重新引入狼群后，麋鹿的行为发生了怎样的变化？

choices.label: Elk began to be more active at night.
choices.labelZh: 麋鹿开始在夜间活动更频繁。
choices.explanationZh: 行为变化是避开溪流附近取食，不是变成夜间活动。

choices.label: Elk began to form larger groups.
choices.labelZh: 麋鹿开始组成更大的群体。
choices.explanationZh: 原文没有说 elk 形成更大的群体。

choices.label: Elk began to feed less near streams.
choices.labelZh: 麋鹿开始减少在溪流附近的觅食。
choices.explanationZh: 狼被重新引入后，elk avoided streamside areas，因为在那里更容易被捕食。

choices.label: Elk began to hide among willow and aspen trees.
choices.labelZh: 麋鹿开始躲藏在柳树和白杨树丛中。
choices.explanationZh: willow/aspen 是因 elk 少吃而恢复的植物，不是 elk 躲藏地点。

questions.promptText: What does the speaker emphasize about beavers in Yellowstone?
questions.promptTextZh: 演讲者强调了黄石公园河狸的什么特点？

choices.label: Their presence benefits many other animal species.
choices.labelZh: 它们的存在有益于许多其他动物物种。
choices.explanationZh: beaver dams created habitats for fish, birds, and amphibians，说明海狸出现惠及多种动物。

choices.label: They are often preyed on by wolves.
choices.labelZh: 它们经常被狼捕食。
choices.explanationZh: speaker 讲 beavers 建坝带来栖息地收益，没有强调它们被狼捕食。

choices.label: They often damage vegetation.
choices.labelZh: 它们经常破坏植被。
choices.explanationZh: 这里说 beavers 改造环境产生 habitat，不是强调破坏 vegetation。

choices.label: They compete with elk for food.
choices.labelZh: 它们与麋鹿竞争食物。
choices.explanationZh: beavers 的重点是帮助鱼、鸟、两栖动物，不是和 elk 争食。

versions.transcript: Listen to a talk on a social sciences podcast. One of the most fascinating aspects of human culture is gift-giving. While it might seem simple, it's actually a deeply social act shaped by cultural norms. Anthropologists have found that gifts aren't just about exchanging goods; they're about building relationships. In many indigenous communities, gift-giving plays a central role in ceremonies and rituals. For example, in the potlatch tradition among indigenous groups in the Pacific Northwest, gifts like food, blankets, or tools are exchanged during communal gatherings to honor guests, mark life events, and reinforce social bonds. These gifts carry meaning and create mutual obligations, helping maintain harmony and unity within the group. Now, interestingly, receiving a gift often comes with an expectation to give back, not immediately, but eventually. Anthropologist Marcel Mauss described this as a spirit of reciprocity. And what's important is that it's not just a one-time transaction of "you gave me something, so I'll give you something." This is often repeated in a continuous loop, creating long-term connections and trust. Over time, this rhythm of giving and returning strengthens relationships and community ties. Okay, now in more formal settings like business and diplomacy, gift-giving can signal goodwill, but cultural sensitivity is key. For instance, while a potted plant might seem thoughtful and eco-friendly, in some cultures it could symbolize sickness, making it unsuitable for formal occasions. So knowing what's appropriate really matters.
versions.transcriptZh: 请听一段社会科学播客的讲座。人类文化最迷人的方面之一是送礼。它看似简单，其实是由文化规范塑造的深刻社会行为。人类学家发现，礼物不只关乎交换物品；更关乎建立关系。在许多原住民社群中，送礼在仪式中起核心作用。例如，太平洋西北原住民群体的夸富宴传统中，在公共聚会交换食物、毯子或工具等礼物，以尊贵客、标记人生事件、强化社会纽带。这些礼物承载意义并产生相互义务，有助维持群体内和谐与团结。有趣的是，收礼常伴随着回礼的期望——不是立刻，而是最终。人类学家马塞尔·莫斯称之为互惠精神。重要的是，这不只是「你给我东西，我就给你东西」的一次性交易。它常在持续循环中重复，创造长期联结与信任。久而久之，这种给予与回报的节奏强化关系与社区纽带。好，在商务与外交等更正式场合，送礼可示善意，但文化敏感是关键。例如，盆栽看似体贴环保，在某些文化中却可能象征疾病，不适合正式场合。所以知道什么得体真的很重要。

versions.transcriptZh: 人类文化中最引人入胜的方面之一就是送礼。 虽然这看起来很简单，但它实际上是一种深受文化规范影响的深刻的社会行为。 人类学家发现，送礼不仅仅是为了交换物品，更是为了建立人际关系。 在许多原住民社区中，送礼在仪式和典礼中扮演着核心角色。 例如，在太平洋西北地区原住民群体的散财宴传统中，食物、毯子或工具等礼物在公共聚会期间进行交换，以尊敬客人、纪念人生事件并加强社会联系。 这些礼物承载着意义并产生相互义务，有助于维持群体内部的和睦与团结。 现在，有趣的是，收到礼物往往伴随着回赠的期望，不是立即，而是最终。 人类学家马塞尔·莫斯将其描述为一种互惠精神。 重要的是，这不仅仅是一次性的交易，即你给了我东西，所以我也给你东西。 这个循环经常在持续的循环中重复，从而建立长期的联系和信任。 随着时间的推移，这种给予和回馈的节奏加强了人际关系和社区联系。 好的，现在在更正式的场合，如商业和外交中，送礼可以表示善意，但文化敏感性是关键。 例如，盆栽植物可能看起来周到且环保，但在某些文化中，它可能象征负面事物，使其不适合正式场合。 因此，了解什么是合适的确实很重要。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
versions.transcript: Listen to a talk in an ecology class. An invasive species is a plant, animal, or other organism that is introduced into an ecosystem, usually by humans. An invasive species can cause harm to its new environment. An example is when humans introduced goats to the Galapagos Islands. The Galapagos are a chain of islands roughly 1,000 kilometers off the coast of Ecuador. Throughout the 1800s, people, mostly whalers and explorers, stopped at the islands during long ocean voyages. At that time, long ocean voyages made it hard to keep fresh meat on ships. So, sailors released goats on some islands as a living food supply. They could hunt later when passing through. They most likely didn't know how much their actions were going to damage the islands. Goats are very adaptable and can survive in harsh environments like the Galapagos. They definitely are not picky eaters. They consume everything from tough shrubs to grasses. So they didn't run out of food easily. With no natural predators, their population exploded. As time went on, the goats' eating habits caused native plants, like one species of cactus, to mostly disappear. And that was a huge problem for native animals like giant tortoises. These tortoises rely on plants like this cactus for food and shade. Without them, many tortoise populations collapsed. So how can we address this problem? Well, in the early 2000s, conservation efforts began to reintroduce tortoises to islands where they had gone extinct. Let's take a look at these efforts and determine how effective they've been.
versions.transcriptZh: 请听一段生态学课的讲座。入侵物种是被引入某一生态系统的植物、动物或其他生物，通常由人类引入。入侵物种可对新环境造成伤害。例子是人类把山羊引入加拉帕戈斯群岛。加拉帕戈斯是距厄瓜多尔海岸约一千公里的一串岛屿。整个十九世纪，主要是捕鲸者与探险家在长途航行中停靠这些岛。当时长途航行难以在船上保存鲜肉。于是水手在一些岛上放养山羊作活体食物储备，以后路过时可猎取。他们多半不知自己的行为会对岛屿造成多大破坏。山羊适应性极强，能在加拉帕戈斯这类严酷环境生存。它们绝不挑食。从坚硬灌木到草都吃，所以不易缺粮。没有天敌，数量爆炸。随着时间推移，山羊的取食习惯使本地植物——如某一种仙人掌——大多消失。这对巨型陆龟等本地动物是大问题。这些陆龟依赖此类仙人掌作食物与遮荫。没有它们，许多陆龟种群崩溃。我们如何应对？二十一世纪初，保护工作开始把陆龟重新引入它们已灭绝的岛屿。我们来看看这些努力，判断成效如何。

transcriptSentences.text: The Galapagos are a chain of islands roughly 1,000 kilometers off the coast of Ecuador.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 加拉帕戈斯是距厄瓜多尔海岸约一千公里的一串岛屿。

transcriptSentences.text: Throughout the 1800s, people, mostly whalers and explorers, stopped at the islands during long ocean voyages.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 整个十九世纪，主要是捕鲸者与探险家在长途航行中停靠这些岛。

transcriptSentences.text: At that time, long ocean voyages made it hard to keep fresh meat on ships.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 当时长途航行难以在船上保存鲜肉。

transcriptSentences.text: So, sailors released goats on some islands as a living food supply.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 于是水手在一些岛上放养山羊，当作活体食物储备。

transcriptSentences.text: They could hunt later when passing through.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 以后路过时可以猎取。

transcriptSentences.text: They most likely didn't know how much their actions were going to damage the islands.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他们多半不知道自己的行为会对岛屿造成多大破坏。

transcriptSentences.text: Goats are very adaptable and can survive in harsh environments like the Galapagos.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 山羊适应性极强，能在加拉帕戈斯这类严酷环境生存。

transcriptSentences.text: They definitely are not picky eaters.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它们绝不挑食。

transcriptSentences.text: They consume everything from tough shrubs to grasses.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 从坚硬灌木到草都吃。

transcriptSentences.text: So they didn't run out of food easily.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以它们不容易缺粮。

transcriptSentences.text: With no natural predators, their population exploded.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 没有天敌，它们的数量爆炸式增长。

transcriptSentences.text: As time went on, the goats' eating habits caused native plants, like one species of cactus, to mostly disappear.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 随着时间推移，山羊的取食习惯使本地植物——如某一种仙人掌——大多消失。

transcriptSentences.text: And that was a huge problem for native animals like giant tortoises.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这对巨型陆龟等本地动物是大问题。

transcriptSentences.text: These tortoises rely on plants like this cactus for food and shade.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这些陆龟依赖此类仙人掌作食物与遮荫。

transcriptSentences.text: Without them, many tortoise populations collapsed.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 没有它们，许多陆龟种群崩溃。

transcriptSentences.text: So how can we address this problem?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 我们如何应对这个问题？

transcriptSentences.text: Well, in the early 2000s, conservation efforts began to reintroduce tortoises to islands where they had gone extinct.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 二十一世纪初，保护工作开始把陆龟重新引入它们已灭绝的岛屿。

transcriptSentences.text: Let's take a look at these efforts and determine how effective they've been.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 我们来看看这些努力，判断成效如何。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a business class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a business class.

Let's talk about lean manufacturing and its impact on efficiency in production processes. Lean manufacturing is a systematic approach to minimizing waste within a manufacturing system while maximizing productivity. While the methodology has been adopted by many companies worldwide, it was developed by a Japanese carmaker in the mid-20th century. But its roots can actually be traced to the supermarket. In the 1950s, Japanese engineers observed that supermarkets in the United States only restocked items as customers purchased them, maintaining just enough inventory to meet demand. This idea of just-in-time inventory management became a core principle of lean manufacturing. By identifying and removing excess inventory and eliminating other inefficiencies, companies could reduce costs and increase their overall productivity. Another important aspect of lean manufacturing is continuous improvement, often referred to as Kaizen. This involves constantly seeking ways to enhance processes, products, and services. Employees at all levels are encouraged to contribute ideas for improvement, fostering a culture of innovation and teamwork. Lean manufacturing also emphasizes the importance of value from the customer's perspective. Companies focus on producing goods that meet customer needs and expectations, ensuring that each step in the production process adds value rather than unnecessary complexity. As you might imagine, implementing lean manufacturing requires a shift in organizational culture. Resistance to change and difficulty in sustaining improvements can get in the way. That said, companies that successfully adopt lean practices experience increased efficiency, reduced costs, and higher customer satisfaction.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段商业课的讲座。

我们来谈精益制造及其对生产流程效率的影响。精益制造是在制造系统内最小化浪费、同时最大化生产率的系统方法。虽已被全球许多公司采用，它由一家日本汽车制造商在二十世纪中叶开发。但其根源其实可追溯到超市。一九五〇年代，日本工程师观察到美国超市只在顾客购买后补货，维持刚好满足需求的库存。这种准时制库存管理理念成为精益制造的核心原则。通过识别并清除过量库存、消除其他低效，公司可降低成本并提高整体生产率。精益制造的另一重要方面是持续改进，常称为改善。这包括不断寻找增强流程、产品与服务的方法。鼓励各层级员工提出改进想法，培育创新与团队文化。精益制造也强调从客户视角看价值的重要性。公司专注生产满足客户需求与期望的商品，确保生产过程每一步都增加价值而非不必要的复杂。可以想见，实施精益制造需要组织文化转变。对变革的阻力与难以维持改进可能成为障碍。尽管如此，成功采用精益做法的公司会体验到效率提高、成本降低与客户满意度上升。

choices.label: An approach to reducing waste and increasing productivity

choices.label: The origins of the concept of lean manufacturing

questions.promptText: How does the speaker organize the talk?

choices.labelZh: 他比较了精益制造的优缺点
choices.explanationZh: 讲座不是优缺点对比结构，而是逐条讲 lean principles。

choices.label: He provides a detailed history of the development of lean manufacturing.
choices.labelZh: 他详细介绍了精益制造的发展历史

transcriptSentences.textZh: 这包括不断寻找方法来改进流程、产品和服务。

transcriptSentences.text: Companies at all levels are encouraged to contribute ideas for improvement, fostering a culture of innovation and teamwork.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 鼓励各级员工贡献改进意见，培养创新和团队合作的文化。

transcriptSentences.text: Lean manufacturing also emphasizes the importance of value from the customer's perspective.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 精益生产还强调从客户角度看待价值的重要性。

transcriptSentences.text: Companies focus on producing goods that meet customer needs and expectations, ensuring that each step in the production process adds value rather than unnecessary complexity.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 公司专注于生产满足客户需求和期望的产品，确保生产过程中的每一步都增加价值，而不是不必要的复杂性。

transcriptSentences.text: As you might imagine, implementing lean manufacturing requires a shift in organizational culture.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 正如你可能想象的，实施精益生产需要组织文化的转变。

transcriptSentences.text: Resistance to change and difficulty in sustaining improvements can get in the way.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 对变革的抵制以及难以持续改进可能会阻碍其发展。

transcriptSentences.text: That said, companies that successfully adopt lean practices experience increased efficiency, reduced costs and higher customer satisfaction.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 尽管如此，成功采用精益实践的公司会体验到效率的提高、成本的降低和客户满意度的提升。

versions.transcript: Listen to a lecture in an art history class. David Hockney, one of Britain's most celebrated painters, is renowned for his use of bold color and constant experimentation. In the 1960s, he gained fame with large acrylic paintings of California swimming pools, works like A Bigger Splash, which captured light, leisure, and everyday moments from modern life with striking clarity. Throughout his career, Hockney embraced innovation, always exploring how technology could expand his artistic vision. Decades later, in 2009, that curiosity led him to digital art. He began on a mobile phone, drawn at first to its portability and ease of use. Digital painting offered freedoms unimaginable with oil paints or even acrylic paints: no drying time, no storage issues, and infinite color choices at a tap of his fingers. Hockney used these features to create vibrant landscapes and intimate still lifes, often sharing them instantly with friends, a spontaneity that echoed his lifelong interest in technology's role in art. Working on a small screen shaped his style: simplified forms, luminous colors, and a fluid process that felt like a dialogue with light and time. Eventually, he moved to a tablet, where a larger screen allowed broader gestures, richer details, and more complex compositions. These works retained his fascination with the theme of daily life, but now they also reflected the freedoms of the digital medium: bolder colors, more clarity, and freshness. Hockney's digital paintings remind us that while tools evolve, art's essence remains: seeing the world always in a new light.
versions.transcriptZh: 请听一段艺术史课的讲座。David Hockney 是英国最负盛名的画家之一，以大胆用色与不断实验著称。一九六〇年代，他以加州泳池的大型丙烯画成名，如《更大的水花》，以惊人清晰捕捉光、闲适与现代生活的日常瞬间。整个职业生涯中，Hockney 拥抱创新，始终探索技术如何拓展艺术视野。数十年后的二零〇九年，这份好奇把他引向数字艺术。他从手机起步，起初被便携与易用吸引。数字绘画提供了油画甚至丙烯难以想象的自由：无需干燥时间、无存储问题，指尖一点即有无限色彩选择。Hockney 用这些特性创作鲜活风景与亲切静物，常即时分享给朋友，这种自发性呼应他对技术在艺术中角色的终身兴趣。在小屏幕上作画塑造了他的风格：简化的形式、明亮的色彩，以及像与光和时间对话的流畅过程。最终他改用平板，更大屏幕允许更开阔的笔触、更丰富的细节与更复杂的构图。这些作品仍保有他对日常生活主题的迷恋，但此刻也反映数字媒介的自由：更大胆的色彩、更清晰与新鲜。Hockney 的数字画提醒我们：工具在变，艺术本质不变——总以新的眼光看世界。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

Today we're revisiting the topic of urban green spaces. Green areas in cities like parks and gardens. These spaces are known to improve air quality and reduce heat in cities. They also support the health of city residents. Creating and maintaining urban green spaces can be challenging, however, especially in densely populated cities. An obvious issue is limited space. In areas where land is expensive or already developed, finding room for parks or gardens can be difficult. One way cities address this is by building green roofs. That's a layer of vegetation planted on top of a building. Green roofs help cool buildings, absorb rainwater, and add greenery without taking up ground space. Cities also often repurpose unused lots, such as old parking areas or vacant lots, turning them into small parks or gardens. Vertical gardens are another innovation. These are walls covered with plants, often using special structures that allow greenery to grow upward. They are useful in places where horizontal space is limited and can improve air quality and insulation. While costs and upkeep of green spaces are legitimate concerns, many cities are adopting green space quotas. Policies that require a minimum amount of greenery in new developments. These quotas mandate builders to include features like trees, rooftop gardens, or courtyards. Though they may raise construction costs, urban planners support them because they ensure that green space is not overlooked in city growth. Quotas help balance development with environmental health and are a step toward more sustainable urban living.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段环境科学课的讲座。

今天我们重访城市绿地话题。城市中的绿色区域，如公园与花园。这些空间以改善空气质量、降低城市热岛效应著称。它们也支持城市居民健康。但创建与维护城市绿地可能具有挑战，尤其在人口密集城市。明显问题是空间有限。在土地昂贵或已开发的地区，找地方建公园或花园可能很难。城市应对的一种方式是建绿色屋顶：建筑物顶部种植的一层植被。绿色屋顶有助冷却建筑、吸收雨水，并在不占地面空间的情况下增加绿意。城市也常把闲置地块——如旧停车场或空地——改造成小公园或花园。垂直花园是另一创新。这些是覆盖植物的墙面，常用特殊结构让绿意向上生长。它们在水平空间有限之处有用，并可改善空气质量与隔热。尽管绿地成本与维护是合理关切，许多城市正采用绿地配额：要求新开发项目中有最低绿化量的政策。这些配额强制建设者纳入树木、屋顶花园或庭院等要素。虽可能提高建设成本，城市规划者支持它们，因为它们确保城市增长中绿地不被忽视。配额有助平衡开发与环境健康，是迈向更可持续城市生活的一步。

versions.transcript: Today, we're revisiting the topic of urban green spaces, green areas in cities like parks and gardens. These spaces are known to improve air quality and reduce heat in cities. They also support the health of city residents. Creating and maintaining urban green spaces can be challenging, however, especially in densely populated cities. An obvious issue is space. In areas where land is expensive or already developed, finding room for parks or gardens can be difficult. One way cities address this is by building green roofs. That's a layer of vegetation planted on top of a building. Green roofs help cool buildings, absorb rainwater, and add greenery without taking up ground space. Cities also often repurpose unused lots, such as abandoned parking areas or vacant lots, turning them into small parks or gardens. Vertical gardens are another innovation. These are walls covered with plants, often using special structures that allow greenery to grow upward. They're useful in places where horizontal space is limited and can improve air quality and insulation. While cost and upkeep of green spaces are legitimate concerns, many cities are adopting green space quotas, policies that require a minimum amount of greenery in new developments. These quotas mandate builders to include features such as trees, rooftop gardens, or courtyards. Though they may raise construction costs, urban planners support them because they ensure that green space is not overlooked in city growth. Quotas help balance development with environmental health and are a step toward more sustainable urban living.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天，我们要重新讨论城市绿地的话题，也就是城市中像公园和花园这样的绿色区域。 众所周知，这些空间可以改善空气质量并降低城市的热度。 它们还能够维护城市居民的健康。 然而，创建和维护城市绿地可能具有挑战性，特别是在人口稠密的城市。 一个显而易见的问题是空间。 在土地昂贵或已经开发完毕的地区，很难为公园或花园找到空间。 城市解决这一问题的一种方法是建造屋顶绿化。 那是种在建筑物顶部的一层植被。 屋顶绿化有助于建筑物降温，吸收雨水，并在不占用地面空间的情况下增加绿化。 城市还经常重新利用闲置土地，比如废弃的停车场或空地，将它们改造成小型公园或花园。 垂直花园是另一项创新。 这些是长满植物的墙壁，通常使用特殊结构让绿植向上生长。 它们在水平空间有限的地方非常有用，并且可以改善空气质量和隔热效果。 虽然绿地的成本和维护是合理的担忧，但许多城市正在采用绿地配额制，即要求新开发项目必须达到最低绿化量的政策。 这些配额强制要求建筑商纳入树木、屋顶花园或庭院等设施。 虽然这些配额可能会增加建筑成本，但城市规划者支持它们，因为它们能确保在城市增长的过程中绿地不会被忽视。 配额有助于平衡发展与环境健康，是迈向更可持续城市生活的一步。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

In recent years, more people have started growing plants in urban spaces, a practice known as urban gardening. This includes cultivating plants on rooftops, balconies, and in community gardens. Urban gardening can help reduce some negative effects of urbanization, such as pollution. One benefit is improved air quality. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, which helps clean the air and makes cities more livable. Another advantage is enhanced food security. By growing their own produce, city residents can access fresh, healthy food and rely less on commercial agriculture. This is especially helpful in food deserts, areas where access to fruits and vegetables is limited. Imagine an abandoned plot in a city, maybe a piece of land where an old factory used to be. Now imagine clearing the land and building a small community center surrounded by garden plots. People from the neighborhood come to workshops to learn how to plant and cultivate spinach, strawberries, tomatoes, whatever produce they want. These neighborhood volunteers then cultivate the garden plots and harvest their produce. As you can imagine, this would bring people together and encourage cooperation and shared responsibility. However, there are challenges to urban gardening, such as soil contamination. In some instances, the soil may contain harmful substances like heavy metals or industrial chemicals. Gardeners often need to test and treat the soil or use raised beds with clean soil to ensure safe growing conditions. Despite these obstacles, cities are adopting policies to support urban gardening and improve residents' quality of life.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段环境科学课的讲座。

近年来，越来越多人开始在城市空间种植植物，这一做法称为城市园艺。包括在屋顶、阳台与社区园地栽培。城市园艺有助于减轻城市化的某些负面影响，例如污染。好处之一是改善空气质量。植物吸收二氧化碳并释放氧气，有助净化空气，使城市更宜居。另一优势是增强粮食安全。城市居民自种农产品，可获得新鲜健康食物，并减少对商业农业的依赖。这在食物沙漠——蔬果获取受限的地区——尤其有用。想象城中一块废弃地，也许是旧工厂原址。再想象清理土地、建起小社区中心，四周是园地。邻里来参加工作坊，学习种植栽培菠菜、草莓、番茄等想种的作物。这些邻里志愿者再照料园地、收获产品。可以想见，这会把人聚在一起，鼓励合作与共同责任。但城市园艺也有挑战，如土壤污染。有时土壤含重金属或工业化学品等有害物。园丁常需检测处理土壤，或用干净土壤的抬高苗床，以确保安全种植条件。尽管有这些障碍，城市正采取政策支持城市园艺，改善居民生活质量。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.

When you think of archaeological fieldwork, you might picture people using tools to dig through dirt and uncover a variety of artifacts, like pottery and jewelry. You might think of a site like Ephesus, an ancient city located in western Turkey. By the way, some say that's the largest excavated site on Earth. Ephesus includes massive remains from different time periods, including Roman, Greek, and Byzantine periods, which are different civilizations spanning millennia. For example, at Ephesus, there are ruins of ancient Greek temples and Roman theaters. Other archaeological sites, though, are more difficult to reach. There's an entire subfield of archaeology that focuses on these sites. It's called underwater archaeology. Underwater archaeology is the study of human history through sites and artifacts found beneath the water's surface. This includes shipwrecks, submerged settlements, harbors, and ports. Researchers have found all kinds of artifacts at underwater sites, including tools, pottery, coins, and other objects. Because water can slow decay, especially of organic materials like wood or textiles, underwater sites often provide exceptionally well-preserved evidence of past human activity. One notable underwater site is the Uluburun shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, dating to about 3,000 years ago. Uluburun was discovered in 1982. Specialized diving and excavation techniques were used at this site, and archaeologists recovered cargo, including copper ingots and luxury goods. These artifacts shed light on ancient trade networks. They suggest that highly complex, multi-regional trade routes connecting central Asia to Europe and Africa existed far earlier than we expected.

请听一段考古学课的讲座。

想到田野考古，你或许会想象人们用工具挖土、发现陶器与珠宝等各类器物。你也许会想到以弗所这类遗址——位于土耳其西部的古城。顺便说，有人说那是地球上最大的发掘遗址。以弗所包含不同时期的大规模遗存，包括罗马、希腊与拜占庭时期，这些是跨越千年的不同文明。例如，以弗所有古希腊神庙与罗马剧场的废墟。不过其他考古遗址更难抵达。有一整支考古学分支专注这些遗址，称为水下考古。水下考古通过水面下发现的遗址与器物研究人类历史。包括沉船、淹没聚落、港口与港湾。研究者在水下遗址发现各类器物，包括工具、陶器、钱币等。因为水可减缓腐烂，尤其对木材或纺织品等有机材料，水下遗址常提供过去人类活动保存异常完好的证据。一处著名水下遗址是土耳其近海的乌鲁布伦沉船，可追溯到约三千年前。乌鲁布伦于一九八二年发现。该遗址使用了专门的潜水与发掘技术，考古学家回收了包括铜锭与奢侈品在内的货物。这些器物揭示古代贸易网络。它们表明连接中亚与欧洲、非洲的高度复杂多区域贸易路线存在时间远早于我们预期。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Imagine a chilly mountain forest. It's early spring, the snow's just melting, and it's still very cold. Now picture a small, bright yellow flower blooming at the edge of the snow. Hard to imagine any flower surviving in those conditions, right? Yet the snow buttercup thrives. How? Well, the snow buttercup's anatomy has a few things going for it. First, a fuzzy stem, like a tiny winter coat that protects it from extreme cold and wind. Plus, a deep root system. The roots keep it anchored in unstable soil on mountains and can reach water that's up to 30 centimeters deep. Now, the snow buttercup needs to protect its cells from ice crystals. To do this, it produces antifreeze proteins. Researchers are studying these proteins, hoping to develop ways to protect other plants, like maybe developing frost-resistant crops for farmers to grow. Okay, so these adaptations allow the snow buttercup to bloom earlier, while most other plants are still dormant for winter. This means exclusive visits from beneficial pollinators like bumblebees and butterflies. The pollinators get food, nectar, from the snow buttercup, while also helping the plant reproduce by spreading its reproductive material, the pollen. The adaptation I find most fascinating is called heliotropic movement. When the flower is open, heliotropic movement means it turns to face the sun throughout the day, staying warm as the sun moves along the sky. Increasing its temperature even a few degrees this way is crucial.

请听一段生物学课的讲座。

想象一片寒冷的山地森林。早春，雪刚融化，仍很冷。再想象一朵小而鲜黄的花在雪缘绽放。很难想象任何花能在那种条件下存活，对吧？然而雪毛茛茁壮生长。怎么做到的？雪毛茛的结构有几处优势。首先，毛茸茸的茎，像一件小冬衣，保护它免受极寒与风。加上深根系。根把它固定在山坡不稳的土壤中，并可触及深达三十厘米的水。雪毛茛还须保护细胞免受冰晶伤害。为此它产生抗冻蛋白。研究者在研究这些蛋白，希望开发保护其他植物的方法，比如也许为农民培育抗霜作物。好，这些适应使雪毛茛更早开花，而多数其他植物仍在冬眠。这意味着能独占熊蜂与蝴蝶等有益传粉者的造访。传粉者从雪毛茛获得食物——花蜜，同时通过传播其繁殖材料——花粉——帮助植物繁殖。我觉得最迷人的适应叫向日运动。花开放时，向日运动意味着它整天转向太阳，随太阳在天空移动而保持温暖。用这种方式哪怕只提高几度温度也至关重要。

versions.transcript: Imagine a chilly mountain forest. It's early spring, the snow is just melting, and it's still very cold. Now picture a small bright yellow flower blooming at the edge of the snow. Hard to imagine any flower surviving in those conditions, right? Yet the snow buttercup thrives. The snow buttercup's anatomy has a few things going for it. First, a fuzzy stem works like a tiny winter coat that protects it from extreme cold and wind. Plus, a deep root system keeps it anchored in unstable mountain soil and can reach water up to 30 centimeters deep. The snow buttercup also produces antifreeze proteins to protect its cells from ice crystals. Researchers are studying these proteins, hoping to develop ways to protect other plants, such as frost resistant crops for farmers to grow. These adaptations allow the snow buttercup to bloom earlier while most other plants are still dormant. That means exclusive visits from beneficial pollinators like bumblebees and butterflies. The adaptation I find most fascinating is heliotropic movement: when the flower is open, it turns to face the sun throughout the day. Staying warm as the sun moves across the sky, even by a few degrees, is beneficial.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a business class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a business class.

Why do some companies thrive while others with similar resources falter? Organizational agility might hold the key. Organizational agility is a company's ability to quickly adapt to market changes by making fast decisions, being flexible and responsive to customer needs, and being able to reconfigure internal structures when needed. Take an example you're probably familiar with: a streaming media company that began as a DVD rental service. It successfully pivoted to online streaming just as internet speeds improved, and later moved into producing original content. These shifts were strategic and fast. They allowed the company to stay ahead of consumer expectations and industry trends. Agility also means responding to customer demands. A well-known clothing retailer, for instance, designed its supply chain to move new styles from concept to store in just a few weeks. If a celebrity wears a bold new look, this retailer can have a similar item on shelves while competitors are still in the design phase. That kind of responsiveness keeps the brand relevant. Agility comes with hurdles, like cultural resistance. In one case, a large industrial firm tried to adopt agile practices across its divisions. This meant forming cross-functional teams, groups made up of people from different departments like engineering, marketing, and operations, who would collaborate on shared goals. But many employees had spent decades in rigid hierarchies with clearly defined roles. Cross-functional teams felt chaotic and unfamiliar. This industrial firm had to invest in training to help employees understand that agility wasn't about abandoning structure, but about building smarter, more responsive systems.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段商业课的讲座。

为何有些公司兴旺，而资源相似的其他公司却步履维艰？组织敏捷性或许是关键。组织敏捷性是公司通过快速决策、灵活响应客户需求、并在需要时重组内部结构来迅速适应市场变化的能力。举一个你大概熟悉的例子：一家从 DVD 租赁起家的流媒体公司。它在网速提升时成功转向在线流媒体，后又进入自制内容。这些转变既有策略又迅速。它们让公司领先于消费者预期与行业趋势。敏捷也意味着响应客户需求。例如一家知名服装零售商设计供应链，使新款从概念到上架仅需数周。若某名人穿出大胆新造型，该零售商可在竞争对手仍处设计阶段时把类似单品摆上货架。这种响应性保持品牌相关。敏捷也有障碍，如文化阻力。一例中，一家大型工业企业试图在各部门采用敏捷做法。这意味着组建跨职能团队——由来自工程、营销、运营等不同部门的人组成、就共同目标协作。但许多员工在角色清晰的僵化等级中工作了数十年。跨职能团队显得混乱陌生。该企业不得不投入培训，帮助员工理解敏捷不是抛弃结构，而是建立更聪明、更响应的系统。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on an archaeology podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on an archaeology podcast.

Throughout the years, archaeologists have discovered many fascinating artifacts on the Greek island of Crete. One example is the Phaistos Disc, an ancient clay artifact that was found in the ruins of the Minoan palace at Phaistos. The Minoan civilization lasted from about 3100 BCE to 1100 BCE, and we think this artifact was made in the second millennium BCE. It was discovered in 1908, and it features many stamped symbols, 241 to be exact, in the shape of a spiral. The symbols include images of things like animals, tools, and so on. These animals, tools, and other images form a pattern in the shape of a spiral. What's so interesting is that these symbols are unlike anything else from the Minoan civilization or any other known writing system. Many experts have tried to decipher these enigmatic symbols. Some suggest they could represent an unknown language. Others think they might represent a calendar or even a religious hymn. Yet no consensus has been reached. Another intriguing thing about the Phaistos Disc is the method used to imprint the symbols. This involved pressing prefabricated stamps into wet clay. This process is really remarkable. It suggests a level of sophistication similar to early printing. Some scholars hypothesize that the disc might be an import from another culture, a lone artifact brought to Crete by traders or travelers. But this is another point of contention surrounding this fascinating artifact.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段考古学播客的讲座。

多年来，考古学家在希腊克里特岛发现了许多迷人器物。一例是费斯托斯圆盘，一件在费斯托斯米诺斯宫殿废墟中发现的古代黏土器物。米诺斯文明约从公元前三一〇〇年持续到公元前一一〇〇年，我们认为这件器物制于公元前第二个千年。它于一九〇八年发现，带有许多压印符号，确切地说是二百四十一个，呈螺旋形。符号包括动物、工具等图像。这些动物、工具与其他图像形成螺旋形图案。特别有趣的是，这些符号与米诺斯文明或任何其他已知书写系统中的任何东西都不像。许多专家试图破译这些神秘符号。有人认为它们可能代表未知语言。另一些人认为可能代表日历甚至宗教赞美诗。但尚未达成共识。费斯托斯圆盘另一引人入胜之处是压印符号的方法。这涉及把预制印章压入湿黏土。这一过程确实非凡。它暗示一种类似早期印刷的复杂程度。一些学者假设圆盘可能是从另一文化进口的，由商人或旅行者带到克里特的孤件。但这是围绕这件迷人器物的又一争议点。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.

I once saw a video of a lionfish with its intimidating long spikes. Then it suddenly turned into a snake. Well, it turns out I was actually watching a mimic octopus. The mimic octopus lives in relatively shallow ocean water, and it's the first animal known to show dynamic mimicry, which means it can shift quickly between multiple imitations. Now, other creatures use mimicry. The owl butterfly's wings have markings resembling an owl's eye, which may keep the butterfly's predators away. But that's how the owl butterfly always looks. With dynamic mimicry, by contrast, an animal can shift its shape in real time. It contorts its body into different formations, often to confuse predators. A mimic octopus can imitate a lionfish or a snake, and it can quickly extend its arms and glide across the seafloor like a flatfish. But what use is changing shape if you can't also change color to look like a flatfish? Well, this octopus has cells called chromatophores just under its skin. Each chromatophore has a pigment inside it that could be red, yellow, etc. Picture thousands of tiny balloons of different colors. If you stretch a balloon, it gets bigger, right? Well, the mimic octopus has muscles surrounding these chromatophores. They tighten to pull the necessary colors bigger and relax to make other colors smaller, making each color more or less visible. While this helps it hide from predators, it also aids in hunting, as unsuspecting prey often perceives the octopus as a non-threatening species.

请听一段生物学课的讲座。

我曾看过一段狮子鱼带着吓人长刺的视频。然后它突然变成了蛇。结果我看的其实是拟态章鱼。拟态章鱼生活在相对浅的海水中，是已知第一种表现动态拟态的动物，意思是它能在多种模仿之间快速切换。其他生物也用拟态。猫头鹰蝶翅膀上有类似猫头鹰眼睛的斑纹，可能让捕食者远离。但猫头鹰蝶一直是那副样子。相比之下，动态拟态中动物可实时改变外形。它把身体扭成不同形态，常为迷惑捕食者。拟态章鱼可模仿狮子鱼或蛇，也能迅速伸展腕足像比目鱼一样滑过海底。但若不能同时变色去像比目鱼，变外形有何用？这章鱼皮肤下有称为色素细胞的细胞。每个色素细胞里有色素，可能是红、黄等。想象成千上万个不同颜色的小气球。你拉伸气球，它会变大，对吧？拟态章鱼有肌肉环绕这些色素细胞。它们收紧把需要的颜色拉大，放松让其他颜色变小，使每种颜色或显或隐。这既助它躲避捕食者，也助狩猎，因毫无戒心的猎物常把章鱼当成无威胁物种。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a science podcast.

Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available. Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and converts it to electricity or heat. The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them. The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero harmful pollutants. Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels. But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Another advantage, and one we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas far from the grid. So what are the disadvantages? Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which of course reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels. That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non-sunny periods. Panel lifespan is quite good at 25 to 30 years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that. Demand is increasing faster than expected. This is a problem because recycling them is expensive, and most panels end up in landfills.

在我们的可再生能源系列中继续谈太阳能，它可以说是可用的最丰富资源。太阳能从太阳光线取能并转化为电或热。主要技术是由光伏电池组成的太阳能电池板，阳光照射时产生电流。太阳能的优势广为人知，最重要的或许是它不产生有害污染物。任何工业活动都会以某种方式产生二氧化碳，制造太阳能电池板本身也需要来自化石燃料的能源。但总体而言，该行业碳足迹远低于煤或天然气，这使其对减少温室气体排放至关重要。另一优势——我们谈得不够多——是太阳能可为远离电网的偏远与服务不足地区提供能源接入。那缺点呢？电池板效率受云层及其他天气影响，这当然减少到达板面的阳光。尽管如此，电池储能系统的创新确实允许储存太阳能供非晴天使用。板的寿命在二十五到三十年相当不错，但效率提升反而矛盾地推动板被更早更换。需求增长快于预期。这成问题，因为回收昂贵，多数板最终进垃圾填埋场。

versions.transcript: Let's move on in our renewable energy series to discuss solar power, which is arguably the most abundant resource available. Solar power takes energy from the sun's rays and converts it to electricity or heat. The primary technology for this is solar panels made up of photovoltaic cells, which generate an electric current when sunlight hits them. The advantages of solar power are well known, and the most important may be the fact that it produces zero harmful pollutants. Any industrial endeavor will produce carbon dioxide in one way or another, and manufacturing solar panels itself requires energy sourced from fossil fuels. But on the whole, the industry has a much lower carbon footprint than coal or natural gas, and this makes it key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Another advantage, and one we don't talk about enough, is that solar power can provide energy access in remote and underserved areas, far from the grid. So what are the disadvantages? Solar panel efficiency is affected by cloud cover and other weather, which of course reduces the amount of sunlight reaching the panels. That said, innovations in battery storage systems do allow for the storage of solar energy for use during non sunny periods. Panel lifespan is quite good at 25 to 30 years, but improvements in efficiency are paradoxically driving panels to be replaced much earlier than that, so waste is increasing faster than expected. This is a problem because recycling them is expensive, and most panels end up in landfills.
versions.transcriptZh: 接下来，在我们的可再生能源系列中，我们将讨论太阳能，这可以说是最丰富的可用资源。 太阳能从太阳光线中获取能量，并将其转化为电能或热能。 这项技术主要采用太阳能电池板，由光伏电池组成，当阳光照射时，这些电池会产生电流。 太阳能的优势众所周知，其中最重要的一点可能是它不会产生任何有害污染物。 任何工业活动都会以这样或那样的方式产生二氧化碳，而制造太阳能电池板本身就需要消耗化石燃料提供的能源。 但总的来说，这个行业的碳足迹远低于燃煤或天然气，这使得它成为减少温室气体排放的关键。 另一个我们很少提及的优势是，太阳能可以在远离电网的偏远和能源不足地区提供能源。 那么，缺点是什么呢？ 太阳能电池板的效率受到云层覆盖和其他天气的影响，这当然会减少到达电池板的阳光量。 话虽如此，电池储能系统的创新确实允许储存太阳能，以便在非晴朗时期使用。 电池板的寿命相当好，有25到30年，但效率的提高却矛盾地导致电池板比预期更早地被更换，因此废弃物增加的速度超出了预期。 这是一个问题，因为回收它们成本高昂，而且大多数电池板最终都被送往垃圾填埋场。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

Soil isn't just dirt; it's alive. In healthy soil, microorganisms like bacteria and fungi help break down organic matter and cycle nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, which plants need to thrive. Not only that, but microbes create sticky substances called extracellular polymeric substances that bind soil particles together. Extracellular polymeric substances are important for maintaining soil structure, which means proper water retention, aeration, and root growth. Without microbes, soil becomes compacted, dry, and less able to support life. Now, when we're trying to reverse damage to a degraded ecosystem, say, a forest that's been logged or farmland that's been overused, microbes can be key players. Scientists engaged in these efforts often begin by studying a reference site. A reference site is a nearby area that shows what the ecosystem should look like in its healthy state. For example, if they're restoring a grassland, they'll look at an untouched patch of native grassland. They'll analyze the soil there, its nutrients, texture, and microbial communities, to determine what's missing in the damaged site. After this research comes the intervention phase. Scientists might introduce microbial inoculants, custom blends of helpful microbes, to the degraded soil. These microbes rebuild structure, cycle nutrients, and support plant growth. In one California vineyard, years of chemical use had depleted microbial diversity and compacted the soil, making it hard for vines to thrive. Researchers introduced various fungi and other beneficial microbes. Within a year, the soil structure improved, water retention increased, and grape yield and quality noticeably rebounded.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段环境科学课的讲座。

土壤不只是泥土；它是活的。在健康土壤中，细菌与真菌等微生物帮助分解有机物，并循环氮、磷等植物茁壮所需的养分。不仅如此，微生物还产生称为胞外聚合物的黏性物质，把土壤颗粒黏合在一起。胞外聚合物对维持土壤结构很重要，意味着适当的保水、通气与根系生长。没有微生物，土壤会板结、干燥、更难支撑生命。当我们试图逆转退化生态系统的损害时——例如被砍伐的森林或过度使用的农田——微生物可以是关键角色。从事这些努力的科学家常从研究参照点开始。参照点是附近显示生态系统健康状态应有模样的区域。例如，若恢复草地，他们会看一块未受干扰的本地草地。他们会分析那里土壤的养分、质地与微生物群落，以确定受损点缺什么。研究之后是干预阶段。科学家可能向退化土壤引入微生物接种剂——有益微生物的定制混合。这些微生物重建结构、循环养分、支持植物生长。在一处加州葡萄园，多年化学品使用耗尽了微生物多样性并板结土壤，使葡萄藤难以茁壮。研究者引入多种真菌及其他有益微生物。一年内，土壤结构改善，保水增强，葡萄产量与质量明显回升。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 例如，若恢复草地，他们会看一块未受干扰的本地草地。

transcriptSentences.text: They'll analyze the soil there, its nutrients, texture, and microbial communities, to determine what's missing in the damaged site.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他们会分析那里土壤的养分、质地与微生物群落，以确定受损点缺什么。

transcriptSentences.text: After this research comes the intervention phase.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 研究之后是干预阶段。

transcriptSentences.text: Scientists might introduce microbial inoculants, custom blends of helpful microbes, to the degraded soil.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 科学家可能向退化土壤引入微生物接种剂——有益微生物的定制混合。

transcriptSentences.text: These microbes rebuild structure, cycle nutrients, and support plant growth.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这些微生物重建结构、循环养分、支持植物生长。

transcriptSentences.text: In one California vineyard, years of chemical use had depleted microbial diversity and compacted the soil, making it hard for vines to thrive.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 在一处加州葡萄园，多年化学品使用耗尽了微生物多样性并板结土壤，使葡萄藤难以茁壮。

transcriptSentences.text: Researchers introduced various fungi and other beneficial microbes.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 研究者引入多种真菌及其他有益微生物。

transcriptSentences.text: Within a year, the soil structure improved, water retention increased, and grape yield and quality noticeably rebounded.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 一年内，土壤结构改善，保水增强，葡萄产量与质量明显回升。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

Imagine working in an office where every employee is smiling and enthusiastic. How would it affect your productivity? You'd probably be more productive. But why? See, happy individuals can spread their positive energy, influencing the mood of those around them. This is called emotional contagion. You know when somebody yawns because they're tired or bored, it can make others around them yawn. Well, in this case, instead of yawns, optimism and motivation are spreading. Emotional contagion can happen because of mirror neurons. Mirror neurons fire when you notice someone else's emotion, which makes you feel it too. Importantly, this happens subconsciously. You aren't aware of it or thinking about it when it happens. Now, happiness doesn't just come from perks. Sure, free snacks can help office morale. But real happiness stems from meaningful work, autonomy, and a sense of appreciation. Leadership really sets the tone for that. In turn, happiness enhances creativity, problem-solving skills, things like that. So, when you're happy, you're not just feeling good, you're thinking better, which motivates you to work better. A study in a leading business magazine takes this further. The authors found that happiness spreads, yes, from a company's leaders to its employees. But what I find remarkable is that the study found that it also extends to the customers or clients. With a positive work environment, the employees feel more committed and engaged. They serve clients better, improving their sense of well-being. And in healthcare settings, that means better health outcomes for clients.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段心理学课的讲座。

想象在每个员工都微笑且热情的办公室工作。这会如何影响你的生产力？你大概会更高效。但为何？快乐的人可以传播积极能量，影响周围人的情绪。这称为情绪传染。你知道有人因疲倦或无聊打哈欠时，会让周围人也打哈欠。而在这种情况下，传播的不是哈欠，而是乐观与动力。情绪传染可因镜像神经元而发生。当你注意到别人的情绪时镜像神经元会放电，使你也感受到它。重要的是，这发生在潜意识中。发生时你并不意识到或思考它。快乐不只来自福利。当然，免费零食可帮助办公室士气。但真正的快乐源于有意义的工作、自主权与被欣赏感。领导层真正为这定调。反过来，快乐增强创造力、问题解决能力之类。因此当你快乐时，你不只感觉良好，你思考得更好，这激励你工作得更好。一篇领先商业杂志的研究更进一步。作者发现快乐会传播，是的，从公司领导到员工。但我觉得非凡的是，研究发现它也延伸到顾客或客户。在积极工作环境中，员工感到更投入、更参与。他们更好地服务客户，提升客户的幸福感。而在医疗环境中，这意味着客户有更好的健康结果。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 反过来，快乐增强创造力、问题解决能力之类。

questions.promptText: What does the speaker mainly discuss?

choices.label: A new way to help employees be happy at work
choices.labelZh: 一种帮助员工在工作中感到快乐的新方法
choices.explanationZh: 不正确。原文没有支持 “A new way to help employees be happy at work”。

choices.labelZh: 一种通过办公室设计提高生产力的策略

questions.promptText: What does the speaker emphasize about mirror neurons?
questions.promptTextZh: 说话者强调了镜像神经元的什么特点？

choices.label: They do not work well when a person is tired.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a marine biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a marine biology class.

Let's talk a little about sea otters and their importance to their own and indeed other ecosystems. We'll start with a few basic facts. The sea otter is a marine mammal often found along the coastal waters of the northern Pacific. It lacks the blubber of other marine mammals like whales, say, or seals, but it stays warm in icy waters thanks to its fur, which is the densest of any animals. It also has unusually large lungs, two and a half times larger than those of similarly sized land mammals, and this helps it stay buoyant and dive efficiently. Sea otters have a loose flap of skin under each foreleg that functions like a pocket, which they use for storing food and tools. That's right, tools. Sea otters are one of the few animals that use tools, using clamshells for digging and rocks to open clamshells. Now, wonderful as they may be, why care about sea otters? Because sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Kelp is a large seaweed that can grow up to 30 meters tall, providing food and shelter for a range of marine life. Kelp forests support a greater variety of marine life than almost any other ocean habitat. Kelp also grows very densely and acts as a natural buffer, protecting shorelines from storm damage. Finally, kelp forests are like rainforests in that they absorb and store carbon dioxide through photosynthesis, mitigating climate change and reducing ocean acidification.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段海洋生物学课的讲座。

我们来稍微谈谈海獭及其对自身乃至其他生态系统的重要性。先从几个基本事实开始。海獭是常出现在北太平洋沿岸水域的海洋哺乳动物。它没有鲸鱼或海豹等其他海洋哺乳动物的鲸脂，但靠毛皮在冰冷水域保暖，其毛皮是所有动物中最密的。它还有异常大的肺，比体型相近的陆生哺乳动物大约两倍半，这有助它保持浮力并高效潜水。海獭每条前肢下有松弛皮瓣，作用像口袋，用来存放食物与工具。没错，工具。海獭是少数使用工具的动物之一，用蛤壳挖掘、用石头打开蛤壳。它们固然奇妙，为何要关心海獭？因为海獭吃海胆，而海胆吃海带。海带是大型海藻，可长到三十米高，为多种海洋生物提供食物与庇护。海带林支持的海洋生物多样性几乎超过任何其他海洋栖息地。海带也生长极密，充当天然缓冲，保护海岸线免受风暴破坏。最后，海带林像雨林一样通过光合作用吸收并储存二氧化碳，缓解气候变化并减轻海洋酸化。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a geography class.

Desertification is the process by which fertile land transforms into desert, typically as a result of drought, deforestation, or unsustainable agricultural practices. One significant driver of desertification is the overexploitation of land for intensive agriculture. This can exhaust soil nutrients, diminish vegetation cover, and accelerate erosion. Without root systems to anchor the soil, wind and water strip away topsoil, leaving behind barren land. In some cases, monoculture farming and excessive irrigation also contribute by disrupting natural soil chemistry. Deforestation further intensifies desertification. When forests are cleared for timber or agricultural expansion, the absence of trees reduces the land's capacity to retain moisture. This loss of canopy cover not only dries out the soil but also disrupts local rainfall patterns, compounding the desert spread. Climate change is another accelerating force. Rising global temperatures and shifting precipitation cycles lead to prolonged droughts and extreme weather events, placing additional stress on soil and vegetation. Once fertile regions are becoming increasingly arid and agriculturally unviable. Desertification can trigger food and water insecurity, and species adapted to specific soil and moisture conditions may struggle to survive. Mitigation efforts include sustainable land management, reforestation, and soil restoration initiatives. Projects like the Great Green Wall in Africa aim to reverse degradation by planting trees and creating green jobs. Addressing desertification is essential not only for environmental health but also for the stability and resilience of human communities worldwide.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段地理课的讲座。

荒漠化是肥沃土地变成沙漠的过程，通常由干旱、森林砍伐或不可持续的农业做法造成。荒漠化的一个重要驱动因素是为集约农业过度开发土地。这会耗尽土壤养分、减少植被覆盖并加速侵蚀。没有根系固定土壤，风和水会剥去表土，留下贫瘠土地。有时单作农业与过度灌溉也通过扰乱自然土壤化学而起作用。森林砍伐进一步加剧荒漠化。当为木材或农业扩张清除森林时，树木的缺失降低土地保水能力。树冠覆盖的丧失不仅使土壤干涸，也扰乱当地降雨模式，加重沙漠扩张。气候变化是另一加速力量。全球气温上升与降水周期变化导致长期干旱与极端天气事件，给土壤与植被施加额外压力。曾经肥沃的地区正变得日益干旱、农业上难以为继。荒漠化可引发粮食与水不安全，适应特定土壤与湿度条件的物种可能难以存活。缓解措施包括可持续土地管理、再造林与土壤修复行动。非洲的绿色长城等项目旨在通过植树与创造绿色就业来逆转退化。应对荒漠化不仅对环境健康至关重要，也对全世界人类社区的稳定与韧性至关重要。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on an art podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on an art podcast. 

Imagine stepping into a gallery where the walls don't just display art—they move with you. One moment, a sculpture spins gently in the breeze. The next, a panel shifts as you walk by. Welcome to the world of kinetic art, a mesmerizing fusion of motion and visual storytelling. Born in the early 20th century, kinetic art is still pushing boundaries, constantly redefining what art can be. Unlike static paintings or marble sculptures, kinetic pieces come alive. Think of Alexander Calder's mobiles, delicately balanced to sway with the air, or Theo Jansen's Strandbeests, giant wind-powered creatures that walk across beaches like living machines. These works don't just sit there; they respond, they evolve. Hungarian artist László Moholy-Nagy, one of the movement's pioneers, believed light and motion could transform how we experience art. Moholy-Nagy created a groundbreaking piece called "Light-Space Modulator," a motorized sculpture of spinning metal and glass, more of a performance than an object. But kinetic art isn't all smooth sailing. Incorporating motors and sensors means dealing with breakdowns, software glitches, and constant upkeep. Some critics argue that the tech can overshadow the artistry, turning installations into flashy gimmicks. Still, the genre thrives. From interactive digital landscapes to whimsical mechanical sculptures, kinetic art invites us into a multi-sensory experience, one that's immersive, unpredictable, and unforgettable.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术播客的讲座。

想象走进一座画廊，墙面不只展示艺术——它们随你而动。这一刻，雕塑在微风中轻旋。下一刻，一块面板在你走过时移动。欢迎来到动态艺术的世界——运动与视觉叙事的迷人融合。诞生于二十世纪初，动态艺术仍在突破边界，不断重新定义艺术可以是什么。与静态绘画或大理石雕塑不同，动态作品活起来。想想亚历山大·考尔德精致平衡、随空气摆动的活动雕塑，或特奥·扬森的海滩兽——像活机器一样走上海滩的巨型风力生物。这些作品不只静坐；它们回应、它们演变。匈牙利艺术家拉斯洛·莫霍利-纳吉——该运动先驱之一——相信光与运动可改变我们体验艺术的方式。莫霍利-纳吉创作了开创性作品《光-空间调制器》，一座旋转金属与玻璃的机动雕塑，更像表演而非物件。但动态艺术并非一帆风顺。融入马达与传感器意味着要应对故障、软件小毛病与不断维护。一些批评者认为技术可能盖过艺术性，把装置变成花哨噱头。尽管如此，这一类型仍兴旺。从互动数字景观到异想天开的机械雕塑，动态艺术邀请我们进入多感官体验——沉浸、不可预测、难忘。

versions.transcript: Imagine stepping into a gallery where the walls don't just display art, they move with you. One moment, a sculpture spins gently in the breeze. The next, a panel shifts as you walk by. Welcome to the world of kinetic art, a mesmerizing fusion of motion and visual storytelling. Born in the early 20th century, kinetic art is still pushing boundaries, constantly redefining what art can be. Unlike static paintings or marble sculptures, kinetic pieces come alive. Think of Alexander Calder's mobiles, delicately balanced to sway with the air, or Theo Janssen's strand beasts, giant wind powered creatures that walk across beaches like living machines. These works don't just sit there, they respond, they evolve. Hungarian artist Laszlo Moholy Nagy, one of the movement's pioneers, believed light and motion could transform how we experience art. Moholy Nagy created a groundbreaking piece called Light Space Modulator, a motorized sculpture of spinning metal and glass, more of a performance than an object. But kinetic art isn't all smooth sailing. Incorporating motors and sensors means dealing with breakdowns, software glitches, and constant upkeep. Some critics argue that the tech can overshadow the artistry, turning installations into flashy gimmicks. Still, the genre thrives. From interactive digital landscapes to whimsical mechanical sculptures, kinetic art invites us into a multi sensory experience, one that's immersive, unpredictable, and unforgettable.
versions.transcriptZh: 想象一下走进这样一个画廊，那里的墙壁不仅仅是展示艺术，它们还会随着你一起移动。 这一刻，一座雕塑在微风中轻轻旋转。 下一秒，当你走过时，一块面板发生了位移。 欢迎来到动力艺术的世界，这是一种动作与视觉叙事的迷人融合。 动力艺术诞生于20世纪初，至今仍在打破边界，不断重新定义艺术的内涵。 与静态绘画或大理石雕塑不同，动力作品是鲜活的。 想想亚历山大·考尔德（Alexander Calder）的动态雕塑，它们精巧平衡，随空气摇曳；或者是泰奥·扬森（Theo Jansen）的仿生兽（strand beasts），这些巨大的风力驱动生物像活的机器一样在海滩上行走。 这些作品不仅仅是摆在那里，它们会回应，会演变。 匈牙利艺术家拉斯洛·莫霍利-纳吉（Laszlo Moholy-Nagy）是这一运动的先驱之一，他相信光线和运动可以改变我们体验艺术的方式。 莫霍利-纳吉创作了一件名为《光空间调制器》（Light Space Modulator）的开创性作品，那是一个由旋转金属和玻璃组成的动力雕塑，与其说它是一个物体，不如说它是一场表演。 但动力艺术并非一帆风顺。 整合电机和传感器意味着要处理故障、软件错误和持续的维护。 一些批评者认为，技术可能会掩盖艺术性，使装置变成花哨的噱头。 尽管如此，这一流派依然蓬勃发展。 从互动数字景观到奇特的机械雕塑，动力艺术邀我们进入一种多感官体验，这种体验是沉浸式的、不可预测且令人难忘的。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

The concept of flow is a fascinating area of study in psychology. It refers to a state of complete immersion and engagement in an activity. It is characterized by a sense of losing oneself in an activity, where time seems to disappear and everything feels effortless. This state is often associated with high levels of performance and satisfaction. Flow occurs when a person's skill level is perfectly matched to the challenge at hand, creating a balance that leads to deep focus and enjoyment. Athletes often experience flow during peak performance moments, where they are fully absorbed in the game and executing actions seamlessly. Artists also report flow states when they are deeply engaged in the creative process. There are several key components to achieving flow. First, the activity must have clear goals and immediate feedback, allowing individuals to understand their progress and adjust their actions accordingly. Second, the person must be fully focused on the activity, minimizing distractions and interruptions. Third, there must be a sense of control over the activity, with the individual feeling capable of meeting the challenges presented. Flow has numerous benefits, including increased productivity, enhanced creativity, and improved well-being. People who regularly experience flow are often happier and more fulfilled, as they spend time engaged in activities that are meaningful and enjoyable. However, achieving flow is not easy. It requires finding activities that match one's skill level to the appropriate level of challenge. Matching an activity with the requisite skill level can be challenging.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段心理学课的讲座。

心流概念是心理学中迷人的研究领域。它指完全沉浸并投入一项活动的状态。其特征是在活动中忘我，时间仿佛消失，一切感觉毫不费力。这种状态常与高水平表现与满足相关。当心流发生时，个人技能水平与手头挑战完美匹配，形成带来深度专注与享受的平衡。运动员常在巅峰表现时刻体验心流，完全沉浸在比赛中并无缝执行动作。艺术家也报告在深度投入创作过程时进入心流状态。达成心流有几个关键要素。第一，活动须有清晰目标与即时反馈，让个体理解进展并相应调整行动。第二，人须完全专注于活动，尽量减少分心与打断。第三，须对活动有控制感，个体感到有能力应对所呈现的挑战。心流有众多益处，包括提高生产力、增强创造力与改善福祉。经常体验心流的人往往更快乐、更充实，因他们把时间花在有意义且愉快的活动上。然而达成心流并不容易。它需要找到技能水平与适当挑战水平相匹配的活动。使活动与所需技能水平匹配可能具有挑战。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Today we're going to look at an interesting intersection between art and music. Now, you might have heard of the Russian abstract painter Wassily Kandinsky. What you might not know is how the work of an avant-garde composer, Arnold Schoenberg, influenced Kandinsky's groundbreaking approach to painting. Okay, early in the 20th century, Wassily Kandinsky was influenced by the music of Arnold Schoenberg, a pioneer in the realm of atonality, a musical approach where there is no key. Atonality was a stark divergence from the conventions of the time, where traditional tonal structures were popular. versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a music history class.
Throughout history, people have created a number of interesting musical instruments. Today, I want to talk about a fascinating instrument called the phonofiddle. If you combined a violin and a gramophone, you'd have the phonofiddle. It's a violin-like instrument with a horn attached to amplify sound. It was developed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries during a time when there was a quest for louder musical instruments. Before electric amplification became the norm, musicians had to come up with ingenious methods to make their sounds heard over larger distances or in noisy environments, and the phonofiddle was one such attempt. Its horn acted kind of like the bell of a trumpet, projecting sound in a way that was surprisingly effective for its time. Picture a street performer on a bustling corner, competing with all the hustle and bustle of busy markets, things like horse-drawn carriages. The phonofiddle's horn would allow their music to cut through all that noise. What's particularly interesting is that the phonofiddle was part of a broader trend toward mechanical amplification in the pre-electric era. It shares similarities with other eccentric instruments like the Stroh violin, which also used a horn. And this exploration of acoustic amplification paved the way for the electric revolution in music. Before we move on to discuss the electric revolution, let's take a closer look at how the phonofiddle was constructed.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段音乐史课的讲座。
历史上人们发明过许多有趣的乐器。今天我想讲一种迷人的乐器：phonofiddle。如果把小提琴和留声机合在一起，差不多就是它：像小提琴，却装着喇叭来放大声音。它出现在十九世纪末二十世纪初，那时人们正追求更响的乐器。在电声放大成为常态之前，乐手要想在更远距离或嘈杂环境中被听见，只能想出各种巧妙办法，phonofiddle 就是其中之一。它的喇叭有点像小号的喇叭口，把声音投射出去，在当时相当有效。想象街头艺人在热闹街角演奏，要压过市场喧闹、马车声等；phonofiddle 的喇叭能让音乐穿过去。特别有意思的是，它属于电气时代之前机械扩音的更大潮流，和同样使用喇叭的 Stroh 小提琴等“古怪”乐器相似。这种对声学放大的探索，为音乐的电气革命铺了路。在讨论电气革命之前，我们先仔细看看 phonofiddle 是怎么做出来的。

transcriptSentences.text: What's particularly interesting is that the phonofiddle was part of a broader trend toward mechanical amplification in the pre-electric era.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
We've been talking about symbiosis, which, to remind you, is a beneficial interaction between two different species. A good example is birds and seed-producing plants. The birds eat the seeds the plants produce, and the plants benefit from birds dispersing those seeds. Okay, so here's a truly remarkable case of symbiosis: the relationship between the spotted salamander, a type of amphibian, and green algae, which are tiny plant-like aquatic organisms. The partnership begins when the salamander lays its eggs in freshwater ponds. The salamander eggs are contained within a jelly-like capsule, and the algae from the pond move in and form an integral part of this jelly-like mass as the embryos develop. All the while, the algae are photosynthesizing, transforming sunlight into usable energy, a process that releases oxygen. This is critical because the embryos need oxygen, and pond water tends to be low in it. And in return, the algae get a nutrient that they need to survive: nitrogen. The embryos produce readily available nitrogen as a waste product, and the algae happily use it. And what's cool is we now know that the algae don't just live in the egg capsule; they can enter the embryo's cells, meaning photosynthesis is occurring inside a vertebrate, a highly advanced animal, a phenomenon almost unheard of. Corals and a few other marine invertebrates do this, but among vertebrates it is extremely rare.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物学课的讲座。
我们一直在谈共生：提醒一下，就是两种不同物种之间的互利关系。一个好例子是鸟类与产籽植物：鸟吃种子，植物则借鸟传播种子。下面是一个真正非凡的共生案例：斑点蝾螈（一种两栖动物）与绿藻（微小的植物样水生生物）。合作从蝾螈在淡水池塘产卵开始。卵包在胶状囊中，池中的藻进入并在胚胎发育时成为这团胶状物的一部分。藻类同时进行光合作用，把阳光变成可用能量并释放氧气——这对胚胎至关重要，因为池水往往缺氧。作为回报，藻得到生存所需的氮：胚胎以废物形式产生易利用的氮，藻乐于吸收。更酷的是，我们现在知道藻不只生活在卵囊里，还能进入胚胎细胞，也就是说光合作用发生在脊椎动物体内——一种高度发达的动物——这几乎闻所未闻。珊瑚和其他少数海洋无脊椎动物会这样，但在脊椎动物中极为罕见。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an ocean sciences class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an ocean sciences class.
Back in the mid-1800s, scientists dredging the ocean floor stumbled on previously unknown life forms: brittle stars, sea cucumbers, even deep-sea corals—creatures living in pitch darkness, near-freezing water, and under crushing pressure. That discovery flipped the old belief that such conditions couldn't support life. But what do these organisms eat? Near the ocean surface, food chains begin with phytoplankton, tiny plants that use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide into energy. These phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed fish, and these in turn feed larger predators. But in the deep ocean, there's no sunlight. So what keeps life going down there? The answer is something scientists call marine snow. This isn't frozen water, but a slow, steady snowfall of organic particles—dead plankton, bits of decaying creatures, and animal waste products—all sinking from above. But marine snow does more than feed deep-sea life. It carries carbon from surface waters down to the deep-sea floor, where some of it can stay locked away for centuries, even millennia. This process helps regulate Earth's climate by pulling carbon from surface waters, and so out of the atmosphere, which interacts with the surface waters. As you probably know, carbon in the atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide gas, has a warming effect on Earth's climate, and the extra carbon released from human activities has caused dangerous global warming. How much carbon does marine snow remove? Roughly 10 billion tons annually, about the same as all human cars.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段海洋科学课的讲座。
十九世纪中叶，科学家疏浚海底时意外发现了前所未知的生命：蛇尾、海参，甚至深海珊瑚——它们生活在漆黑、近乎冰点、高压的环境中。这一发现推翻了“这种条件不能支持生命”的旧观念。但它们吃什么？靠近海面，食物链从浮游植物开始：微小植物利用阳光把二氧化碳转化为能量，再养活浮游动物、鱼类，以及更大的捕食者。深海没有阳光，生命靠什么维持？答案是科学家所说的“海雪”。那不是冰，而是缓慢沉降的有机颗粒——死亡的浮游生物、腐烂残骸、动物排泄物——从上层沉下来。海雪不仅养活深海生物，还把碳从表层水带到深海底，有的可封存数百年甚至上千年。这一过程把碳从表层水、进而从与表层相互作用的大气中抽离，有助于调节地球气候。你们知道，大气中的二氧化碳有温室效应，人类活动额外排放的碳已造成危险的全球变暖。海雪每年带走大约一百亿吨碳，大致相当于人类所有汽车的排放量。

versions.transcript: Back in the mid 1800s, scientists dredging the ocean floor stumbled on previously unknown life forms: brittle stars, sea cucumbers, even deep sea corals, creatures living in pitch darkness, near freezing water, and under crushing pressure. That discovery flipped the old belief that such conditions couldn't support life. But what do these organisms eat? Near the ocean surface, food chains begin with phytoplankton, tiny plants that use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide into energy. These phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed fish, and these in turn feed larger predators. But in the deep ocean, sunlight doesn't reach, so phytoplankton cannot grow there. Instead, many deep sea organisms depend on something called marine snow. It is a constant shower of organic matter: dead plankton, bits of decaying creatures, and animal waste products, all sinking from above. But marine snow does more than feed deep sea life. It carries carbon from surface waters down to the deep sea floor, where some of it can stay locked away for centuries, even millennia. This process helps regulate Earth's climate by pulling carbon from surface waters, and so out of the atmosphere, which interacts with the surface waters. As you probably know, carbon in the atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide gas, has a warming effect on Earth's climate, and the extra carbon released from human activities has caused dangerous global warming. How much carbon does marine snow remove? Roughly 10 billion tons annually, about the same as all human cars.
versions.transcriptZh: 回到19世纪中期，科学家们在疏浚海底时，偶然发现了以前未知的生命形式：海蛇尾、海参，甚至深海珊瑚，这些生物生活在漆黑、接近冰点的水和巨大的压力之下。 这一发现颠覆了此前认为这种条件无法支持生命的旧观念。 但是这些生物吃什么呢？ 在海洋表面附近，食物链始于浮游植物，这些微小的植物利用阳光将二氧化碳转化为能量。 这些浮游植物喂养浮游动物，浮游动物喂养鱼类，而鱼类又喂养更大的捕食者。 但在深海，阳光无法到达，因此浮游植物无法在那里生长。 相反，许多深海生物依赖于一种叫做“海洋雪”的东西。 它是有机物质的持续“降雪”：死亡的浮游生物、腐烂生物的碎片和动物排泄物，都从上方沉降下来。 但海洋雪不仅仅为深海生物提供食物。 它将碳从表层水域带到深海海底，其中一部分碳可以被封存数百年，甚至数千年。 这个过程通过将碳从表层水域，从而从与表层水域相互作用的大气中抽取出来，帮助调节地球的气候。 正如你可能知道的，大气中的碳，以二氧化碳气体的形式存在，对地球气候有增温效应，而人类活动释放的额外碳已导致危险的全球变暖。 海洋雪能去除多少碳？ 每年大约100亿吨，与所有人类汽车的排放量大致相同。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on a music podcast.
versions.transcript: Listen to a talk on a music podcast. Have you ever wondered how music influences our eating habits? Well, it turns out that the kind of music playing in the background when we dine can significantly shape our culinary experience. Recent research has demonstrated that fast music, music with a rapid tempo, can make us eat more quickly, while slower tunes encourage us to savor our meals. And, you know, my doctor's been telling me eating slowly is good for digestion and health. It's important to chew the food well. Anyway, music isn't just about speed. It's about taste perception as well. For instance, a study found that high-pitched music can enhance the sweetness of a dish, while a lower pitch might accentuate its bitterness. Restaurants have started to take note of these findings and are curating playlists to improve their patrons' dining experiences. This auditory seasoning, as some call it, is becoming an essential part of the ambiance. Now, some argue that auditory manipulation can detract from the authenticity of the food experience. It can make diners more susceptible to overeating or misjudging the quality of their meal. This isn't just theory. Take the example of a high-end restaurant that experimented with soundscapes by playing ocean sounds. They found that diners rated seafood dishes more favorably, feeling as if they were right by the sea. While this kind of thing might revolutionize dining, some diners prefer a more genuine taste experience, free from any auditory influence.
versions.transcriptZh: 请听一段音乐播客的讲座。你是否想过音乐如何影响我们的饮食习惯？结果发现，用餐时背景播放的音乐类型可显著塑造我们的味觉体验。最近研究表明，快音乐——节奏快的音乐——可让我们吃得更快，而较慢的曲调鼓励我们细细品味。而且，你知道，我的医生一直告诉我慢吃对消化与健康有益。把食物嚼好很重要。无论如何，音乐不只关乎速度。也关乎味觉感知。例如，一项研究发现高音音乐会增强菜肴甜味，而较低音高可能突出苦味。餐厅已开始注意这些发现，并策划播放列表以改善顾客用餐体验。这种有人称为听觉调味的做法正成为氛围的重要部分。现在有人认为听觉操控会削弱食物体验的真实性。它可使用餐者更易过量进食或误判餐食质量。这不只是理论。以一家高端餐厅为例，它通过播放海洋声做声景实验。他们发现用餐者对海鲜菜肴评价更积极，感觉仿佛就在海边。尽管这类做法可能革命化用餐，一些用餐者更偏好不受任何听觉影响的更真实味觉体验。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a geography class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a geography class.

One tool that's useful in many fields is a geographic information system, or GIS. GIS is a computer system that can collect and store lots of data about specific locations. GIS software can also analyze and display data.

You're probably familiar with GPS, which also uses location data. GPS is used for navigation and positioning. It relies on hardware like satellites, right? Our phones use GPS to get directions to places.

On the other hand, GIS is software-based and is used for making decisions. Picture a trucking company delivering furniture. They'd use GPS to track where trucks are headed. The company might use GIS, though, to analyze the amount of fuel the trucks use on particular routes. They'd analyze traffic patterns, elevation changes, and things like that to make decisions about shipping routes.

Geographers can use GIS to study the interactions between humans and the environment. Say some farms start using a new fertilizer. GIS can analyze the location of those farms, including nearby streams. GIS can then analyze rainfall patterns in those locations by combining and analyzing all these data. GIS helps researchers predict where the fertilizer is likely to end up and whether it could pollute a stream. That's quite useful.

GIS software can also create maps of important buildings and sites in historic districts of cities and assess things like how nearby development would impact the historic district. This aids with conservation and managing these important locations.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段地理课的讲座。

许多领域都有用的一种工具是地理信息系统，即 GIS。GIS 是可收集并存储关于特定地点大量数据的计算机系统。GIS 软件也能分析并展示数据。

你大概熟悉 GPS，它也使用位置数据。GPS 用于导航与定位。它依赖卫星等硬件，对吧？我们的手机用 GPS 获取去某处的路线。

另一方面，GIS 基于软件，用于做决策。想象一家送家具的卡车公司。他们会用 GPS 追踪卡车去向。公司却可能用 GIS 分析卡车在特定路线上的燃油用量。他们会分析交通模式、海拔变化之类，以决定运输路线。

地理学家可用 GIS 研究人类与环境的互动。比方说一些农场开始使用新肥料。GIS 可分析那些农场的位置，包括附近溪流。GIS 再通过合并并分析所有这些数据，分析那些地点的降雨模式。GIS 帮助研究者预测肥料可能去向，以及是否会污染溪流。这相当有用。

GIS 软件也能绘制城市历史街区中重要建筑与地点的地图，并评估附近开发会如何影响历史街区之类。这有助于保护与管理这些重要地点。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.
A remarkable discovery was made in the 1970s. I'm referring to the Bactrian Gold, which dates to around the first century BCE and includes over twenty thousand objects. It's called Bactrian Gold, but the treasure includes jewelry, coins, and ornaments. It came from six burial mounds belonging to five women and one man. They would have been wealthy nomads from Central Asia or northwestern China. The discovery was so important to archaeologists that it was compared to the discovery of King Tut's tomb in Egypt. Bactrian Gold was found at a major crossroads of the Silk Road, the ancient trade routes that connected Europe and Asia. The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of trade routes. It facilitated the exchange not only of goods, but also of ideas, art, and technology. The Bactrian Gold artifacts show Greek, Indian, and Chinese influences, and some pieces combine elements from several cultures. These many influences passed through the region because it was a crossroads. The discovery provides significant insight into how interconnected the ancient world truly was. It serves as a testament to the Silk Road's role in fostering culture and commerce long before the modern era.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段考古学课的讲座。
二十世纪七十年代有一次惊人的发现。我说的是“大夏黄金”，年代约在公元前一世纪，包含两万多件物品。虽叫大夏黄金，宝物却包括珠宝、钱币和装饰品，来自六座墓冢，属于五名女性和一名男性，应是中亚或中国西北的富裕游牧者。发现对考古学家如此重要，甚至被比作埃及图坦卡蒙墓的发现。大夏黄金出土于丝绸之路的重要十字路口——连接欧亚的古代商路网络。丝路不是一条路，而是庞大的贸易路线网，促进的不仅是货物交换，还有思想、艺术与技术。大夏黄金文物显示出希腊、印度和中国的影响，有的单件还融合多种文化元素。正因为地处十字路口，这些影响才汇聚于此。这一发现深刻说明古代世界何等互联，也证明丝路在现代之前很久就推动了文化与商业交流。
