versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
Let's step into the curious world of Trompe l'oeil. A painting technique that doesn't just play with perspective, it plays with your perception. The term, French for "deceive the eye," hints at its magic. Paintings so convincing they make you question what's real. Trompe l'oeil paintings often look three-dimensional and blur the boundaries between what's real and what isn't. Though its roots stretch back to ancient Greece and Rome, Trompe l'oeil truly flourished during the Renaissance. Artists like Andrea Mantegna used the technique to make ceilings look like open skies, creating the impression that rooms were open to the heavens. By the 17th century, Trompe l'oeil had become a popular form of interior decoration. Consider the work of Dutch artist Samuel van Hoogstraten, whose paintings gave viewers the illusion of stepping into another room or looking through a window. These paintings played tricks on the viewer's sense of space and depth, creating a sense of wonder. Not everyone is enchanted. Some view Trompe l'oeil as a clever trick, technically impressive but emotionally hollow. It's a fair critique. When art leans heavily on illusion, it risks being seen as spectacle rather than substance. Still, the technique endures, and today's artists push it further, using digital tools to bend reality in ways that go beyond paint and canvas. Trompe l'oeil isn't just about fooling the eye anymore, it's about challenging how we see.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课的讲座。
让我们踏入错视画的奇妙世界。这一绘画技法不只玩弄透视，还玩弄你的感知。该法语术语意为「欺骗眼睛」，暗示其魔力。画作如此逼真，让人质疑何为真实。错视画常看起来三维，模糊真实与非真实的边界。尽管其根源可追溯到古希腊罗马，错视画在文艺复兴时期真正兴盛。安德里亚·曼特尼亚等艺术家用该技法让天花板看起来像开阔天空，造成房间通向天际的印象。到十七世纪，错视画已成为流行的室内装饰形式。想想荷兰艺术家塞缪尔·范·霍赫斯特拉滕的作品，其画给观者一种踏入另一房间或透过窗户眺望的错觉。这些画捉弄观者的空间与深度感，制造惊奇。并非人人着迷。有人视错视画为巧妙把戏，技术惊人但情感空洞。这是公平的批评。当艺术过度依赖幻觉时，有被看作奇观而非实质的风险。尽管如此，该技法仍延续，今日艺术家进一步推进，用数字工具以超出颜料与画布的方式弯曲现实。错视画不再只是愚弄眼睛，而是挑战我们如何观看。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 错视画通常看起来是三维的，模糊了虚实之间的界限。

transcriptSentences.text: Though its roots stretch back to ancient Greece and Rome, trompe l'oeil truly flourished during the Renaissance.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 尽管其根源可以追溯到古希腊和古罗马，但错视画真正繁荣是在文艺复兴时期。

transcriptSentences.text: Artists like Andrea Mantegna used the technique to make ceilings look like open skies, creating the impression that rooms were open to the heavens.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 像安德烈亚·曼特尼亚（Andrea Mantegna）这样的艺术家利用这种技术使天花板看起来像开阔的天空，营造出房间通向天堂的印象。

transcriptSentences.text: By the seventeenth century, trompe l'oeil had become a popular form of interior decoration.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 到了十七世纪，错视画已成为一种流行的室内装饰形式。

transcriptSentences.text: Consider the work of Dutch artist Samuel van Hoogstraten, whose paintings gave viewers the illusion of stepping into another room or looking through a window.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 想想荷兰艺术家塞缪尔·范·霍格斯特拉滕（Samuel van Hoogstraten）的作品，他的画作给观众一种走进另一个房间或透窗远眺的错觉。

transcriptSentences.text: These paintings play tricks on the viewer's sense of space and depth, creating a sense of wonder.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这些画作戏弄了观众对空间和深度的感知，创造出一种奇迹感。

transcriptSentences.text: Not everyone is enchanted.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 不过并不是每个人都为此着迷。

transcriptSentences.text: Some view trompe l'oeil as a clever trick, technically impressive but emotionally hollow.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 有些人将错视画视为一种聪明的把戏，在技术上令人印象深刻，但在情感上却很空洞。

transcriptSentences.text: It's a fair critique.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这是一个公平的评价。

transcriptSentences.text: When art leans heavily on illusion, it risks being seen as spectacle rather than substance.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 当艺术过度依赖错觉时，它就有可能被视为一种奇观而非实质。

transcriptSentences.text: Still, the technique endures, and today's artists push it further, using digital tools to bend reality in ways that go beyond paint and canvas.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 尽管如此，这种技术依然存在，今天的艺术家们更是进一步推动了它，利用数字工具以超越画笔和画布的方式弯曲现实。

transcriptSentences.text: Trompe l'oeil isn't just about fooling the eye anymore.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 错视画不再仅仅是关于欺骗眼睛了。

transcriptSentences.text: It's about challenging how we see.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它是关于挑战我们观看的方式。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Man: Trilobites were a group of ancient sea creatures. They are classified as arthropods. They are extinct now. Among modern animals, horseshoe crabs probably resemble trilobites the most. As arthropods, both trilobites and horseshoe crabs have segmented bodies, joints in their legs, and hard exoskeletons, kind of like shells. So we have known for years that trilobites had two compound eyes. There are different kinds of compound eyes, but for many trilobites, it meant that their eyes had thousands of tiny lenses. This is helpful for detecting motion, like noticing other creatures swimming around. Other types of compound eyes provided, say, sharper images. But having thousands of lenses was most common for trilobites. But in a recent study, researchers examined a trilobite fossil that was damaged. Part of its head was missing. This allowed them to notice, in the middle of the trilobite's forehead, three tiny dark spots. They said, hmm, these do not seem random. In fact, the tiny spots are evidence of a median eye, that is, a third eye. Most arthropods have median eyes, which are not really like compound eyes. They are simpler. But a median eye had never been found in trilobites before. Why? Well, researchers had believed it was only there during the larval stage, early in the development of a young trilobite, so researchers thought adult fossils would not have it. But it would have been hidden underneath a thin, dark layer of shell, which was missing in this fossil. So you would not see it in a fossil whose entire head was intact.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物学课的讲座。

男：三叶虫是一类古代海洋生物。归入节肢动物。现已灭绝。在现代动物中，鲎大概最像三叶虫。作为节肢动物，三叶虫与鲎都有分节身体、腿关节与硬外骨骼，有点像壳。我们多年已知三叶虫有两只复眼。复眼有不同类型，但对许多三叶虫而言，意味着眼睛有数千微小晶状体。这有助于探测运动，比如察觉周围游动的其他生物。其他类型复眼则提供更清晰的图像之类。但拥有数千晶状体对三叶虫最常见。最近一项研究中，研究者检查了一块受损的三叶虫化石。头部一部分缺失。这让他们注意到三叶虫前额中央有三个微小暗斑。他们说，嗯，这些似乎不是随机的。实际上，小斑点是中眼的证据，也就是第三只眼。多数节肢动物有中眼，与复眼并不相同，更简单。但三叶虫中此前从未发现中眼。为什么？研究者曾以为它只存在于幼体阶段，即幼年三叶虫发育早期，因此认为成体化石不会有。但它本会被藏在一层薄而暗的壳下，而这件化石缺失了那层壳。所以头部完整的化石上你看不到它。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 作为节肢动物，三叶虫和鲟鱼都有分节的身体、有关节的腿和坚硬的外骨骼，有点像壳。

transcriptSentences.text: So we've known for years that trilobites had two compound eyes.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 多年来我们一直知道三叶虫有两只复眼。

transcriptSentences.text: There are different kinds of compound eyes, but for many trilobites, it meant that their eyes had thousands of tiny lenses.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 复眼有很多种，但对于许多三叶虫来说，这意味着它们的眼睛有成千上万个微小的透镜。

transcriptSentences.text: This is helpful for detecting motion, like noticing other creatures swimming around.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这有助于探测运动，比如注意到周围游动的其他生物。

transcriptSentences.text: Other types of compound eyes provided, say, sharper images.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 比方说，其他类型的复眼能提供更清晰的图像。

transcriptSentences.text: But having thousands of lenses was most common for trilobites.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但拥有数千个透镜是三叶虫最常见的特征。

transcriptSentences.text: But in a recent study, researchers examined a trilobite fossil that was damaged.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但在最近的一项研究中，研究人员检查了一个受损的三叶虫化石。

transcriptSentences.text: Part of its head was missing.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它头部的一部分缺失了。

transcriptSentences.text: This allowed them to notice, in the middle of the trilobite's forehead, 3 tiny dark spots, they said.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 据他们说，这使得他们注意到在三叶虫前额的正中央有三个微小的黑点。

transcriptSentences.text: These don't seem random.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这些看起来并非偶然出现。

transcriptSentences.text: In fact, the tiny spots are evidence of a median eye, that is, a third eye.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 事实上，这些小点是中眼（即第三只眼）存在的证据。

transcriptSentences.text: Most arthropods have median eyes, which aren't really like compound eyes.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 大多数节肢动物都有中眼，它们与复眼不太一样。

transcriptSentences.text: They're simpler.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它们结构更简单。

transcriptSentences.text: But a median eye had never been found in trilobites before.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但以前从未在三叶虫身上发现过中眼。

transcriptSentences.text: Why?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 为什么呢？

transcriptSentences.text: Well, researchers had believed it was only there during the larval stage, early in the development of a young trilobite.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 嗯，研究人员曾认为它只存在于幼虫阶段，即幼年三叶虫发育的早期。

transcriptSentences.text: So researchers thought adult fossils wouldn't have it.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以研究人员认为成体化石不会有这种结构。

transcriptSentences.text: But it would have been hidden underneath a thin, dark layer of shell, which was missing in this fossil.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但它其实一直隐藏在一层薄薄的深色外壳下，而在这个化石中这层壳缺失了。

transcriptSentences.text: So you wouldn't see it in a fossil whose entire head was intact.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以，在一个头部完整的化石中，你是看不到它的。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on an art podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on an art podcast.

Woman: Humans have been expressing themselves through art for thousands of years. Consider ancient cave paintings that have been discovered throughout the world, some of them more than 40,000 years old. Caves in Sulawesi, Indonesia, that include figurative art are an example of this. Some forms of art, though, have much more recent origins. Take, for example, decalcomania, a really cool art technique that originated in the eighteenth century. So what is decalcomania? At its core, it is a simple process. You begin by spreading paint onto a surface, like a sheet of paper. Then you press another surface, let's say canvas, onto the paper. So you press the two surfaces together. At this point, you pull them apart while the paint is still wet. The resulting image is often rich with organic abstract patterns. Decalcomania was first used to decorate pottery in the eighteenth century, but it really took off in the twentieth century, especially with the Surrealist movement. Artists like Max Ernst loved this technique because it helped them tap into the subconscious and explore the unexpected. Ernst was enchanted by the process that allowed him to create shapes that the artist could not fully control. What's especially intriguing about decalcomania is the balance it strikes between control and chaos. Sure, the artist chooses the colors and the materials, but once the process is complete, the final result is mostly up to chance.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术播客的讲座。

女：人类通过艺术表达自我已有数千年。想想世界各地发现的古代洞穴壁画，有些超过四万年。印度尼西亚苏拉威西含具象艺术的洞穴即是一例。不过有些艺术形式起源近得多。例如印花转印法，一种源于十八世纪的很酷技法。什么是印花转印法？核心上过程简单。先把颜料涂在一个表面，比如一张纸。再把另一表面——比如画布——压到纸上。两表面压合。此时趁颜料未干把它们拉开。所得图像常充满有机抽象图案。印花转印法十八世纪先用于装饰陶器，但真正兴起在二十世纪，尤其随超现实主义运动。马克斯·恩斯特等艺术家热爱此法，因它助他们触及潜意识、探索意外。恩斯特着迷于让他创造出艺术家无法完全控制的形状的过程。印花转印法特别引人入胜之处在于控制与混沌之间的平衡。当然，艺术家选择颜色与材料，但过程完成后，最终结果多半取决于偶然。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
We've been talking about symbiosis, which, to remind you, is a beneficial interaction between two different species. A good example is birds and seed-producing plants. The birds eat the seeds the plants produce, and the plants benefit from birds dispersing those seeds. Okay, so here's a truly remarkable case of symbiosis: the relationship between the spotted salamander, a type of amphibian, and green algae, which are tiny plant-like aquatic organisms. The partnership begins when the salamander lays its eggs in freshwater ponds. The salamander eggs are contained within a jelly-like capsule, and the algae from the pond move in and form an integral part of this jelly-like mass as the embryos develop. All the while, the algae are photosynthesizing, transforming sunlight into usable energy, a process that releases oxygen. This is critical because the embryos need oxygen, and pond water tends to be low in it. And in return, the algae get a nutrient that they need to survive: nitrogen. The embryos produce readily available nitrogen as a waste product, and the algae happily use it. And what's cool is we now know that the algae don't just live in the egg capsule; they can enter the embryo's cells, meaning photosynthesis is occurring inside a vertebrate, a highly advanced animal, a phenomenon almost unheard of. Corals and a few other marine invertebrates do this, but among vertebrates it is extremely rare.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物学课的讲座。
我们一直在谈共生：提醒一下，就是两种不同物种之间的互利关系。一个好例子是鸟类与产籽植物：鸟吃种子，植物则借鸟传播种子。下面是一个真正非凡的共生案例：斑点蝾螈（一种两栖动物）与绿藻（微小的植物样水生生物）。合作从蝾螈在淡水池塘产卵开始。卵包在胶状囊中，池中的藻进入并在胚胎发育时成为这团胶状物的一部分。藻类同时进行光合作用，把阳光变成可用能量并释放氧气——这对胚胎至关重要，因为池水往往缺氧。作为回报，藻得到生存所需的氮：胚胎以废物形式产生易利用的氮，藻乐于吸收。更酷的是，我们现在知道藻不只生活在卵囊里，还能进入胚胎细胞，也就是说光合作用发生在脊椎动物体内——一种高度发达的动物——这几乎闻所未闻。珊瑚和其他少数海洋无脊椎动物会这样，但在脊椎动物中极为罕见。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
When we look at paintings, we often think of them as standalone creations, but they aren't always. Sometimes they converse with each other in surprising ways. Lubaina Himid, a British artist, was born in 1954 in what's now Tanzania in East Africa, and she was raised in London. London's where she also developed her career as an artist. According to Himid herself, her career expanded after 2010 when her work was shown at a gallery called Hollybush Gardens, a gallery in London. After that exhibit, critics paid more attention, and Himid began showing her work at larger museums and internationally outside of the United Kingdom. In her 1984 work titled Freedom and Change, Lubaina Himid shows two Black women dancing, or maybe running. They're holding hands in the air, and they just look so joyful. The scene reimagines a famous 1922 painting by the Spanish artist Pablo Picasso called Two Women Running on the Beach. Picasso's painting shows two women—white women—also dancing or running. They're in similar positions with similar facial expressions as the Black women in Himid's later work. This is an interesting reversal. By that I mean, Picasso was known for incorporating African elements into his work, like tribal masks. So I think it's only equitable that Himid then incorporated Picasso's elements into her own work. Makes it a fair back and forth, a conversation in a way, you see? It's just something that wasn't seen that often.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课的讲座。
我们看画时，常以为画作是独立创作，其实并不总是如此。有时它们会以出人意料的方式彼此“对话”。英国艺术家 Lubaina Himid 1954 年生于今东非坦桑尼亚，在伦敦长大，也在伦敦发展艺术生涯。据她本人说，2010 年作品在伦敦 Hollybush Gardens 画廊展出后，事业得到扩展；此后评论界更关注她，她也开始在更大博物馆以及英国以外的国际场合展出。在 1984 年的作品《自由与改变》中，Himid 画了两名黑人女性在跳舞，或许是在奔跑，手牵手举在空中，神情欢快。这一场景重新演绎了西班牙艺术家毕加索 1922 年的名画《海滩上奔跑的两个女人》。毕加索画中是两名白人女性，同样在舞动或奔跑，姿势与表情和 Himid 画中的黑人女性相似。这是一种有趣的反转：毕加索以把非洲元素——如部落面具——融入作品而闻名，因此我认为 Himid 把毕加索的元素融入自己的作品，也完全公平。某种意义上，这是一次来回的对话，而这种做法过去并不常见。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
Sea turtles are endangered marine species, and survival rates for sea turtle hatchlings are extremely low: about one in a thousand reaches adulthood. Even under natural conditions survival is difficult, and human activity makes it worse. One of the most significant problems is artificial light. Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches in tropical and subtropical waters. For millions of years, newly hatched turtles have relied on moonlight and starlight reflected off the water to find the sea. However, where beachfront development overlaps with nesting beaches, bright lights from hotels, streets, and homes overwhelm these natural cues. Older lighting technologies, such as fluorescent bulbs and cool-white lights, emit short-wavelength light that hatchlings are especially sensitive to, causing them to crawl inland instead of toward the sea. Many die from dehydration or traffic. Fortunately, there is a solution. Some older bulbs have been replaced with red or amber lights. These colors have longer wavelengths that are nearly invisible to hatchlings, allowing them to follow moonlight and starlight toward the water. Unlike dangers such as climate change and plastic pollution, which are global problems requiring broader action, light pollution can be addressed locally through small-scale efforts.

海龟是濒危海洋物种，幼龟存活率极低：大约一千只中只有一只能长到成年。即使在自然条件下也很难，人类活动更使情况恶化。最严重的问题之一是人工光。海龟在热带、亚热带沙滩产卵。数百万年来，刚出壳的幼龟靠水面反射的月光和星光找到大海。然而当滨海开发与筑巢沙滩重叠时，酒店、街道和住宅的强光淹没了这些自然线索。荧光灯、冷白光等较旧的照明发出短波光，幼龟特别敏感，会爬向内陆而不是大海，许多死于脱水或交通事故。幸好有解决办法：一些旧灯泡换成了红色或琥珀色灯，波长更长，幼龟几乎看不见，从而能跟随月光星光朝水走。与气候变化、塑料污染这类需要全球行动的问题不同，光污染可以通过本地小规模努力来解决。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on a history podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a history podcast.
Let's step back to the early twentieth century, a time when the world was changing rapidly and sounds from the past were fading away. One person who was deeply concerned was John Lomax, a pioneer in the field of audio recording who traveled across the United States with a phonograph in tow. His mission was to capture the voices and music of Indigenous and folk communities before they disappeared. His recordings were key to preserving a vast range of songs. A Cherokee lullaby sung by a grandmother to put a baby to sleep is not just a song; it is a piece of cultural heritage. One major challenge Lomax faced was the weight and fragility of the phonograph, which made travel to remote areas difficult. Lomax's efforts inspired similar projects, creating rich archives of many cultures. His recordings also laid the groundwork for ethnomusicology, a field dedicated to the study of music from cultural and social perspectives.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段历史播客中的谈话。
让我们回到二十世纪初：世界变化迅速，过去的声音正在消逝。对此深感忧虑的是 John Lomax——音频录制领域的先驱，他带着留声机走遍美国，使命是在原住民与民间社群的声音和音乐消失前把它们录下来。这些录音对保存大量歌曲至关重要。一位切罗基祖母哄婴儿入睡时唱的摇篮曲，不只是一首歌，更是文化遗产。Lomax 面临的一大困难是留声机笨重易损，不利深入偏远地区。他的努力激励了类似项目，形成多文化丰富档案，也为民族音乐学——从文化与社会视角研究音乐的领域——奠定了基础。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an archaeology class.
A remarkable discovery was made in the 1970s. I'm referring to the Bactrian Gold, which dates to around the first century BCE and includes over twenty thousand objects. It's called Bactrian Gold, but the treasure includes jewelry, coins, and ornaments. It came from six burial mounds belonging to five women and one man. They would have been wealthy nomads from Central Asia or northwestern China. The discovery was so important to archaeologists that it was compared to the discovery of King Tut's tomb in Egypt. Bactrian Gold was found at a major crossroads of the Silk Road, the ancient trade routes that connected Europe and Asia. The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of trade routes. It facilitated the exchange not only of goods, but also of ideas, art, and technology. The Bactrian Gold artifacts show Greek, Indian, and Chinese influences, and some pieces combine elements from several cultures. These many influences passed through the region because it was a crossroads. The discovery provides significant insight into how interconnected the ancient world truly was. It serves as a testament to the Silk Road's role in fostering culture and commerce long before the modern era.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段考古学课的讲座。
二十世纪七十年代有一次惊人的发现。我说的是“大夏黄金”，年代约在公元前一世纪，包含两万多件物品。虽叫大夏黄金，宝物却包括珠宝、钱币和装饰品，来自六座墓冢，属于五名女性和一名男性，应是中亚或中国西北的富裕游牧者。发现对考古学家如此重要，甚至被比作埃及图坦卡蒙墓的发现。大夏黄金出土于丝绸之路的重要十字路口——连接欧亚的古代商路网络。丝路不是一条路，而是庞大的贸易路线网，促进的不仅是货物交换，还有思想、艺术与技术。大夏黄金文物显示出希腊、印度和中国的影响，有的单件还融合多种文化元素。正因为地处十字路口，这些影响才汇聚于此。这一发现深刻说明古代世界何等互联，也证明丝路在现代之前很久就推动了文化与商业交流。

versions.label: Wofo M42
versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a lecture in an education class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a lecture in an education class.
Earlier, we were discussing the concept of modeling. Remember, modeling is when a teacher demonstrates a skill or process so students can observe and learn from that example. For instance, if you're teaching essay writing, you might write a paragraph in front of the class, explaining your choices as you go. Modeling shows students how to do something by providing a clear example. Now, let's talk about a related but distinct concept: scaffolding. Scaffolding is a teaching strategy that provides temporary supports to help learners accomplish tasks they might not manage independently. The term comes from construction. Just as scaffolds support workers until a building can stand on its own, instructional scaffolds support students until they gain mastery. For example, after modeling an essay, you might give students an outline, sentence starters, and model paragraphs. As they grow more confident, you gradually remove these supports, encouraging them to organize ideas and write independently. This gradual release fosters autonomy while ensuring progress. The key difference? Modeling shows the process—it's about demonstration. Scaffolding, on the other hand, is about support. It helps students take steps toward independence. Both strategies complement each other. Modeling sets the stage, and scaffolding guides learners through the performance. When applied thoughtfully, scaffolding transforms challenging tasks into achievable steps, while modeling provides the blueprint for success.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段教育学课的讲座。
前面我们讨论了 modeling（示范）。记住，示范是教师演示技能或过程，让学生观察并学习。比如教写作文，你可以当着全班写一段，边写边解释选择。示范通过清晰例子告诉学生怎么做。现在谈一个相关但不同的概念：scaffolding（支架）。支架是一种教学策略，提供临时支持，帮助学生完成尚难独立完成的任务。术语来自建筑：脚手架支撑工人，直到建筑能自立；教学支架支撑学生，直到他们掌握。例如示范完作文后，可以给提纲、句首提示和范文段落；学生更有信心后，逐渐撤掉这些支持，鼓励他们自己组织并写作。这种逐步放手既促进自主，又保证进步。关键区别？示范展示过程——是演示；支架则是支持，帮助学生一步步走向独立。两者互补：示范搭台，支架引领表演。运用得当，支架把难任务拆成可完成的步骤，示范则提供成功的蓝图。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an ocean sciences class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an ocean sciences class.
Back in the mid-1800s, scientists dredging the ocean floor stumbled on previously unknown life forms: brittle stars, sea cucumbers, even deep-sea corals—creatures living in pitch darkness, near-freezing water, and under crushing pressure. That discovery flipped the old belief that such conditions couldn't support life. But what do these organisms eat? Near the ocean surface, food chains begin with phytoplankton, tiny plants that use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide into energy. These phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed fish, and these in turn feed larger predators. But in the deep ocean, there's no sunlight. So what keeps life going down there? The answer is something scientists call marine snow. This isn't frozen water, but a slow, steady snowfall of organic particles—dead plankton, bits of decaying creatures, and animal waste products—all sinking from above. But marine snow does more than feed deep-sea life. It carries carbon from surface waters down to the deep-sea floor, where some of it can stay locked away for centuries, even millennia. This process helps regulate Earth's climate by pulling carbon from surface waters, and so out of the atmosphere, which interacts with the surface waters. As you probably know, carbon in the atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide gas, has a warming effect on Earth's climate, and the extra carbon released from human activities has caused dangerous global warming. How much carbon does marine snow remove? Roughly 10 billion tons annually, about the same as all human cars.

十九世纪中叶，科学家疏浚海底时意外发现了前所未知的生命：蛇尾、海参，甚至深海珊瑚——它们生活在漆黑、近乎冰点、高压的环境中。这一发现推翻了“这种条件不能支持生命”的旧观念。但它们吃什么？靠近海面，食物链从浮游植物开始：微小植物利用阳光把二氧化碳转化为能量，再养活浮游动物、鱼类，以及更大的捕食者。深海没有阳光，生命靠什么维持？答案是科学家所说的“海雪”。那不是冰，而是缓慢沉降的有机颗粒——死亡的浮游生物、腐烂残骸、动物排泄物——从上层沉下来。海雪不仅养活深海生物，还把碳从表层水带到深海底，有的可封存数百年甚至上千年。这一过程把碳从表层水、进而从与表层相互作用的大气中抽离，有助于调节地球气候。你们知道，大气中的二氧化碳有温室效应，人类活动额外排放的碳已造成危险的全球变暖。海雪每年带走大约一百亿吨碳，大致相当于人类所有汽车的排放量。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a music history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a music history class.
Throughout history, people have created a number of interesting musical instruments. Today, I want to talk about a fascinating instrument called the phonofiddle. If you combined a violin and a gramophone, you'd have the phonofiddle. It's a violin-like instrument with a horn attached to amplify sound. It was developed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries during a time when there was a quest for louder musical instruments. Before electric amplification became the norm, musicians had to come up with ingenious methods to make their sounds heard over larger distances or in noisy environments, and the phonofiddle was one such attempt. Its horn acted kind of like the bell of a trumpet, projecting sound in a way that was surprisingly effective for its time. Picture a street performer on a bustling corner, competing with all the hustle and bustle of busy markets, things like horse-drawn carriages. The phonofiddle's horn would allow their music to cut through all that noise. What's particularly interesting is that the phonofiddle was part of a broader trend toward mechanical amplification in the pre-electric era. It shares similarities with other eccentric instruments like the Stroh violin, which also used a horn. And this exploration of acoustic amplification paved the way for the electric revolution in music. Before we move on to discuss the electric revolution, let's take a closer look at how the phonofiddle was constructed.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段音乐史课的讲座。
历史上人们发明过许多有趣的乐器。今天我想讲一种迷人的乐器：phonofiddle。如果把小提琴和留声机合在一起，差不多就是它：像小提琴，却装着喇叭来放大声音。它出现在十九世纪末二十世纪初，那时人们正追求更响的乐器。在电声放大成为常态之前，乐手要想在更远距离或嘈杂环境中被听见，只能想出各种巧妙办法，phonofiddle 就是其中之一。它的喇叭有点像小号的喇叭口，把声音投射出去，在当时相当有效。想象街头艺人在热闹街角演奏，要压过市场喧闹、马车声等；phonofiddle 的喇叭能让音乐穿过去。特别有意思的是，它属于电气时代之前机械扩音的更大潮流，和同样使用喇叭的 Stroh 小提琴等“古怪”乐器相似。这种对声学放大的探索，为音乐的电气革命铺了路。在讨论电气革命之前，我们先仔细看看 phonofiddle 是怎么做出来的。

versions.transcript: Throughout history, people have created a number of interesting musical instruments. Today, I want to talk about a fascinating instrument called the phonofiddle. If you combined a violin and a gramophone, you'd have the phonofiddle. It's a violin like instrument with a horn attached to amplify sound. It was developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, during a time when there was a quest for louder musical instruments. Before electric amplification became the norm, musicians had to come up with ingenious methods to make their sounds heard over larger distances or in noisy environments. And the phonofiddle was one such attempt. Its horn acted kind of like the bell of a trumpet, projecting sound in a way that was surprisingly effective for its time. Picture a street performer on a bustling corner, competing with all the hustle and bustle of busy markets, things like horse drawn carriages. The phonofiddle's horn would allow their music to cut through all that noise. What's particularly interesting is that the phonofiddle was part of a broader trend toward mechanical amplification in the pre electric era. It shares similarities with other eccentric instruments, like the Stroh violin, which also used a horn. And this exploration of acoustic amplification paved the way for the electric revolution in music. Before we move on to discuss the electric revolution, let's take a closer look at how the phonofiddle was constructed.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk about Premack's principle and rewards.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk about Premack's principle and rewards.
Ever wonder why some rewards motivate better than others when you're trying to change behavior? Most people think of rewards as tangible things: money, candy, or gift cards. Psychologists call these extrinsic rewards because they come from an external source. But in the 1960s, psychologist David Premack had a different idea. Instead of giving people tangible things, why not use activities people already enjoy? This became Premack's principle. Here are the basics. You can use something someone already likes to do, or a high-probability behavior, to motivate an activity they avoid, or a low-probability behavior. If a child loves playing outside but hates cleaning their room, you make outdoor play the reward for cleaning: first clean, then play. Premack believed this strategy works better than candy or money because it taps into intrinsic rewards, things that feel good because we genuinely enjoy them. Tangible rewards often lose their appeal, but favorite activities stay motivating. By linking something less appealing to something naturally fun, you create a lasting incentive that feels personal and meaningful. If you're trying to get yourself to the gym more often, you might promise yourself extra time on a hobby you love after your workout. You're connecting the new habit to something that already matters to you. That's why Premack's principle is still relevant today, and not just for parents and teachers.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段关于普雷马克原则与奖励的讲座。
有没有想过为什么有些奖励比另一些更能推动行为改变？多数人想到的奖励是有形的：金钱、糖果或礼品卡。心理学家称之为外部奖励，因为来自外部。但在1960年代，心理学家大卫·普雷马克有不同想法：与其给有形物品，不如用人们已经喜欢的活动。这就是普雷马克原则。基本做法是：用高概率行为（你本来就爱做的事）作为做低概率行为（你不太想做的事）的奖励。比如，你不爱去健身房，但爱看剧，就可以规定：先锻炼，再看一集。外部奖励往往很快失去吸引力，而把喜爱的活动当作奖励，更可持续。所以想改变习惯时，不必总找新礼物，可以调度你已经享受的活动。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 以下是其基本内容。

transcriptSentences.text: You can use something someone already likes to do, or a high probability behavior, to motivate an activity they avoid, or a low probability behavior.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 你可以利用某人已经喜欢做的事情，或者说高概率行为，来激励他们回避的活动，或者说低概率行为。

transcriptSentences.text: Here's an example.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 举个例子。

transcriptSentences.text: If a child loves playing outside but hates cleaning their room, you make outdoor play the reward for cleaning.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 如果一个孩子喜欢在外面玩耍但讨厌打扫房间，你就可以将户外玩耍作为打扫房间的奖励。

transcriptSentences.text: First clean, then play.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 先打扫，后玩耍。

transcriptSentences.text: It's simple but powerful.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它简单却强大。

transcriptSentences.text: Premack believed this strategy works better than candy or money because it motivates by tapping into what psychologists call intrinsic rewards, things that feel good because we genuinely enjoy them.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 普雷马克认为，这种策略比糖果或金钱更有效，因为它通过利用心理学家所说的内在奖励来激励，即那些我们真正喜欢、感觉良好的事物。

transcriptSentences.text: Tangible rewards often lose their appeal, but favorite activities stay motivating.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 有形的奖励常常会失去吸引力，但最喜欢的活动却能持续激励人心。

transcriptSentences.text: By linking something less appealing to something naturally fun, you create a lasting incentive that feels personal and meaningful.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 通过将不太吸引人的事物与自然有趣的活动联系起来，你就能创造出一种持久的、个人化且有意义的激励。

transcriptSentences.text: Think about it.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 想想看。

transcriptSentences.text: If you're trying to get yourself to the gym more often, you might promise yourself extra time on a hobby you love after your workout.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 如果你想让自己更经常去健身房，你可能会在锻炼后答应自己，给自己更多时间投入到你喜欢的一个爱好上。

transcriptSentences.text: You're not bribing yourself with something artificial or external.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 你不是在用人工的或外部的东西贿赂自己。

transcriptSentences.text: You're connecting the new habit to something that already matters to you.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 你正在将新习惯与对你来说已经很重要的事情联系起来。

transcriptSentences.text: That's why Premack's principle is still relevant today and not just for parents and teachers.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这就是为什么普雷马克原则在今天仍然适用，而且不仅仅适用于父母和老师。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk about termite mounds and natural climate-control architecture.
Have you ever thought of termites as architects? It might sound a bit far-fetched, but these tiny insects construct some of the most impressive structures in the animal kingdom: massive mounds with complex ventilation systems that function as natural air conditioning. These mounds, sometimes towering over three meters high, can be found in the savannas of Africa and Australia. How do termites, with their small size and limited resources, build such marvels? It is all about teamwork and their incredible use of natural principles. Termite mounds are not just heaps of dirt. They are intricately designed with a network of tunnels and chimneys that manage airflow. By exploiting temperature differences between the inside and outside of the mound, these structures regulate heat and moisture, essentially working as natural air conditioners. The ventilation system allows fresh air to flow in and out, maintaining a stable environment inside that is crucial for the survival of its inhabitants. But there is a downside. During heavy rains, the structures can be prone to collapse, a significant issue for the colony. Yet termites have adapted by rebuilding quickly, demonstrating resilience. By observing these industrious creatures, architects and engineers have been inspired to develop sustainable building designs for humans. Termite mounds show how nature's design principles can be harnessed to create energy-efficient structures. It is a fascinating blend of biology and architecture, where the humble termite stands as a pioneer in sustainable living.

请听一段关于白蚁丘与自然气候调节建筑的讲座。
你有没有想过白蚁其实是建筑师？这听起来或许有点牵强，但这些小昆虫建造了动物界中一些最惊人的结构：带有复杂通风系统、能像天然空调一样运作的巨大蚁丘。这些蚁丘有时高达三米以上，分布在非洲和澳大利亚的稀树草原。体型弱小、资源有限的白蚁如何建成这样的奇迹？关键在于协作，以及它们对自然原理的巧妙利用。白蚁丘不只是土堆。它们内部有精密的隧道与烟囱网络来管理气流。通过利用蚁丘内外的温差，这些结构调节热量与湿度，本质上就是天然空调。通风系统让新鲜空气进出，维持对巢群生存至关重要的稳定内部环境。不过也有缺点：大雨时结构可能塌陷，对群落是严重问题。白蚁却能迅速重建，展现韧性。观察这些勤劳的生物后，建筑师与工程师受到启发，开发出更可持续的人类建筑方案。白蚁丘表明，自然的设计原则可以被用来建造节能结构。这是生物学与建筑学的迷人结合，谦卑的白蚁成了可持续生活的先驱。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
We've been talking about symbiosis, which, to remind you, is a beneficial interaction between two different species. A good example is birds and seed-producing plants. The birds eat the seeds the plants produce, and the plants benefit from birds dispersing those seeds. Okay, so here's a truly remarkable case of symbiosis: the relationship between the spotted salamander, a type of amphibian, and green algae, which are tiny plant-like aquatic organisms. The partnership begins when the salamander lays its eggs in freshwater ponds. The salamander eggs are contained within a jelly-like capsule, and the algae from the pond move in and form an integral part of this jelly-like mass as the embryos develop. All the while, the algae are photosynthesizing, transforming sunlight into usable energy, a process that releases oxygen. This is critical because the embryos need oxygen, and pond water tends to be low in it. And in return, the algae get a nutrient that they need to survive: nitrogen. The embryos produce readily available nitrogen as a waste product, and the algae happily use it. And what's cool is we now know that the algae don't just live in the egg capsule; they can enter the embryo's cells, meaning photosynthesis is occurring inside a vertebrate, a highly advanced animal, a phenomenon almost unheard of. Corals and a few other marine invertebrates do this, but among vertebrates it is extremely rare.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物学课的讲座。
我们一直在谈共生：提醒一下，就是两种不同物种之间的互利关系。一个好例子是鸟类与产籽植物：鸟吃种子，植物则借鸟传播种子。下面是一个真正非凡的共生案例：斑点蝾螈（一种两栖动物）与绿藻（微小的植物样水生生物）。合作从蝾螈在淡水池塘产卵开始。卵包在胶状囊中，池中的藻进入并在胚胎发育时成为这团胶状物的一部分。藻类同时进行光合作用，把阳光变成可用能量并释放氧气——这对胚胎至关重要，因为池水往往缺氧。作为回报，藻得到生存所需的氮：胚胎以废物形式产生易利用的氮，藻乐于吸收。更酷的是，我们现在知道藻不只生活在卵囊里，还能进入胚胎细胞，也就是说光合作用发生在脊椎动物体内——一种高度发达的动物——这几乎闻所未闻。珊瑚和其他少数海洋无脊椎动物会这样，但在脊椎动物中极为罕见。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
When we look at paintings, we often think of them as standalone creations, but they aren't always. Sometimes they converse with each other in surprising ways. Lubaina Himid, a British artist, was born in 1954 in what's now Tanzania in East Africa, and she was raised in London. London's where she also developed her career as an artist. According to Himid herself, her career expanded after 2010 when her work was shown at a gallery called Hollybush Gardens, a gallery in London. After that exhibit, critics paid more attention, and Himid began showing her work at larger museums and internationally outside of the United Kingdom. In her 1984 work titled Freedom and Change, Lubaina Himid shows two Black women dancing, or maybe running. They're holding hands in the air, and they just look so joyful. The scene reimagines a famous 1922 painting by the Spanish artist Pablo Picasso called Two Women Running on the Beach. Picasso's painting shows two women—white women—also dancing or running. They're in similar positions with similar facial expressions as the Black women in Himid's later work. This is an interesting reversal. By that I mean, Picasso was known for incorporating African elements into his work, like tribal masks. So I think it's only equitable that Himid then incorporated Picasso's elements into her own work. Makes it a fair back and forth, a conversation in a way, you see? It's just something that wasn't seen that often.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课的讲座。
我们看画时，常以为画作是独立创作，其实并不总是如此。有时它们会以出人意料的方式彼此“对话”。英国艺术家 Lubaina Himid 1954 年生于今东非坦桑尼亚，在伦敦长大，也在伦敦发展艺术生涯。据她本人说，2010 年作品在伦敦 Hollybush Gardens 画廊展出后，事业得到扩展；此后评论界更关注她，她也开始在更大博物馆以及英国以外的国际场合展出。在 1984 年的作品《自由与改变》中，Himid 画了两名黑人女性在跳舞，或许是在奔跑，手牵手举在空中，神情欢快。这一场景重新演绎了西班牙艺术家毕加索 1922 年的名画《海滩上奔跑的两个女人》。毕加索画中是两名白人女性，同样在舞动或奔跑，姿势与表情和 Himid 画中的黑人女性相似。这是一种有趣的反转：毕加索以把非洲元素——如部落面具——融入作品而闻名，因此我认为 Himid 把毕加索的元素融入自己的作品，也完全公平。某种意义上，这是一次来回的对话，而这种做法过去并不常见。

Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

Today we're revisiting the topic of urban green spaces. Green areas in cities like parks and gardens. These spaces are known to improve air quality and reduce heat in cities. They also support the health of city residents. Creating and maintaining urban green spaces can be challenging, however, especially in densely populated cities. An obvious issue is limited space. In areas where land is expensive or already developed, finding room for parks or gardens can be difficult. One way cities address this is by building green roofs. That's a layer of vegetation planted on top of a building. Green roofs help cool buildings, absorb rainwater, and add greenery without taking up ground space. Cities also often repurpose unused lots, such as old parking areas or vacant lots, turning them into small parks or gardens. Vertical gardens are another innovation. These are walls covered with plants, often using special structures that allow greenery to grow upward. They are useful in places where horizontal space is limited and can improve air quality and insulation. While costs and upkeep of green spaces are legitimate concerns, many cities are adopting green space quotas. Policies that require a minimum amount of greenery in new developments. These quotas mandate builders to include features like trees, rooftop gardens, or courtyards. Though they may raise construction costs, urban planners support them because they ensure that green space is not overlooked in city growth. Quotas help balance development with environmental health and are a step toward more sustainable urban living.

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.
Today I've got a topic that might just electrify your imagination: lightning in the atmosphere of Venus. You might wonder why we should care about lightning on another planet. Well, understanding lightning on Venus could give us clues about the planet's dynamic weather systems. Okay, so the Soviet Venera space missions set out to explore Venus, one of Earth's closest neighbors. What these missions found was surprising: evidence of lightning in Venus's thick, sulfuric acid-laden clouds. So picture this: the sky is perpetually cloaked in clouds. Lightning flickers through the gloom. It's practically the setting for a science fiction movie. But this isn't fiction; it's real science. And here's where it gets interesting: the presence of lightning suggests that the atmosphere of Venus is more dynamic than we once assumed. Why does this matter? Lightning can play a crucial role in atmospheric chemistry, affecting the formation of molecules and influencing weather patterns. On Earth, lightning is known to create compounds like nitrogen oxides, which are essential for plant life. While Venus doesn't have plant life, understanding its atmospheric processes helps scientists build models that can be applied to other planets, including our own. Moreover, studying Venusian lightning can help us predict future changes in its atmosphere. If lightning is as prevalent as the Venera mission suggests, it could mean that Venus is more geologically active than previously assumed. This suggests new ideas for research. Could other planets with similar conditions harbor surprising phenomena, or even forms of life?
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段天文学课的讲座。
今天我有个可能点燃你想象的话题：金星大气中的闪电。你也许会想为何我们该关心另一颗行星上的闪电。理解金星上的闪电可给我们关于该行星动态天气系统的线索。好，苏联金星号空间任务出发探索金星——地球最近邻之一。这些任务发现令人惊讶：在金星厚重、充满硫酸的云层中有闪电的证据。想象一下：天空永远被云笼罩。闪电在昏暗中闪烁。几乎是科幻电影的场景。但这不是虚构；是真科学。有趣之处在于：闪电的存在表明金星大气比我们曾经假定的更动态。这为何重要？闪电可在大气化学中起关键作用，影响分子形成并影响天气模式。在地球上，已知闪电会生成氮氧化物等化合物，它们对植物生命至关重要。尽管金星没有植物生命，理解其大气过程帮助科学家建立可应用于包括我们自己在内的其他行星的模型。此外，研究金星闪电可帮助我们预测其大气的未来变化。若闪电如金星号任务所暗示的那样普遍，可能意味着金星比先前假定的地质上更活跃。这提示新的研究方向。条件相似的其他行星是否可能有令人惊讶的现象，甚至生命形式？

Listen to a talk in a science podcast.

When we study ecosystems, we're not just looking at a collection of plants and animals scattered across a landscape. We're diving into a dynamic web of interactions, all of which shape the structure and function of the natural world. One particularly fascinating concept within this field is that of keystone species. In architecture, a keystone is a central stone that locks an arch together. Remove it, and the arch collapses. Similarly, a keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its environment. It can't be removed without threatening the whole ecosystem. A striking example is the gray wolf in Yellowstone National Park in the U.S. In the early 20th century, wolves were eradicated from the region due to widespread hunting through government predator control programs, driven by concerns over livestock and human safety. Without wolves, elk populations—you probably know elk are a type of deer that wolves hunt and eat—um, the elk population surged dramatically with their main predator gone. And all these elk, which eat many kinds of vegetation, began overgrazing, which suppressed the growth of trees and other plants in the area. This destabilized the whole ecosystem. Birds had fewer places to nest, mice and rabbits couldn't use plants to hide from predators, and even bees had fewer flowers to feed from. When wolves were reintroduced in the 1990s, their presence reshaped the landscape. Elk populations decreased, which allowed plant and tree populations to recover, and in turn, all the animals who depended on them.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on a social science podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a social science podcast.

Man: Today, we're exploring a fascinating concept in social psychology known as pluralistic ignorance. Pluralistic ignorance describes a situation where the majority of members in a group privately reject a norm or standard, but incorrectly assume that most others accept it. This often results in everyone conforming to a norm they don't truly agree with. A classic example occurs in workplace overtime culture. Many employees might prefer to leave work on time, but they stay late because everyone else is committed to working extra hours. In reality, most colleagues also wish to leave on time, but fear appearing less dedicated. Research highlights this dynamic when employees are asked privately about their preferences. Many express a desire for better work-life balance, despite their public behavior suggesting enthusiasm for long hours. Pluralistic ignorance has broad implications beyond the workplace. Notably, it can perpetuate social stereotypes and hinder societal change, as individuals might hesitate to voice dissenting opinions, thinking they are in the minority. However, overcoming pluralistic ignorance has powerful benefits. When even one person speaks up, it can embolden others to express their true beliefs, potentially leading to a shift in group norms and to more honest, authentic communities. There is a challenge, and it's a big one. Being the first to speak out often requires courage, as it can put one's social standing among peers at risk.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段社会科学播客的讲座。

男：今天我们探讨社会心理学中一个迷人概念：多元无知。多元无知描述这样一种情形：群体中多数成员私下拒绝某规范或标准，却错误地假定多数他人接受它。这常导致人人从众于自己并不真正认同的规范。经典例子出现在职场加班文化中。许多员工可能更想准时下班，却因别人都坚持加班而留下。实际上多数同事也想准时走，但怕显得不够敬业。研究在私下询问员工偏好时凸显了这一动态。许多人表达希望更好的工作生活平衡，尽管公开行为暗示对长时间工作的热情。多元无知的影响远超职场。尤其它可延续社会刻板印象、阻碍社会变革，因为个人可能犹豫表达异议，以为自己是少数。但克服多元无知有强大益处。哪怕一人发声，也可鼓舞他人表达真实信念，潜在导致群体规范转变与更诚实真实的共同体。挑战很大。第一个发声常需要勇气，因为可能危及自己在同辈中的社会地位。

versions.transcriptZh: 今天，我们将探讨社会心理学中一个引人入胜的概念，即“多元无知”。 多元无知描述了这样一种情境：一个群体中的大多数成员在内心深处抵制某种规范或标准，但却错误地认为大多数其他人是接受它的。 这通常导致每个人都顺从了一个他们并非真正认同的规范。 职场加班文化就是一个典型的例子。 许多员工可能更希望按时下班，但他们选择加班，因为他们认为其他所有人都在致力于额外的工作。 实际上，大多数同事也希望按时下班，但害怕表现得不够敬业。 研究强调了这种动态关系。 当员工被私下询问他们的意愿时，许多人表达了对更好工作与生活平衡的渴望，尽管他们的公开行为表现出对长时间工作的热情。 多元无知的影响远不止于职场。 值得注意的是，它会使社会偏见根深蒂固，并阻碍社会变革，因为个人可能会因认为自己属于少数派而犹豫是否要发表不同政见。 然而，克服多元无知具有强大的益处。 当哪怕只有一个人大声说出想法时，它也能鼓励其他人表达真实的信念，从而可能导致群体规范的转变，并建立更诚实、真实的社区。 但挑战也是巨大的。 成为第一个发声的人往往需要勇气，因为这可能会冒着失去同龄人中社会地位的风险。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 今天，我们将探讨社会心理学中一个引人入胜的概念，即“多元无知”。

transcriptSentences.text: Pluralistic ignorance describes a situation where the majority of members in a group privately reject a norm or standard, but assume, incorrectly, that most others accept it.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 多元无知描述了这样一种情境：一个群体中的大多数成员在内心深处抵制某种规范或标准，但却错误地认为大多数其他人是接受它的。

transcriptSentences.text: This often results in everyone conforming to a norm they don't truly agree with.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这通常导致每个人都顺从了一个他们并非真正认同的规范。

transcriptSentences.text: A classic example occurs in workplace overtime culture.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 职场加班文化就是一个典型的例子。

transcriptSentences.text: Many employees might prefer to leave work on time, but they stay late because they believe everyone else is committed to working extra hours.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 许多员工可能更希望按时下班，但他们选择加班，因为他们认为其他所有人都在致力于额外的工作。

transcriptSentences.text: In reality, most colleagues also wish to leave on time, but fear appearing less dedicated.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 实际上，大多数同事也希望按时下班，但害怕表现得不够敬业。

transcriptSentences.text: Research highlights this dynamic.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 研究强调了这种动态关系。

transcriptSentences.text: When employees are asked privately about their preferences, many express a desire for better work life balance, despite their public behavior suggesting enthusiasm for long hours.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 当员工被私下询问他们的意愿时，许多人表达了对更好工作与生活平衡的渴望，尽管他们的公开行为表现出对长时间工作的热情。

transcriptSentences.text: Pluralistic ignorance has broad implications well beyond the workplace.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 多元无知的影响远不止于职场。

transcriptSentences.text: Notably, it can perpetuate social stereotypes and hinder societal change, as individuals might hesitate to voice dissenting opinions, thinking they're in the minority.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 值得注意的是，它会使社会偏见根深蒂固，并阻碍社会变革，因为个人可能会因认为自己属于少数派而犹豫是否要发表不同政见。

transcriptSentences.text: However, overcoming pluralistic ignorance has powerful benefits.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 然而，克服多元无知具有强大的益处。

transcriptSentences.text: When even one person speaks up, it can embolden others to express their true beliefs, potentially leading to a shift in group norms and to more honest, authentic communities.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 当哪怕只有一个人大声说出想法时，它也能鼓励其他人表达真实的信念，从而可能导致群体规范的转变，并建立更诚实、真实的社区。

transcriptSentences.text: But there's a challenge, and it's a big one.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但挑战也是巨大的。

transcriptSentences.text: Being the first to speak out often requires courage, as it can risk one's social standing among one's peers.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 成为第一个发声的人往往需要勇气，因为这可能会冒着失去同龄人中社会地位的风险。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
So, I've been thinking about the painter Georges de La Tour.
You may not have heard his name as frequently as some of his contemporaries, like Caravaggio.
You're probably familiar with Caravaggio, but Georges de La Tour holds a special place in the Baroque movement.
His candlelit scenes set an atmosphere that feels both intimate and mysterious.
La Tour's paintings often focus on the play of light and shadow, with candlelight serving as the primary source of illumination.
One of the key elements of La Tour's style is his use of chiaroscuro.
Chiaroscuro is a technique that employs stark contrast between light and dark.
By using chiaroscuro, La Tour was able to bring a sense of realism and focus to his subjects.
They were often ordinary people engaged in mundane tasks.
Now, the oil painting The Penitent Magdalene is a well-known painting of his.
In The Penitent Magdalene, a woman sits by a table, gazing at a burning candle, which is in front of a small mirror.
The light from the candle, which is reflected in the mirror, creates a soft glow, highlighting her contemplative state.
The light creates a chiaroscuro effect, since only the side of her face is brightly lit while the rest of the painting is quite dark.
As we move forward, we will explore how La Tour's work was rediscovered in the early 20th century, shedding new light, quite literally, on his contributions to Baroque art.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课上的讲解。
我一直在思考画家乔治·德·拉图尔。
你们听到他的名字的频率可能不如他的同时代画家，比如卡拉瓦乔。
你们可能熟悉卡拉瓦乔，但乔治·德·拉图尔在巴洛克运动中占有特殊地位。
他笔下的烛光场景营造出既亲密又神秘的氛围。
拉图尔的画作常常聚焦于光影的变化，以烛光作为主要光源。
拉图尔风格的关键元素之一是他对明暗对照法的运用。
明暗对照法是一种运用明暗强烈对比的技巧。
通过使用明暗对照法，拉图尔能够使画中人物更具真实感，并突出主体。
这些人物通常是从事日常事务的普通人。
油画《忏悔的抹大拉的玛利亚》是他的一幅著名作品。
在《忏悔的抹大拉的玛利亚》中，一名女子坐在桌旁，凝视着一根燃烧的蜡烛，蜡烛前面是一面小镜子。
蜡烛的光线映照在镜子中，形成柔和的光晕，突出了她沉思的状态。
光线形成了明暗对照效果，因为她的脸只有侧面被明亮地照亮，而画作的其余部分相当昏暗。
接下来，我们将探讨拉图尔的作品如何在20世纪初重新受到关注，从字面意义上说，这为他对巴洛克艺术的贡献带来了新的认识。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
For most of human history, people have needed to focus on the present, like cave dwellers.
Cave dwellers had to think about surviving today, not someday years in the future.
As a result, human brains aren't cut out for the long-term thinking that's required today.
Instead, we experience hyperbolic discounting.
A bigger future reward is worth a lot less because it's far off, and we choose the smaller reward right now instead.
Still, there are things we can do to avoid hyperbolic discounting.
For one, you can be realistic about your future self.
You might choose the immediate reward of watching TV today instead of the future reward of finishing an annoying but essential task like doing laundry.
You might picture your future self, tomorrow's you, as having lots of energy and motivation to get that laundry done.
Is that realistic? Probably not.
More likely, you'll be frustrated and maybe out of clean clothes.
Seeing that can motivate you to do your laundry today.
Another approach is to break down a big goal into smaller chunks.
Maybe you have a big project due in a month, and even though finishing it will be a big relief, it seems far away, right?
It's easier to choose playing video games right now instead of chipping away at your project.
So try looking at your project as a sequence of shorter tasks that are each manageable.
You can handle one task today, can't you?
Sure. And then give yourself a small reward for that.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段心理学课上的讲解。
在人类历史的大部分时期，人们都必须关注当下，就像穴居人一样。
穴居人必须考虑如何在今天生存，而不是几年后某一天的事情。
因此，人类的大脑并不擅长如今所需要的长期思考。
相反，我们会经历双曲贴现。
未来更大的奖励因为距离现在很远而显得价值低得多，于是我们会选择眼下较小的奖励。
不过，我们可以采取一些措施来避免双曲贴现。
首先，你可以现实地看待未来的自己。
你可能会选择今天看电视这一即时奖励，而不是完成洗衣服这种烦人但必要的任务所带来的未来奖励。
你可能会想象未来的自己，也就是明天的你，会有充足的精力和动力把衣服洗完。
这现实吗？可能并不现实。
更有可能的是，你会感到沮丧，甚至没有干净衣服可穿。
意识到这一点可以促使你今天就洗衣服。
另一种方法是把一个大目标分解成较小的部分。
也许你有一个一个月后截止的大项目，尽管完成它会让你如释重负，但截止日期看起来还很遥远，对吧？
与一点点完成项目相比，人们更容易选择现在玩电子游戏。
所以，试着把项目看成一系列较短且各自可完成的任务。
你今天可以完成一项任务，对吧？
当然。然后为此给自己一个小奖励。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: A bigger future reward is worth a lot less because it's far off, and we choose the smaller reward right now instead.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 未来更大的奖励因为距离现在很远而显得价值低得多，于是我们会选择眼下较小的奖励。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Still, there are things we can do to avoid hyperbolic discounting.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 不过，我们可以采取一些措施来避免双曲贴现。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: For one, you can be realistic about your future self.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 首先，你可以现实地看待未来的自己。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: You might choose the immediate reward of watching TV today instead of the future reward of finishing an annoying but essential task like doing laundry.

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: You might picture your future self, tomorrow's you, as having lots of energy and motivation to get that laundry done.

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Is that realistic?

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Probably not.

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Seeing that can motivate you to do your laundry today.

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Another approach is to break down a big goal into smaller chunks.

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Maybe you have a big project due in a month, and even though finishing it will be a big relief, it seems far away, right?

versions.transcript: For most of human history, people have needed to focus on the present, like cave dwellers. Cave dwellers had to think about surviving today, not someday years in the future. As a result, human brains aren't cut out for the long term thinking that's required today. Instead, we experience hyperbolic discounting. We see a bigger future reward as worth a lot less because it's far off, and choose the smaller reward right now instead. Still, there are things we can do to avoid hyperbolic discounting. For one, you can be realistic about your future self. What's the immediate reward of watching TV today, instead of the future reward of finishing an annoying, but essential task like doing laundry? You might picture your future self, tomorrow's you, as having lots of energy and motivation to get that laundry done. Is that realistic? Probably not. More likely, you'll be frustrated and maybe out of clean clothes. Seeing that can motivate you to do your laundry today. Another approach is to break down a big goal into smaller chunks. Maybe you have a big project due in a month, and even though finishing will be a big relief, it seems far away, right? It's easier to choose playing video games right now, instead of chipping away at your project. So, try looking at your project as a sequence of shorter tasks that are each manageable. You can handle one task today, can't you? Sure. And then give yourself a small reward for that.

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
You might be surprised, but plants can flourish in seemingly inhospitable environments, for example, in rocky crevices in high mountains, enduring relentless winds and temperatures that plunge below freezing.
One such plant is the alpine saxifrage, an emblem of nature's ingenuity and adaptability.
Let's discuss the extraordinary adaptations that enable this unassuming yet tenacious plant to thrive where few others venture.
The alpine saxifrage employs a unique survival strategy by anchoring itself within rock crevices, a refuge from the most severe weather.
These crevices provide natural insulation against the biting cold, conserving precious moisture, which is often scarce in alpine climates.
And that's not all.
The leaves of alpine saxifrage have a specialized waxy coating, which limits moisture loss, a critical adaptation for survival in regions where water remains largely trapped as ice.
Furthermore, the wax serves another purpose. It reflects excess sunlight that the plant doesn't require, thereby shielding it from damaging ultraviolet rays.
A trade-off exists in this resilience, however.
The alpine saxifrage's slow growth renders it vulnerable to disturbances.
Human activities such as hiking and climbing pose a threat to its delicate habitat, reminding us of the fragile equilibrium between nature's resilience and its susceptibility to external influences.
So, if you see it in the mountains, appreciate and protect the alpine saxifrage, one of nature's silent survivors, weathering storms in its rocky refuge.
Its presence serves as a reminder of the remarkable adaptations life employs to persist against formidable odds.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物课上的讲解。
你可能会感到惊讶，但植物可以在看似不适宜生存的环境中茁壮成长，例如在高山的岩石缝隙中，忍受持续不断的强风和降至冰点以下的温度。
高山虎耳草就是这样一种植物，是大自然创造力和适应性的象征。
我们来讨论一下，这种不起眼却顽强的植物所具备的非凡适应性，这些适应性使它能在很少有其他植物涉足的地方生长。
高山虎耳草采用独特的生存策略，将自己扎根在岩石缝隙中，以躲避最恶劣的天气。
这些缝隙可以抵御刺骨的寒冷，提供天然隔热，并保存珍贵的水分，而水分在高山气候中往往十分稀缺。
而且还不止这些。
高山虎耳草的叶片有一层特殊的蜡质涂层，可以减少水分流失；在水大多以冰的形式被困住的地区，这是生存所需的关键适应性。
此外，这层蜡还有另一个作用。它能反射植物不需要的多余阳光，从而保护植物免受有害紫外线的伤害。
不过，这种适应能力也存在代价。
高山虎耳草生长缓慢，因此容易受到干扰的影响。
徒步和攀岩等人类活动会威胁其脆弱的栖息地，提醒我们自然的韧性与其易受外部影响之间存在着脆弱的平衡。
所以，如果你在山中看到它，请欣赏并保护高山虎耳草——这种在岩石庇护所中经受风雨的大自然无声幸存者。
它的存在提醒我们，生命会运用非凡的适应性，在极其不利的条件下延续下去。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Furthermore, the wax serves another purpose.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 此外，这层蜡还有另一个作用。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: It reflects excess sunlight that the plant doesn't require, thereby shielding it from damaging ultraviolet rays.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它能反射植物不需要的多余阳光，从而保护植物免受有害紫外线的伤害。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: A trade-off exists in this resilience, however.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 不过，这种适应能力也存在代价。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: The alpine saxifrage's slow growth renders it vulnerable to disturbances.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 高山虎耳草生长缓慢，因此容易受到干扰的影响。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Human activities such as hiking and climbing pose a threat to its delicate habitat, reminding us of the fragile equilibrium between nature's resilience and its susceptibility to external influences.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 徒步和攀岩等人类活动会威胁其脆弱的栖息地，提醒我们自然的韧性与其易受外部影响之间存在着脆弱的平衡。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: So, if you see it in the mountains, appreciate and protect the alpine saxifrage, one of nature's silent survivors, weathering storms in its rocky refuge.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以，如果你在山中看到它，请欣赏并保护高山虎耳草——这种在岩石庇护所中经受风雨的大自然无声幸存者。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Speaker
transcriptSentences.text: Its presence serves as a reminder of the remarkable adaptations life employs to persist against formidable odds.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它的存在提醒我们，生命会运用非凡的适应性，在极其不利的条件下延续下去。

versions.label: Wofo M45
versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
You've probably seen it: writing on a building or some other structure, like when someone tags a wall by spraying a quick signature on it.
Often a person will use spray paint to create graffiti.
Spray paint comes in an aerosol can.
You shake it and then press down on a small dispenser valve while aiming it at a surface you want to paint.
Now, aerosol cans themselves were developed in the 1920s.
Initially, they were used to dispense insect repellent, or bug spray.
Years later, an inventor named Edward Seymour used aerosol cans to spray paint in the 1940s.
This was actually his wife's idea.
Anyway, Seymour was trying to paint radiators efficiently, and spray paint did the job.
Spray paint has a number of everyday uses.
A construction company could use a stencil, a thin sheet with a design cut out of it, to spray-paint their company logo onto their trucks and other equipment.
They can use the same stencil multiple times, so it's less expensive than other, more costly methods to label their equipment.
Then there's street art, like graffiti.
Historically, it's a frowned-upon activity.
But you know, attitudes change.
These days, there are specific spray paints for graffiti artists.
It's quite cool.
They're more expensive, but artists can get a whole range of colors.
Paints are made so that they're less likely to drip down the side of a building, or what have you.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课上的讲解。
你们可能见过这种东西：建筑物或其他结构上的文字，比如有人在墙上喷出一个简短签名作为涂鸦标记。
人们常常会用喷漆创作涂鸦。
喷漆装在气雾罐中。
你先摇匀罐子，然后对准想要喷涂的表面，按下小型分配阀。
气雾罐本身是在20世纪20年代研制出来的。
最初，它们被用来喷洒驱虫剂，也就是杀虫喷雾。
多年以后，一位名叫爱德华·西摩的发明家在20世纪40年代用气雾罐喷漆。
这其实是他妻子的主意。
总之，西摩当时想高效地给暖气片上漆，而喷漆完成了这项工作。
喷漆有许多日常用途。
建筑公司可以使用模板，也就是一张刻有图案的薄片，把公司的标志喷到卡车和其他设备上。
同一个模板可以多次使用，因此比其他成本更高的设备标记方法便宜。
此外，还有像涂鸦这样的街头艺术。
从历史上看，这一直是一种不受认可的活动。
不过，态度是会改变的。
如今，有专门供涂鸦艺术家使用的喷漆。
这相当酷。
这些喷漆更贵，但艺术家可以获得各种各样的颜色。
这些涂料经过特殊制造，不太容易沿着建筑物侧面滴落，或出现类似情况。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a music podcast.
Welcome to Echoes of Culture, where we explore how music tells the story of who we are, where we've been, and where we're going. Today, we're diving into a fascinating idea: how musical composition mirrors the societies from which it emerges. It is more than just sounds. It is a reflection of cultural values, technological progress, and social change. Let's rewind to the Baroque period. Picture the grandeur of European courts, ornate architecture, lavish clothing, and a love for complexity. Composers weren't just writing music. They were crafting sonic tapestries that mirrored the opulence of their time, an elaborate counterpoint, intricate ornamentation. These weren't just stylistic choices. They were reflections of a society that valued structure, hierarchy, and beauty in excess. Fast forward to the 20th century and the musical landscape shifts dramatically. Jazz bursts onto the scene in the United States, and it's not just a new genre. It's a movement. Born in African-American communities, jazz carried the pulse of a society in flux. Its improvisational nature and blending of traditions spoke to a yearning for freedom, innovation, and equality. Jazz became the soundtrack of the civil rights movement, echoing the struggles and triumphs of a people demanding to be heard. And it's not just Western music that tells these stories. In sub-Saharan Africa, traditional music is deeply communal, less about individual display and more about shared experience. The emphasis on group expression is woven into the rhythms, the call and response interaction between performers and audiences, and communal participation.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段音乐播客中的讲解。
欢迎来到《文化回声》，我们探讨音乐如何讲述我们是谁、从哪里来、要到哪里去。今天要谈一个有意思的想法：音乐创作如何映射它所产生的社会。它不只是声音，更是文化价值、技术进步和社会变迁的反映。让我们回到巴洛克时期。想象欧洲宫廷的宏伟、华丽的建筑、奢华的服饰，以及对复杂的热爱。作曲家不只是在写曲子，他们在编织声音织锦，映照那个时代的奢华：精巧的对位、繁复的装饰音。这些不只是风格选择，而是一个看重结构、等级和极度美感的社会的反映。快进到二十世纪，音乐面貌急剧变化。爵士在美国爆发，它不只是新的体裁，更是一场运动。诞生于非裔美国人社区，爵士带着一个变动中社会的脉搏。它的即兴本质和传统融合，表达了对自由、创新和平等的渴望。爵士成为民权运动的配乐，回响着一个要求被听见的群体的挣扎与胜利。讲述这些故事的也不只是西方音乐。在撒哈拉以南非洲，传统音乐深深扎根于共同体，较少展示个人，更多是共同体验。对群体表达的强调织进节奏、表演者与听众的呼应，以及共同参与之中。

versions.transcript: Welcome to Echoes of Culture, where we explore how music tells the story of who we are, where we've been, and where we're going. Today, we're diving into a fascinating idea: how musical composition mirrors the societies from which it emerges. Music is more than just sounds. It is a reflection of cultural values, technological progress, and social change. Let's rewind to the Baroque period. Picture the grandeur of European courts, ornate architecture, lavish clothing, and a love for complexity. Composers weren't just writing music. They were crafting sonic tapestries that mirrored the opulence of their time: elaborate counterpoint, intricate ornamentation. These weren't just stylistic choices. They were reflections of a society that valued structure, hierarchy, and beauty in excess. Fast forward to the 20th century, and the musical landscape shifts dramatically. Jazz bursts onto the scene in the United States. And it's not just a new genre. It's a movement. Born in African American communities, jazz carried the pulse of a society in flux. Its improvisation, syncopation, and call and response patterns expressed freedom, resilience, and social change. Jazz became connected with broader struggles for identity and equality. In many cultures in sub Saharan Africa, music also shows how deeply sound can reflect social life. Rhythm, repetition, and communal performance often place the group at the center rather than a single isolated performer. Music is woven into ceremonies, storytelling, work, and community gatherings. So when we study musical composition, we are also studying the values and structures of the cultures that produce it.
versions.transcriptZh: 欢迎收听《文化回响》，在这里我们探索音乐如何讲述关于我们是谁、我们曾去过哪里以及我们将走向何方的故事。 今天，我们将深入探讨一个迷人的观点：音乐创作如何映射出它所诞生的社会。 音乐不仅仅是声音。 它是文化价值、技术进步和社会变革的反映。 让我们回到巴洛克时期。 想象一下欧洲宫廷的宏伟、华丽的建筑、奢侈的服饰以及对复杂性的热爱。 作曲家们不仅仅是在谱写音乐。 他们正在精心编制映射时代华丽感的声学织锦：复杂的复调对位，精致的装饰音。 这些不仅仅是风格上的选择。 它们反映了一个重视结构、等级制度和极致美感的社会。 快进到20世纪，音乐版图发生了巨大的变化。 爵士乐在美国舞台上爆发式兴起。 它不仅仅是一种新的流派。 它是一个运动。 爵士乐诞生于非裔美国人社区，承载着一个处于变迁中的社会脉搏。 它的即兴创作、切分音以及呼应模式表达了自由、韧性和社会变革。 爵士乐与更广泛的追求身份认同和平等的斗争联系在了一起。 在撒哈拉以南非洲的许多文化中，音乐也展示了声音如何深刻地反映社会生活。 节奏、重复和集体表演通常将群体置于中心，而不是单一孤立的表演者。 音乐交织在仪式、故事叙说、劳动和社区聚会之中。 因此，当我们研究音乐创作时，我们也在研究产生它的文化的价值观和结构。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a biology class.
About 66 million years ago, a catastrophic event wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs. This mass extinction didn't just change animal life, it transformed plant life too. Before the extinction, giant plant-eating dinosaurs like sauropods acted as ecosystem engineers. Their enormous size gave them the power to reshape landscapes. They trampled vegetation, knocked down trees, and even created open clearings as they moved across the land. These disturbances kept forests open, allowing sunlight to flood the ground. In that world, seeds were small, and fruits were rare. Why small? Because abundant light favoured rapid germination. Tiny seeds sprouted quickly without needing large energy reserves. Producing small seeds was also energy efficient for plants, enabling them to make thousands of seeds and spread widely, often by wind. When dinosaurs disappeared, forests rebounded and became dense and shady. With less light on the forest floor, plants faced intense competition. Larger seeds had an advantage because they stored more energy for seedlings to push through low-light conditions. But these heavier seeds couldn't travel far by wind, creating a new challenge. The solution? Fleshy fruits. By evolving sweet, colorful coverings, plants attracted small mammals and birds, survivors of the extinction who ate the fruits and carried seeds across vast areas. This animal-assisted dispersal replaced wind as the main strategy. So the extinction of the dinosaurs set the stage for the world of apples, berries and bananas we enjoy today.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段生物课上的讲解。
大约六千六百万年前，一场灾难性事件消灭了非鸟类恐龙。这场大灭绝不只改变了动物，也改变了植物。灭绝之前，像蜥脚类这样的巨型植食恐龙扮演着生态系统工程师的角色。巨大体型让它们能重塑地貌：踩踏植被、推倒树木，移动时还能开辟空地。这些扰动让森林保持开阔，阳光得以照到地面。在那个世界里，种子很小，果实很少。为什么小？因为充足的光照有利于快速发芽。小种子不必储存大量能量就能很快萌发。对植物来说，结小种子也更节省能量，可以一次结出成千上万颗，并常常靠风传播。恐龙消失后，森林恢复并变得浓密阴暗。林下光线减少，植物竞争加剧。较大的种子更有优势，因为它们储存了更多能量，帮助幼苗在低光环境中生长。但这些更重的种子无法靠风走远，于是出现了新问题。解决办法是什么？肉质果实。植物进化出甜美、色彩鲜艳的外皮，吸引大灭绝后存活下来的小型哺乳动物和鸟类；它们吃下果实，把种子带到很远的地方。这种借助动物的传播取代风，成为主要策略。所以恐龙的灭绝，铺垫出我们今天所享用的苹果、浆果和香蕉的世界。

transcriptSentences.text: Why small?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 为什么小？

transcriptSentences.text: Because abundant light favoured rapid germination.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 因为充足的光照有利于快速发芽。

transcriptSentences.text: Tiny seeds sprouted quickly without needing large energy reserves.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 小种子不必储存大量能量就能很快萌发。

transcriptSentences.text: Producing small seeds was also energy efficient for plants, enabling them to make thousands of seeds and spread widely, often by wind.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 对植物来说，结小种子也更节省能量，可以一次结出成千上万颗，并常常靠风传播。

transcriptSentences.text: When dinosaurs disappeared, forests rebounded and became dense and shady.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 恐龙消失后，森林恢复并变得浓密阴暗。

transcriptSentences.text: With less light on the forest floor, plants faced intense competition.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 林下光线减少，植物竞争加剧。

transcriptSentences.text: Larger seeds had an advantage because they stored more energy for seedlings to push through low-light conditions.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 较大的种子更有优势，因为它们储存了更多能量，帮助幼苗在低光环境中生长。

transcriptSentences.text: But these heavier seeds couldn't travel far by wind, creating a new challenge.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但这些更重的种子无法靠风走远，于是出现了新问题。

transcriptSentences.text: The solution?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 解决办法是什么？

transcriptSentences.text: Fleshy fruits.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 肉质果实。

transcriptSentences.text: By evolving sweet, colorful coverings, plants attracted small mammals and birds, survivors of the extinction who ate the fruits and carried seeds across vast areas.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 植物进化出甜美、色彩鲜艳的外皮，吸引大灭绝后存活下来的小型哺乳动物和鸟类；它们吃下果实，把种子带到很远的地方。

transcriptSentences.text: This animal-assisted dispersal replaced wind as the main strategy.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这种借助动物的传播取代风，成为主要策略。

transcriptSentences.text: So the extinction of the dinosaurs set the stage for the world of apples, berries and bananas we enjoy today.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以恐龙的灭绝，铺垫出我们今天所享用的苹果、浆果和香蕉的世界。

questions.promptText: What is the main focus of the talk?
questions.promptTextZh: 这段讲解的主要焦点是什么？

choices.label: How birds and small mammals adapted to new forest conditions
choices.labelZh: 鸟类和小型哺乳动物如何适应新的森林环境
choices.explanationZh: 错误。鸟类和小型哺乳动物是传播种子的媒介，不是本讲的主线。

choices.label: How some dinosaurs evolved into plant-eaters
choices.labelZh: 一些恐龙如何演化成植食动物
choices.explanationZh: 错误。蜥脚类在灭绝前已经是植食恐龙，没有讲它们如何演化成植食者。

choices.label: Why mammals became dominant after the dinosaur extinction
choices.labelZh: 恐龙灭绝后哺乳动物为何占据优势
choices.explanationZh: 错误。没有解释哺乳动物为何成为优势类群。

choices.label: How the extinction of dinosaurs influenced plant evolution
choices.labelZh: 恐龙灭绝如何影响了植物演化
choices.explanationZh: 正确。全篇把恐龙消失与森林变密、种子变大、肉质果实出现连在一起。

questions.promptText: According to the speaker, what enabled dinosaurs to act as "ecosystem engineers"?
questions.promptTextZh: 根据说话者的说法，恐龙凭什么能充当“生态系统工程师”？

choices.label: Their massive size
choices.labelZh: 它们巨大的体型
choices.explanationZh: 正确。说话者说巨大体型让它们能重塑地貌。

choices.label: Their specialized diets
choices.labelZh: 它们特殊的食性
choices.explanationZh: 错误。提到植食只是身份，不是工程师作用的原因。

choices.label: Their teeth and digestive systems
choices.labelZh: 它们的牙齿和消化系统
choices.explanationZh: 错误。没有谈牙齿或消化系统。

choices.label: Their large energy reserves
choices.labelZh: 它们大量的能量储备
choices.explanationZh: 错误。大量能量储备说的是后来的大种子，不是恐龙。

questions.promptText: What major change occurred in forests after the dinosaurs disappeared?
questions.promptTextZh: 恐龙消失后，森林发生了什么重大变化？

choices.label: Forests became more open and sunny
choices.labelZh: 森林变得更开阔、更明亮
choices.explanationZh: 错误。开阔向阳是恐龙还在时的状态。

choices.label: Forests died and were replaced by grasslands
choices.labelZh: 森林消亡，被草原取代
choices.explanationZh: 错误。没有说森林被草原取代。

choices.label: Forests became dense and shady
choices.labelZh: 森林变得浓密阴暗
choices.explanationZh: 正确。恐龙消失后森林恢复，变得浓密阴暗。

choices.label: Forest trees began producing more seeds
choices.labelZh: 林木开始结出更多种子
choices.explanationZh: 错误。变化是种子变大并靠果实传播，不是简单结更多种子。

questions.promptText: What is the speaker explaining when he points out that large seeds cannot be easily spread by wind?
questions.promptTextZh: 说话者指出大种子不易被风传播时，是在解释什么？

choices.label: Why some trees evolved to produce fleshy fruits
choices.labelZh: 为什么有些树进化出肉质果实
choices.explanationZh: 正确。大种子走不远带来新难题，解决办法是进化出吸引动物的肉质果实。

choices.label: Why large seeds need a lot of energy
choices.labelZh: 为什么大种子需要很多能量
choices.explanationZh: 错误。大种子储存能量是为了在低光下生长，不是这段“不能靠风传播”所解释的点。

choices.label: Why dinosaurs and some tall tree species became extinct around the same time
choices.labelZh: 为什么恐龙和一些高大树种大约同时灭绝
choices.explanationZh: 错误。没有说高大树种与恐龙同时灭绝。

choices.label: Why large seeds need to sprout quickly in order to survive
choices.labelZh: 为什么大种子必须快速发芽才能存活
choices.explanationZh: 错误。需要快速发芽的是恐龙时代的小种子。

versions.transcript:
Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.
Honey bees are social insects, forming highly organized colonies where teamwork is essential. Inside a hive, most bees are workers, but different workers have different jobs. For example, some specialize in maintaining the hive, while others head out to forage for food like nectar and pollen.

Now, researchers wanted to know if forager bees shared their workload evenly among themselves, or did some work harder than others? To find out, they tagged thousands of foragers with tiny microtransponders. Think of it like giving each bee its own identification badge. And they tracked every trip in and out of the hive.

The results were surprising. About 20% of the forager bees made more than half of all the trips. These harder-working forager bees, called elite foragers, were foraging nonstop, while many others spent most of their time inside the hive.

Interesting, right? But the researchers also wanted to know whether or not this hard-working behavior was an intrinsic, permanent characteristic. To find out, the scientists ran a second experiment. They removed most of the elite foragers from the hive. And what happened? Initially, overall foraging activity dropped, which makes sense. But a day later, foragers that had been relatively inactive suddenly stepped up and started foraging like crazy. The colony bounced back quickly.

Apparently, those less active foragers functioned like a reserve workforce, with each bee monitoring the colony's needs and adjusting its activity level accordingly. It's a wonderful example of flexibility, with individual bees working in concert to ensure the hive's survival.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听生物学课上的一段讲座。
蜜蜂是社会性昆虫，会组成高度组织化的蜂群，团队合作至关重要。在蜂巢里，大多数蜜蜂是工蜂，但不同工蜂有不同工作。例如，有些专门维护蜂巢，另一些则外出觅食，采集花蜜和花粉。
研究人员想知道：觅食蜂之间的工作量是否平均分担，还是有些蜜蜂比别的更卖力？为了弄清楚，他们给成千上万只觅食蜂贴上了微小的微型应答器。可以把它想成给每只蜜蜂发了一张身份牌。然后他们追踪了每只蜜蜂进出蜂巢的每一次出行。
结果出人意料。大约20%的觅食蜂完成了全部出行的一半以上。这些更卖力的觅食蜂被称为精英觅食蜂，它们几乎不停地外出觅食，而许多其他蜜蜂大部分时间都待在巢里。
很有意思，对吧？但研究人员还想知道，这种卖力行为是不是一种内在、固定的特质。于是他们做了第二个实验：把大多数精英觅食蜂从蜂巢里拿走。结果怎样？一开始，整体觅食活动下降了，这说得通。但一天之后，原先相对不活跃的觅食蜂突然加码，开始拼命觅食。蜂群很快就恢复了。
显然，那些不太活跃的觅食蜂就像一支后备劳动力，每只蜜蜂都会监测蜂群的需求，并相应调整自己的活动水平。这是灵活性的绝佳例子：个体蜜蜂协同工作，确保蜂巢生存。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
Before we begin, here's a little background. Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian artist and inventor who lived during the Renaissance, a period of renewed interest in science, art, and human knowledge. He is best known for paintings such as the Mona Lisa, but he also studied anatomy, engineering, and mechanics, often combining these interests in his work.

And today, we'll talk about one of his lesser-known works, his design of a robot. In 1495, Leonardo designed what we now call Leonardo's Robot, or the Mechanical Knight. So, to be clear, this was long before the term robot entered our vocabulary.

Leonardo was fascinated with human anatomy, not really surprising for a painter. And this fascination directly influenced his robotic design, a synthesis of his varied interests. Leonardo sketched an intricate, human-like robot that would mimic human actions. The knight was meant to be wearing armour, and was designed to move its arms, raise its visor, and even hug a person.

This knight might not have been built during Leonardo's lifetime, but the designs highlight mechanical understanding that was remarkable for the period. They reveal an in-depth understanding of gears, pulleys, principles of weight distribution.

These sketches made by Leonardo were actually rediscovered in the 1950s by a Leonardo scholar. This scholar studied these sketches, but it wasn't until 2002 that the most complete physical reconstruction of the robot was made. This robot was able to walk and wave, an incredible feat considering how long ago Leonardo created his sketches.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课上的讲解。
在开始之前，先补充一点背景。列奥纳多·达·芬奇是文艺复兴时期的意大利艺术家和发明家。文艺复兴是科学、艺术和人类知识重新受到重视的时期。他最著名的是《蒙娜丽莎》这类画作，但他也研究解剖学、工程学和机械学，并常常把这些兴趣结合到作品中。
今天我们要讲的是他较不为人所知的一项作品：机器人设计。1495年，达·芬奇设计了我们现在所说的“达·芬奇机器人”，或称机械骑士。需要说明的是，这远早于“机器人”这个词进入我们的词汇。
达·芬奇对人体解剖非常着迷，对一位画家来说这并不奇怪。而这种着迷直接影响了他的机器人设计，把多种兴趣综合在一起。他画出了一个结构精密、外形像人的机器人，能够模仿人类动作。这个骑士要穿铠甲，并能活动手臂、掀起面甲，甚至拥抱一个人。
这个骑士未必在达·芬奇生前就被造出来，但这些设计显示出当时相当出色的机械理解。它们体现了对齿轮、滑轮和重量分布原理的深入把握。
达·芬奇的这些草图实际上是在20世纪50年代被一位达·芬奇研究者重新发现的。这位学者研究了这些草图，但直到2002年，才做出了最完整的实体复原。这个机器人能够行走和挥手，考虑到达·芬奇画出草图是那么久以前，这真是了不起的成就。

transcriptSentences.text: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian artist and inventor who lived during the Renaissance, a period of renewed interest in science, art, and human knowledge.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 列奥纳多·达·芬奇是文艺复兴时期的意大利艺术家和发明家。文艺复兴是科学、艺术和人类知识重新受到重视的时期。

transcriptSentences.text: He is best known for paintings such as the Mona Lisa, but he also studied anatomy, engineering, and mechanics, often combining these interests in his work.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他最著名的是《蒙娜丽莎》这类画作，但他也研究解剖学、工程学和机械学，并常常把这些兴趣结合到作品中。

transcriptSentences.text: And today, we'll talk about one of his lesser-known works, his design of a robot.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 今天我们要讲的是他较不为人所知的一项作品：机器人设计。

transcriptSentences.text: In 1495, Leonardo designed what we now call Leonardo's Robot, or the Mechanical Knight.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 一四九五年，达·芬奇设计了我们现在所说的“达·芬奇机器人”，或称机械骑士。

transcriptSentences.text: So, to be clear, this was long before the term robot entered our vocabulary.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 需要说明的是，这远早于“机器人”这个词进入我们的词汇。

transcriptSentences.text: Leonardo was fascinated with human anatomy, not really surprising for a painter.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 达·芬奇对人体解剖非常着迷，对一位画家来说这并不奇怪。

transcriptSentences.text: And this fascination directly influenced his robotic design, a synthesis of his varied interests.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 而这种着迷直接影响了他的机器人设计，把多种兴趣综合在一起。

transcriptSentences.text: Leonardo sketched an intricate, human-like robot that would mimic human actions.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他画出了一个结构精密、外形像人的机器人，能够模仿人类动作。

transcriptSentences.text: The knight was meant to be wearing armour, and was designed to move its arms, raise its visor, and even hug a person.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这个骑士要穿铠甲，并能活动手臂、掀起面甲，甚至拥抱一个人。

transcriptSentences.text: This knight might not have been built during Leonardo's lifetime, but the designs highlight mechanical understanding that was remarkable for the period.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这个骑士未必在达·芬奇生前就被造出来，但这些设计显示出当时相当出色的机械理解。

transcriptSentences.text: They reveal an in-depth understanding of gears, pulleys, principles of weight distribution.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它们体现了对齿轮、滑轮和重量分布原理的深入把握。

transcriptSentences.text: These sketches made by Leonardo were actually rediscovered in the 1950s by a Leonardo scholar.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 达·芬奇的这些草图实际上是在二十世纪五十年代被一位达·芬奇研究者重新发现的。

transcriptSentences.text: This scholar studied these sketches, but it wasn't until 2002 that the most complete physical reconstruction of the robot was made.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这位学者研究了这些草图，但直到二〇〇二年，才做出了最完整的实体复原。

transcriptSentences.text: This robot was able to walk and wave, an incredible feat considering how long ago Leonardo created his sketches.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这个机器人能够行走和挥手，考虑到达·芬奇画出草图是那么久以前，这真是了不起的成就。
