versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on a cultural studies podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a cultural studies podcast.
Okay, in Thailand, there's a city called Lopburi. Lopburi is one of the oldest cities in Thailand. Lots of ancient sites, ruins, etc. Now, Lopburi is also inhabited by free-roaming monkeys, long-tailed macaques specifically, many of whom live in the ruins of an ancient temple. And every year, there's a celebration in Lopburi for them, called the Monkey Buffet Festival.

In the week before the Monkey Buffet Festival, locals in Lopburi hand out so-called invitations to the monkeys, along with a cashew as a snack for them. Now, these monkeys are very intelligent. You might not think they understand the invitation or what it's for, but who knows? The festival happens each year, so it wouldn't surprise me if they remember the tradition and what comes next.

So, what does come next? The Monkey Buffet Festival itself starts with dance performances at the temple ruins where the monkeys live. Human dancers dress in monkey costumes and perform—entertaining for the locals and tourists watching, no doubt. But the real purpose is to get the monkeys' attention. And it works. Thousands of monkeys come into the area.

That's when the buffet begins. People have placed stacks of pineapples, bananas, watermelons—thousands of kilograms of fruit—on large tables and pyramids, almost like a fruit buffet in a, well, a luxury hotel. The monkeys jump into the feast with enthusiasm. It's a way to thank them for helping attract tourists to the city.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听文化研究播客中的一段讲解。
好的，在泰国有一座名叫华富里的城市。华富里是泰国最古老的城市之一，有许多古迹、遗址等。华富里还有许多自由活动的猴子，具体来说是长尾猕猴，其中很多生活在一座古寺庙的遗址中。当地每年都会为它们举行庆祝活动，叫作“猴子自助餐节”。
猴子自助餐节前一周，华富里居民会向猴子发出所谓的“邀请函”，同时给它们一颗腰果作为零食。这些猴子非常聪明。你也许觉得它们不明白邀请函是什么、有什么用，但谁知道呢？这个节日每年都会举办，所以如果它们记得这个传统以及接下来会发生什么，我一点也不会惊讶。
那么，接下来会发生什么？猴子自助餐节先在猴子生活的寺庙遗址举行舞蹈表演。人类舞者穿上猴子服装表演，毫无疑问也会给现场居民和游客带来娱乐，但真正的目的是吸引猴子的注意。这个办法确实有效，成千上万只猴子会来到这一带。
随后，自助餐开始。人们把一堆堆菠萝、香蕉和西瓜——总计数千公斤的水果——摆在大桌子和金字塔形架子上，看起来几乎像豪华酒店里的水果自助餐。猴子们兴高采烈地冲进这场盛宴。这是人们感谢猴子帮助这座城市吸引游客的一种方式。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.
For your group assignment next week, I've asked you to document your individual contributions. Some of you asked me why. The reason isn't only that I want to give everyone a fair grade. The main reason is actually rooted in psychology.

In the late 1800s, a French agricultural engineer named Max Ringelmann conducted a simple experiment. He asked people to pull on a rope, first alone, and then in groups. What he found was surprising. When people pulled in groups, the total force was less than the sum of individual efforts when pulling alone. In other words, people weren't pulling their weight when others were involved. This effect is called social loafing.

Its existence was confirmed in later research. In a study in the late 1970s, researchers asked participants to cheer as loudly as they could, both alone and in groups. And individuals in groups made less noise per person than when cheering alone.

But here's the good news. Social loafing often has a solution. In a study in the 1990s, participants were asked to brainstorm uses for a common object, like a brick, under two situations. In one situation, participants worked in groups, but were told their ideas would be individually identified and evaluated. In another situation, ideas were pooled anonymously. The result? When people knew their contributions would be linked to them personally, they generated higher-quality responses. This shows that accountability and visibility can significantly decrease loafing.

So basically, documenting your individual work for your upcoming group assignment will likely improve your overall project results.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段心理学课上的讲解。
下周的小组作业，我要求你们记录自己各自做出的贡献。有些同学问我为什么。原因不只是我想给每个人一个公平的成绩，主要原因其实来自心理学。
19世纪末，一位名叫马克斯·林格尔曼的法国农业工程师做了一个简单实验。他让人们先独自拉绳子，再以小组形式拉绳子。结果出人意料：人们集体拉绳时产生的总力量，小于每个人单独拉绳时力量的总和。换句话说，有其他人在场时，人们并没有完全尽到自己的那份力。这种效应叫作“社会惰化”。
后来的研究证实了这种现象。20世纪70年代末的一项研究让参与者分别在独自和集体两种情况下尽可能大声地欢呼。结果，以小组形式欢呼时，平均到每个人发出的声音比独自欢呼时更小。
不过，好消息是社会惰化往往有解决办法。20世纪90年代的一项研究让参与者在两种情况下集思广益，想出砖块之类普通物品的用途。一种情况下，参与者以小组形式工作，但被告知每个人的想法都会被单独标明并接受评价；另一种情况下，所有想法匿名汇总。结果如何？当人们知道自己的贡献会与本人对应时，他们给出的答案质量更高。这说明，责任明确、贡献可见能够显著减少社会惰化。
所以，简单来说，记录你在即将进行的小组作业中各自完成的工作，很可能会改善整个项目的成果。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a history class.
You may be familiar with Roman numerals, where the capital letter I means one, the letter X means ten, and so on. They were used in Europe until around the sixteenth century, when they were gradually replaced by the Arabic numerals we use today. We typically say Arabic numerals, but it would be more precise to call them Hindu-Arabic numerals or Indo-Arabic numerals. While Arab mathematicians did bring this numeral system to Europe, it actually originated in India. So, what do Arabic numerals offer that Roman numerals do not? For one thing, Arabic numerals are a place-value system. Place value means that a symbol's value changes depending on its place within a number. Consider the number five. In fifty, or five-zero, it is in the tens place, whereas in five hundred, or five-zero-zero, it is in the hundreds place. In that sense, one of the fives is worth more than the other. In the Roman system, however, a symbol's value doesn't change. This is why Arabic numerals are generally more efficient for handling large numbers. The Arabic system also introduced the idea of zero. We might not think about it much today, but it was a big breakthrough back then. Without the concept of zero, there'd be no advanced mathematics. versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on an astronomy podcast.
When I was growing up, Pluto was known as the ninth planet in our solar system. Alas, Pluto was demoted to dwarf-planet status in 2006, and not only because it's so small, maybe half the width of the United States. It's mainly because in 2006, it was decided that planets had to meet three criteria. They had to orbit the Sun and be round in shape. Check and check. But they also had to be the main object in their orbit. Which, well, Pluto is in the Kuiper Belt. The Kuiper Belt contains many other bodies that orbit the Sun, so Pluto lost its planet status as a result. Many scientists dismissed Pluto as just a ball of ice anyway. However, about ten years later, the New Horizons spacecraft sent back new images and data showing that Pluto is far more complex than previously thought. We're talking volcanoes and dunes. I mean, get this: Pluto has a deep basin with three types of ice, and New Horizons' images suggest there's convection in the basin of ice. With convection, warmer ice rises to the surface, then cools and sinks at the edge of the basin. So the surface is continuously rejuvenating, renewing itself. Moreover, under the basin of ice there may be something astonishing: a saltwater ocean. Life could exist there. This means many neighboring bodies in the Kuiper Belt could also have oceans and potentially be habitable.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段天文学播客中的讲解。
我小时候，冥王星被认为是太阳系的第九颗行星。遗憾的是，2006年冥王星被降为矮行星，而且不只是因为它很小——宽度大约只有美国的一半。主要原因是，2006年人们确定行星必须满足三项标准：必须绕太阳运行，并且形状近似球形。冥王星这两项都符合。但行星还必须是其轨道上的主要天体。问题在于，冥王星位于柯伊伯带，那里还有许多绕太阳运行的其他天体，因此冥王星失去了行星地位。许多科学家原本也只把它看成一个冰球。然而大约十年后，“新视野号”探测器传回的新图像和数据表明，冥王星远比原先想象的复杂，上面有火山和沙丘。更令人惊讶的是，冥王星有一个包含三种冰的深盆地，“新视野号”的图像显示冰盆中存在对流：较暖的冰上升到表面，冷却后又在盆地边缘下沉，因此表面会不断更新。此外，冰盆下方还可能存在一个咸水海洋，那里甚至可能有生命。这意味着柯伊伯带中的许多邻近天体也可能拥有海洋，并具有适宜生命存在的条件。

transcriptSentences.textZh: 遗憾的是，二〇〇六年冥王星被降为矮行星，而且不只是因为它很小——宽度大约只有美国的一半。

transcriptSentences.text: It's mainly because in 2006, it was decided that planets had to meet three criteria.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 主要原因是，二〇〇六年人们确定行星必须满足三项标准。

transcriptSentences.text: They had to orbit the Sun and be round in shape.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 必须绕太阳运行，并且形状近似球形。

transcriptSentences.text: Check and check.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这两项都符合。

transcriptSentences.text: But they also had to be the main object in their orbit.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但行星还必须是其轨道上的主要天体。

transcriptSentences.text: Which, well, Pluto is in the Kuiper Belt.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 问题在于，冥王星位于柯伊伯带。

transcriptSentences.text: The Kuiper Belt contains many other bodies that orbit the Sun, so Pluto lost its planet status as a result.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 那里还有许多绕太阳运行的其他天体，因此冥王星失去了行星地位。

transcriptSentences.text: Many scientists dismissed Pluto as just a ball of ice anyway.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 许多科学家原本也只把它看成一个冰球。

transcriptSentences.text: However, about ten years later, the New Horizons spacecraft sent back new images and data showing that Pluto is far more complex than previously thought.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 然而大约十年后，“新视野号”探测器传回的新图像和数据表明，冥王星远比原先想象的复杂。

transcriptSentences.text: We're talking volcanoes and dunes.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 上面有火山和沙丘。

transcriptSentences.text: I mean, get this: Pluto has a deep basin with three types of ice, and New Horizons' images suggest there's convection in the basin of ice.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 更令人惊讶的是，冥王星有一个包含三种冰的深盆地，“新视野号”的图像显示冰盆中存在对流。

transcriptSentences.text: With convection, warmer ice rises to the surface, then cools and sinks at the edge of the basin.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 对流时，较暖的冰上升到表面，冷却后又在盆地边缘下沉。

transcriptSentences.text: So the surface is continuously rejuvenating, renewing itself.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 因此表面会不断更新、自我更新。

transcriptSentences.text: Moreover, under the basin of ice there may be something astonishing: a saltwater ocean.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 此外，冰盆下方还可能存在一个令人惊讶的东西：咸水海洋。

transcriptSentences.text: Life could exist there.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 那里甚至可能有生命。

transcriptSentences.text: This means many neighboring bodies in the Kuiper Belt could also have oceans and potentially be habitable.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这意味着柯伊伯带中的许多邻近天体也可能拥有海洋，并具有适宜生命存在的条件。

choices.labelZh: 为了解释冥王星的地位为什么发生变化
choices.explanationZh: 正确。冥王星位于拥有许多其他天体的柯伊伯带，无法成为轨道上的主要天体，因此被降为矮行星。

choices.label: To illustrate Pluto's size
choices.labelZh: 为了说明冥王星的大小
choices.explanationZh: 错误。大小只作为背景信息出现，柯伊伯带并不是用来说明冥王星尺寸的。

choices.label: To emphasize how far Pluto is from the Sun
choices.labelZh: 为了强调冥王星离太阳有多远
choices.explanationZh: 错误。讲座没有用柯伊伯带强调日距，重点是轨道区域内还有许多其他天体。

choices.label: To make a point about Pluto's shape
choices.labelZh: 为了说明冥王星的形状
choices.explanationZh: 错误。冥王星呈球形且已满足形状标准，柯伊伯带解释的是第三项轨道标准。

questions.promptText: How did new data change scientists' understanding of Pluto?

choices.label: It has a longer orbit than previously thought.

choices.explanationZh: 错误。新数据讨论的是地表和内部特征，没有修正其轨道长度。

choices.label: It has a wider variety of features than previously thought.

choices.explanationZh: 正确。“新视野号”发现火山、沙丘、多种冰和对流，说明冥王星比原先想象的复杂得多。

choices.explanationZh: 错误。讲座没有比较冥王星过去与现在的体积。

questions.promptText: What point does the speaker make about convection in Pluto's ice basin?
questions.promptTextZh: 说话者对冥王星冰盆中的对流说明了什么？

choices.explanationZh: 错误。讲座说的是冰下海洋，没有把它解释为表面冰正在融化。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a social sciences class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a social sciences class.
Have you ever wondered why certain urban neighborhoods flourish while others stagnate?
A fascinating theory known as the creative class offers one explanation.
Coined by sociologist Richard Florida, this concept suggests that cities with a high concentration of creative professionals, including artists, scientists, and entrepreneurs, tend to experience more significant economic growth and revitalization.
The idea is that these individuals drive innovation and attract others like them, creating a vibrant dynamic atmosphere.
However, it's important to note that such a transformation isn't without its drawbacks.
When these creative hubs thrive economically, it can inadvertently lead to gentrification.
That is, it can cause rising property values and living costs.
This often displaces long-standing residents who can no longer afford to live in their own neighborhoods.
This process can erode the unique cultural fabric that made the area attractive in the first place.
Despite this, cities continue to pursue the creative class strategy.
They invest in cultural infrastructure, like galleries and performance spaces, to lure creative professionals.
Yet, critics argue that this focus on attracting the creative class might overshadow the needs of other community members, particularly those in lower-income brackets.
It's a delicate balancing act that cities must navigate carefully, fostering economic vitality while ensuring inclusivity and equity.
So, next time you stroll through a bustling urban district filled with lively cafes and art installations, consider the multifaceted dynamics at play that underpin its success.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段社会科学课上的讲解。
你是否想过，为什么某些城市社区蓬勃发展，而另一些则停滞不前？
一个名为“创意阶层”的有趣理论提供了一种解释。
这个概念由社会学家理查德·佛罗里达提出，认为拥有高密度创意专业人士（包括艺术家、科学家和企业家）的城市，往往经历更显著的经济增长和复兴。
其核心思想是，这些个体推动创新并吸引同类人才，从而营造出充满活力的氛围。
然而，值得注意的是，这种转变并非没有弊端。
当这些创意中心经济繁荣时，可能会无意中导致绅士化。
也就是说，它会导致房产价值和生活成本上升。
这往往会迫使那些再也负担不起在自己社区居住的长期居民离开。
这个过程可能会侵蚀最初使该地区具有吸引力的独特文化肌理。
尽管如此，城市仍在继续推行“创意阶层”战略。
它们投资于文化基础设施，如画廊和表演空间，以吸引创意专业人士。
然而，批评者认为，这种对吸引创意阶层的关注可能会掩盖其他社区成员的需求，尤其是那些低收入群体的需求。
这是城市必须谨慎把握的微妙平衡，既要促进经济活力，又要确保包容性和公平性。
因此，下次当你漫步在一个充满热闹咖啡馆和艺术装置的繁华城区时，请思考一下支撑其成功的多方面动态因素。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
When you think of abstract expressionism, you probably imagine colorful, chaotic canvases. Maybe you're familiar with Jackson Pollock, a leader of the movement. But how about Norman Lewis? Probably not. Norman Lewis is associated with abstract expressionism, although he wasn't included in major publications about the movement. Nor did his work sell very well. If you ask me, that's an injustice. Lewis won awards and was well regarded by critics. And so, he wasn't really recognized for his work until after his death in 1979. Lewis' career began in 1930. At that time, his major focus wasn't abstract expressionism, but social realism. Social realism refers to works that draw attention to socio-political issues. Maybe you've seen the painting American Gothic by Grant Wood, the one showing an older man and woman, farmers, standing in front of their home, looking very serious, and the man is holding a pitchfork? Anyway, Norman Lewis' social realist works focused on life in Harlem, New York City, where he lived. It also led him to be a member of a group of fellow black artists called the 306 Group. The 306 Group worked together in Harlem. As Lewis' career went on, around 1950, his work became more abstract. So, it's around 1950 that Lewis began focusing more on beauty and harmony in his art. This is where we get into abstract expressionism. He focused on beauty and harmony in his art, and less on the political side of things as he had earlier. His painting, Migratory Birds, shows that. There's an abstract depiction of birds with delicate white marks and an orange brown background.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听艺术史课上的一段讲解。
说到抽象表现主义，你脑海里大概会浮现色彩斑斓、看起来很混乱的画布。你也许熟悉这个运动的领军人物杰克逊·波洛克。但诺曼·刘易斯呢？大概不熟。诺曼·刘易斯与抽象表现主义有关，不过当时关于这一运动的重要出版物并没有收录他。他的作品也卖得不好。要我说，这不公平。刘易斯得过奖，也受到评论家的认可。因此，直到他 1979 年去世之后，他的作品才真正被承认。刘易斯的职业生涯始于 1930 年。那时，他的主要关注点并不是抽象表现主义，而是社会现实主义。社会现实主义指的是那些把注意力引向社会政治问题的作品。你也许见过格兰特·伍德的画作《美国哥特式》，画面上是一对年长的男女农民，站在自家屋前，神情非常严肃，男人手里还拿着一把干草叉？总之，诺曼·刘易斯的社会现实主义作品聚焦于他生活的纽约哈莱姆区的生活。这也让他加入了一个由黑人艺术家组成的团体，叫做 306 团体。306 团体在哈莱姆一起工作。随着刘易斯事业的推进，大约在 1950 年，他的作品变得更加抽象。所以，大约从 1950 年起，刘易斯开始更关注艺术中的美与和谐。我们由此进入抽象表现主义。他在艺术中更强调美与和谐，而不再像早年那样侧重政治。他的画作《候鸟》就说明了这一点。画面是对鸟的抽象描绘，有纤细的白色笔触，背景则是橙棕色。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Narrator
transcriptSentences.text: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 请听艺术史课上的一段讲解。

transcriptSentences.text: When you think of abstract expressionism, you probably imagine colorful, chaotic canvases.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 说到抽象表现主义，你脑海里大概会浮现色彩斑斓、看起来很混乱的画布。

transcriptSentences.text: Maybe you're familiar with Jackson Pollock, a leader of the movement.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 你也许熟悉这个运动的领军人物杰克逊·波洛克。

transcriptSentences.text: But how about Norman Lewis?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但诺曼·刘易斯呢？

transcriptSentences.text: Probably not.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 大概不熟。

transcriptSentences.text: Norman Lewis is associated with abstract expressionism, although he wasn't included in major publications about the movement.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 诺曼·刘易斯与抽象表现主义有关，不过当时关于这一运动的重要出版物并没有收录他。

transcriptSentences.text: Nor did his work sell very well.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他的作品也卖得不好。

transcriptSentences.text: If you ask me, that's an injustice.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 要我说，这不公平。

transcriptSentences.text: Lewis won awards and was well regarded by critics.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 刘易斯得过奖，也受到评论家的认可。

transcriptSentences.text: And so, he wasn't really recognized for his work until after his death in 1979.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 因此，直到他 1979 年去世之后，他的作品才真正被承认。

transcriptSentences.text: Lewis' career began in 1930.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 刘易斯的职业生涯始于 1930 年。

transcriptSentences.text: At that time, his major focus wasn't abstract expressionism, but social realism.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 那时，他的主要关注点并不是抽象表现主义，而是社会现实主义。

transcriptSentences.text: Social realism refers to works that draw attention to socio-political issues.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 社会现实主义指的是那些把注意力引向社会政治问题的作品。

transcriptSentences.text: Maybe you've seen the painting American Gothic by Grant Wood, the one showing an older man and woman, farmers, standing in front of their home, looking very serious, and the man is holding a pitchfork?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 你也许见过格兰特·伍德的画作《美国哥特式》，画面上是一对年长的男女农民，站在自家屋前，神情非常严肃，男人手里还拿着一把干草叉？

transcriptSentences.text: Anyway, Norman Lewis' social realist works focused on life in Harlem, New York City, where he lived.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 总之，诺曼·刘易斯的社会现实主义作品聚焦于他生活的纽约哈莱姆区的生活。

transcriptSentences.text: It also led him to be a member of a group of fellow black artists called the 306 Group.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这也让他加入了一个由黑人艺术家组成的团体，叫做 306 团体。

transcriptSentences.text: The 306 Group worked together in Harlem.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 306 团体在哈莱姆一起工作。

transcriptSentences.text: As Lewis' career went on, around 1950, his work became more abstract.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 随着刘易斯事业的推进，大约在 1950 年，他的作品变得更加抽象。

transcriptSentences.text: So, it's around 1950 that Lewis began focusing more on beauty and harmony in his art.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 所以，大约从 1950 年起，刘易斯开始更关注艺术中的美与和谐。

transcriptSentences.text: This is where we get into abstract expressionism.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 我们由此进入抽象表现主义。

transcriptSentences.text: He focused on beauty and harmony in his art, and less on the political side of things as he had earlier.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他在艺术中更强调美与和谐，而不再像早年那样侧重政治。

transcriptSentences.text: His painting, Migratory Birds, shows that.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他的画作《候鸟》就说明了这一点。

transcriptSentences.text: There's an abstract depiction of birds with delicate white marks and an orange brown background.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 画面是对鸟的抽象描绘，有纤细的白色笔触，背景则是橙棕色。

choices.explanationZh: 讲者说刘易斯受到评论家认可，失望针对的是市场和主流出版物的忽视，不是评论家。

questions.promptTextZh: 说话人为什么提到一幅名叫《美国哥特式》、画着一对年长男女的作品？

choices.label: To indicate a painting that influenced artists in Harlem
choices.labelZh: 指出一幅影响了哈莱姆艺术家的画作
choices.explanationZh: 没有说这幅画影响了哈莱姆的艺术家。

choices.labelZh: 对比社会现实主义与抽象表现主义
choices.explanationZh: 举这幅画是为了说明什么是社会现实主义，不是拿它直接对比两种风格。

choices.labelZh: 给出社会现实主义作品的一个例子
choices.explanationZh: 讲完社会现实主义的定义后，立刻用《美国哥特式》当大家可能见过的例子。

choices.label: To introduce a sociopolitical issue of Lewis' lifetime
choices.labelZh: 引出刘易斯生活时代的一个社会政治问题
choices.explanationZh: 这幅画被用来举例说明社会现实主义，没有借它讨论刘易斯时代的某个具体议题。

questions.promptText: According to the speaker, what happened around 1950?
questions.promptTextZh: 根据说话人的说法，大约 1950 年发生了什么？

choices.label: Lewis became the leader of the 306 Group.
choices.labelZh: 刘易斯成了 306 团体的领袖。
choices.explanationZh: 只说他是成员，没说 1950 年当上领袖。

choices.label: Lewis began working with other Black artists in New York.
choices.labelZh: 刘易斯开始与纽约的其他黑人艺术家合作。
choices.explanationZh: 加入 306 团体是更早的社会现实主义阶段，不是 1950 年才开始。

choices.labelZh: 刘易斯用《候鸟》来做政治表态。
choices.explanationZh: 《候鸟》被用来说明他转向美与和谐，减少了政治性。

choices.label: Lewis began to focus more on abstract expressionism.
choices.labelZh: 刘易斯开始更多地关注抽象表现主义。
choices.explanationZh: 讲者说大约 1950 年作品更抽象，并开始关注美与和谐，由此进入抽象表现主义。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a history class.
So there's an ancient invention, the Archimedes screw. The Archimedes screw is credited to the Greek mathematician Archimedes in about 250 BCE, although it's possible that, uh, ancient Egyptians were actually using it first. Archimedes might have learned about it from the Egyptians, but we don't really know.

Now, the Archimedes screw isn't something used to, like, assemble a piece of furniture. Picture a much larger screw than one for furniture. Like any screw, it has threads, the continuous ridge that spirals around it. The threads are one long spiral from one end of the screw to the other, okay? And that long screw fits inside the length of a long tube. That's the Archimedes screw. It's used to lift water from a low area up to higher ground. You'd put one end of it down into the low water and the other end up higher at an angle, not straight up and down, but at a more horizontal angle. Then turn it. Water gets into the tube and onto the threads. When you turn the screw, the water is transported upward.

This was an effective way, for example, to get water from rivers or lakes to irrigate fields for crops, an impactful technology in agriculture. Also, there's evidence that in ancient Spain, they used the Archimedes screw to pump water out of mines. Besides Spanish mines, it was used elsewhere to pump water out of ships in antiquity as well, and in wastewater treatment plants even today.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听历史课上的一段讲解。
有一种古代发明，叫阿基米德螺旋泵。一般认为，希腊数学家阿基米德在大约公元前 250 年发明了它。不过，也有可能，呃，古埃及人其实更早就在使用它。阿基米德或许是从埃及人那里了解到这种装置的，但我们并不确切知道。

阿基米德螺旋泵可不是用来组装家具之类东西的螺丝。想象一根比家具螺丝大得多的螺杆。和任何螺丝一样，它有螺纹，也就是环绕它盘旋的连续凸起。这道螺纹形成一条长长的螺旋，从螺杆的一端一直延伸到另一端，明白吗？这根长螺杆沿着一根长管的内部安装。这就是阿基米德螺旋泵。它用来把水从低处提升到较高的地方。使用时，把一端放入低处的水中，另一端斜着抬高；并不是竖直朝上，而是以更接近水平的倾角放置。然后转动它。水会进入管内，落在螺纹上。转动螺杆时，水就会被向上输送。

例如，这是一种从河流或湖泊中取水灌溉农田的有效方法，是一项对农业影响很大的技术。另外，有证据表明，在古代西班牙，人们使用阿基米德螺旋泵排出矿井中的水。除了西班牙的矿井之外，古代其他地方也用它排出船内的积水，甚至到今天，污水处理厂仍在使用它。

questions.promptText: What does the speaker mainly discuss?

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
Paintings can deteriorate over time. Color can gradually be lost and so on. So, let's talk about painting restoration, the ways in which professional conservators bring a painting back to its original glory. The first time I watched a conservator clean a painting, it was really eye-opening. She leaned in with a cotton swab and started moving it across a dark corner like she was erasing pencil marks. At one point she lifted off a thin layer of old varnish. Varnish is the originally transparent coating the artist had applied over the finished painting to protect it. But varnish can brown from collecting dirt over time and so can become less transparent. After the varnish was removed the color under it popped back like someone had turned the lights on. Another part that was super interesting. They sometimes use gels, not liquids, to clean. A gel holds the cleaning agent in place so it stays put. It doesn't soak into cracks or drift into areas you never meant to touch. Think of it as putting the chemistry on a short leash. Now if this sounds slow, it is. But that slowness is the point. Museums used to prize dramatic before and after reveals. But nowadays the goal is more like good editing. Remove what doesn't belong, keep what does. And leave a clear record so the next team can undo or improve what you did.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课上的讲解。
画作会随时间劣化，颜色可能逐渐褪失。那么我们来谈谈绘画修复，也就是专业修复师如何让画作重现原貌。我第一次看修复师清理画作时，印象非常深。她用棉签俯身处理一个暗角，动作像是在擦铅笔痕。有一刻她揭下一层薄薄的旧光油。光油是画家在完稿后涂上的透明保护层。但光油会因积尘变黄，变得不那么透明。光油去掉后，底下的颜色像被人打开了灯一样跳了出来。另一点也很有意思。他们有时用凝胶而不是液体来清洗。凝胶能把清洁剂固定在原处。它不会渗进裂缝，也不会漂到你根本不想碰的区域。可以想成把化学反应用短绳拴住。这听起来慢，确实慢。但慢正是重点。博物馆过去偏爱戏剧性的前后对比。如今的目标更像高明的剪辑：去掉不该留下的，保留该留下的，并留下清晰记录，让下一组人能撤销或改进你的工作。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
Soil fertility doesn't just depend on minerals or fertilizers. It also depends on microbes, especially bacteria that live around plant roots. These microbes break down organic matter and release nutrients that plants can absorb. But for these processes to work well, bacteria often need to act together, not just individually. One way they coordinate their behavior is through quorum sensing, figuring out if there's enough of them around. Bacteria release and detect chemical signals. Think of it like leaving notes on a shared bulletin board. One note doesn't make much difference, but when enough notes accumulate, everyone in the community notices. That's when the group, the bacteria, shift from working alone to coordinated action. An example of this kind of coordination is the formation of biofilms—sticky communities that cling to soil particles or root surfaces. Building biofilms benefits both the microbes and plants, because it improves the microbes' ability to capture and retain nutrients. But building a biofilm is expensive for the bacteria in energy terms, so it's beneficial for them to wait until there's a large enough group before committing. If they start too early, there may not be enough cells to sustain the structure, which would make it a waste of energy. Quorum sensing helps them decide when it's worth pooling effort. And plants can actually influence this system. Roots release chemical compounds that magnify microbial signals. This helps recruit the helpful microbes that the plants need.

请听一段生态学课上的讲解。
土壤肥力不只取决于矿物质或肥料，还取决于微生物，尤其是生活在植物根系周围的细菌。这些微生物分解有机物，释放植物能吸收的养分。但要让这些过程顺利进行，细菌往往需要协同行动，而不是各自为战。它们协调行为的一种方式是群体感应，也就是判断周围同类是否足够多。细菌释放并检测化学信号。可以想象成在共享布告栏上留言。一条留言没什么作用，但当留言足够多时，社区里的每个成员都会注意到。那时，细菌群体就会从单打独斗转向协同行动。这种协同的一个例子是生物膜的形成，也就是附着在土壤颗粒或根表的黏性群落。形成生物膜对微生物和植物都有利，因为它提高了微生物捕获和保存养分的能力。但形成生物膜对细菌来说能耗很高，所以最好等到群体足够大再投入。如果开始得太早，细胞数量可能不足以维持结构，就会浪费能量。群体感应帮助它们判断何时值得合力。而植物其实也能影响这套系统。根系会释放化学物质来放大微生物信号，从而招募植物需要的有益微生物。

transcriptSentences.speaker: Narrator
transcriptSentences.text: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 请听一段生态学课上的讲解。

transcriptSentences.text: Soil fertility doesn't just depend on minerals or fertilizers.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 土壤肥力不只取决于矿物质或肥料。

transcriptSentences.text: It also depends on microbes, especially bacteria that live around plant roots.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它还取决于微生物，尤其是生活在植物根系周围的细菌。

transcriptSentences.text: These microbes break down organic matter and release nutrients that plants can absorb.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这些微生物分解有机物，释放植物能吸收的养分。

transcriptSentences.text: But for these processes to work well, bacteria often need to act together, not just individually.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但要让这些过程顺利进行，细菌往往需要协同行动，而不是各自为战。

transcriptSentences.text: One way they coordinate their behavior is through quorum sensing, figuring out if there's enough of them around.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 它们协调行为的一种方式是群体感应，也就是判断周围同类是否足够多。

transcriptSentences.text: Bacteria release and detect chemical signals.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 细菌释放并检测化学信号。

transcriptSentences.text: Think of it like leaving notes on a shared bulletin board.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 可以想象成在共享布告栏上留言。

transcriptSentences.text: One note doesn't make much difference, but when enough notes accumulate, everyone in the community notices.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 一条留言没什么作用，但当留言足够多时，社区里的每个成员都会注意到。

transcriptSentences.text: That's when the group, the bacteria, shift from working alone to coordinated action.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 那时，细菌群体就会从单打独斗转向协同行动。

transcriptSentences.text: An example of this kind of coordination is the formation of biofilms—sticky communities that cling to soil particles or root surfaces.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这种协同的一个例子是生物膜的形成，也就是附着在土壤颗粒或根表的黏性群落。

transcriptSentences.text: Building biofilms benefits both the microbes and plants, because it improves the microbes' ability to capture and retain nutrients.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 形成生物膜对微生物和植物都有利，因为它提高了微生物捕获和保存养分的能力。

transcriptSentences.text: But building a biofilm is expensive for the bacteria in energy terms, so it's beneficial for them to wait until there's a large enough group before committing.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 但形成生物膜对细菌来说能耗很高，所以最好等到群体足够大再投入。

transcriptSentences.text: If they start too early, there may not be enough cells to sustain the structure, which would make it a waste of energy.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 如果开始得太早，细胞数量可能不足以维持结构，就会浪费能量。

transcriptSentences.text: Quorum sensing helps them decide when it's worth pooling effort.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 群体感应帮助它们判断何时值得合力。

transcriptSentences.text: And plants can actually influence this system.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 而植物其实也能影响这套系统。

transcriptSentences.text: Roots release chemical compounds that magnify microbial signals.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 根系会释放化学物质来放大微生物信号。

transcriptSentences.text: This helps recruit the helpful microbes that the plants need.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这有助于招募植物需要的有益微生物。

choices.labelZh: 它们如何对肥料作出反应

choices.explanationZh: 原文说一条留言没用，但 enough notes accumulate 后大家都会注意到，用来比喻化学信号累积到阈值才触发群体行动。

choices.labelZh: 说明微生物有记忆

choices.explanationZh: 这句讲的是细菌之间，与植物交流在后文根系释放物质处。

choices.labelZh: 指出植物和微生物共享养分
choices.explanationZh: 共享的是布告栏上的信息，不是养分。

questions.promptTextZh: 细菌为什么可能推迟形成生物膜？

choices.label: To save energy
choices.labelZh: 为了节约能量
choices.explanationZh: 原文说 building a biofilm is expensive…in energy terms，太早开始可能浪费能量，所以等到群体够大再做，是为了省能量。

choices.labelZh: 为了收集足够养分
choices.explanationZh: 等待的是细胞数量，不是先攒养分。

choices.labelZh: 吸引有益微生物
choices.explanationZh: 原文 Roots release chemical compounds… This helps recruit the helpful microbes that the plants need，即吸引植物需要的有益菌。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on an architecture podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on an architecture podcast.
The great pyramids in Egypt were basically built by piling one stone on top of another. Many of the stones used to build them contain huge numbers of one specific type of fossil shell. These shells resemble the size and shape of small coins, and the scientific name of the shells reflects this. The organisms that form these shells are called nummulites. That's a word with the same root as the word numismatics, which is the study of money. And coins are money, right? Okay, so considering that these shells, while small, are still large enough to collect in your hand, it may come as a surprise that they were created by a unicellular organism. A creature that consisted of just one single huge cell, not a multicellular organism like clams or oysters. Amazing, right? Large numbers of these shell-making organisms once lived on a tropical seafloor millions of years ago in what's now Egypt. Over time, huge numbers of these shells were buried beneath many additional layers. The weight of the overlying layers compacted the limey sediment closer together until it turned into a solid rock known as limestone. But limestone that was rich in nummulites wasn't suitable for construction in all sections of the pyramids, so other types of stone had to be quarried as well. Okay, next up. Let's look at the pyramid structure and why different kinds of stone were used for different parts.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段建筑播客。
埃及的大金字塔基本上是把石头一层层垒起来建成的。用来建造它们的许多石头里，含有大量某一种特定的化石贝壳。这些贝壳的大小和形状像小硬币，其学名也反映了这一点。形成这些贝壳的生物叫货币虫。这个词和 numismatics（钱币学）同源，而钱币就是钱，对吧？这些贝壳虽然小，却大到能放在手里把玩，所以它们其实由单细胞生物创造，可能让人意外。那种生物只有一个大细胞，不是蛤蜊或牡蛎那样的多细胞生物。很神奇吧？数不清的造壳生物曾生活在数百万年前、如今埃及一带的热带海底。随着时间推移，大量贝壳被埋在更多沉积层之下。上覆地层的重量把灰质沉积压实，最终变成称为石灰岩的坚硬岩石。但富含货币虫的石灰岩并不适合金字塔所有部位的建造，因此还需要开采其他类型的石头。好，接下来我们看看金字塔的结构，以及为什么不同部位要用不同石材。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in a music appreciation class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a music appreciation class.
Have you ever wondered why music has such a strong emotional impact on us? Sometimes it comes from the way our brains respond to what's called dissonance. Dissonance occurs when two or more notes clash. They sound together in a way that creates tension or instability. Imagine hitting two piano keys that are right next to each other. It creates a sound that feels unresolved. Why does this matter? Well, music thrives on the tension between opposites. So dissonance is what creates a sense of unease that begs the solution, to move to harmony. And when that resolution comes, say those two notes resolve into a harmonious chord, it feels like a breath of fresh air. This combination of tension and release forms the emotional push and pull of music. Here's something you might not know though. The use of dissonance hasn't always been welcome. There were long periods in European history during which dissonance in music was considered sinful by the religious authorities at the time. But then, in the 1700s, the German composer Johann Sebastian Bach came along. Bach started using dissonance more dynamically, and it became central to compositions. And today, modern genres like jazz and experimental music rely heavily on the unique emotions dissonance creates. Let's listen to some modern music.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段音乐欣赏课上的讲解。
你是否想过，为什么音乐对我们的情绪影响如此强烈？有时这来自大脑对所谓不协和音的反应。当两个或多个音符冲突时，就产生不协和。它们同时响起，制造出紧张或不稳定感。想象一下，同时按下相邻的两个钢琴键。听起来悬而未决。这为什么重要？因为音乐恰恰建立在对立面的张力之上。不协和音制造出一种不安，逼着我们寻找解决，也就是走向和谐。当解决到来，比如那两个音符落到一个和谐的和弦上，会让人松一口气。紧张与释放的组合，构成了音乐的情绪推拉。不过有一点你可能不知道。不协和音的使用并不一直受欢迎。欧洲历史上有很长时期，宗教当局认为音乐中的不协和是罪恶的。到了十八世纪，德国作曲家约翰·塞巴斯蒂安·巴赫出现。巴赫更动态地使用不协和音，它于是成为作曲的核心。今天，爵士和实验音乐等现代风格，都重度依赖不协和音创造的独特情绪。我们来听一些现代音乐。

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in a film class.
As you know, Hollywood California is associated with movies. Early Hollywood, through the 1920s or so, was the period of silent films, with no recorded dialogue. Maybe you've heard of Charlie Chaplin, a famous silent film star. He was prolific early in the century. Movies remained silent until the first full-length sound film with spoken dialogue throughout was called The Jazz Singer. But that, The Jazz Singer, came out later, not till 1927. One important filmmaker's career spanned the silent film era and later. Her name was Dorothy Arzner. Arzner's career was unusual for a woman at that time. I can think of maybe one other female director who had a long Hollywood career in those days. Well, Dorothy Arzner started out by typing scripts and then editing film. Then, in 1922, she had an opportunity to edit and direct for a silent film called Blood and Sand. It irritates me that she was not credited as an editor or director for Blood and Sand. It's unfair. She made decisions that saved the movie studio thousands of dollars. She deserved acknowledgment. From there, Arzner made about 20 films and was credited for her work. In fact, she was the first woman to direct a sound film. Many of her films deal with, shall we say, unconventional romance stories, unexpected characters meeting, falling in love, getting married. Arzner's films introduced several women actors who would go on to become hugely successful in comedies and dramas themselves.

请听一段电影课上的讲解。
你们都知道，加州好莱坞与电影紧密相连。到二十世纪二十年代前后，早期好莱坞是默片时期，没有录制对白。你们可能听说过查理·卓别林，著名的默片明星。他在本世纪初非常高产。电影一直保持无声，直到第一部从头到尾都有对白的全长有声片《爵士歌手》问世。不过《爵士歌手》出现得更晚，要到一九二七年。有一位重要电影人的生涯横跨默片与后来的有声时代。她就是多萝西·阿兹纳。以当时女性而言，阿兹纳的职业生涯很不寻常。那个年代在好莱坞拥有漫长导演生涯的女性，我能想到的大概只有一位。多萝西·阿兹纳从打字剧本起步，后来剪辑影片。一九二二年，她有机会为默片《血与沙》担任剪辑和导演。让我恼火的是，《血与沙》没有给她剪辑或导演署名。这不公平。她做出的决定为电影公司省下数千美元。她应得认可。此后阿兹纳拍了大约二十部电影，并获得署名。事实上，她是第一位执导有声电影的女性。她的许多影片处理的是，怎么说呢，非传统的爱情故事，意想不到的角色相遇、相爱、结婚。阿兹纳的影片启用了多位女演员，她们后来在喜剧和正剧中都大获成功。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk on a history podcast.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a history podcast.
Have you had a zipper betray you, stuck halfway, misaligned, and suddenly you're negotiating with your jacket like it's got a personality? That kind of failure is annoying, but it's only noticeable because properly functioning zippers are seen as a given. The modest zipper is actually a big deal. When its earliest form was invented in the late 19th century, people weren't super impressed. Hooks and buttons had been around forever, and people thought they worked well enough, and the first versions of the zipper weren't sleek. They were fussy, they jammed. Basically, they malfunctioned much more commonly than they do today. In other words, they weren't a must-have. What made the zipper take off was a new design that was invented by a Swedish-American engineer named Gideon Sundback. Sundback's idea was to create uniform metal teeth. With these teeth, all of the exact same size, the slider could now reliably glide into place in a single motion. The zipper's impact on everyday life has been huge since. Designers of bags and clothes stopped planning around slow or fragile closures. Suitcases could now pack more stuff without being as bulky. Because luggage no longer needed unwieldy straps and buckles. So traveling became more convenient. Outdoor clothing became easier to seal with one hand. That meant you could close a pocket while holding something else. We're now so used to this convenience that we take it for granted.

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk on a social sciences podcast.
So, different cultures around the world have their own sports, right? In some cases, people in many parts of the world enjoy the same sport, like maybe hockey, field hockey or ice hockey. But other sports are quite tied to the roots of a particular area. A city in England called Gloucester is known for its sizable cheese industry. And in Gloucester, um, there's a village, Brockworth. In the village of Brockworth, there's a sport that's an annual tradition involving cheese. Participants stand at the top of a hill, then someone rolls a wheel of cheese down the hill. The participants run down the hill after it, tumbling, sliding, crashing into one another on the way down. This annual cheese rolling competition has taken place at least since the early 1800s. There's no definitive explanation for why it started. Some say its origins were in barrel racing. Barrel racing? I would look more seriously at the fact that this area of England is a major cheese producer, you know? Now, maybe it's a stretch to call cheese rolling a sport. Chasing a wheel of cheese down a hill is a pretty odd activity, but if you think about it, other sports. Is it that much stranger than hitting a ball with a stick, or standing on two sticks and sliding down a mountain covered in snow? These are activities involved in sports that we consider legitimate. Maybe we're just more used to those ones though.

versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an art history class.
When I show students a small bowl by the Native American potter Lucy Lewis, they often say it feels modern, like minimalist almost. Lucy Lewis was a 20th century Native American artist, and her pottery looks contemporary, but it's anchored in traditional Native American techniques. How so? Well, Lewis learned to build clay pots from women in her community. As a kid, Lewis made pottery for tourists, sold to travelers passing through. She found ideas in publications, books, especially a local painting style that dated back to the 11th century. Of traditional black-on-white geometric designs, she saw in book illustrations, and she revived that style. Lewis painted black and white on her plates, bowls, etc. She used fine line work and balanced symmetry to interpret the old designs in a personalized way. As an adult, she became an award-winning artist, but she lived in a remote area in the southwestern United States. Due to her location, she didn't have any contact with museums or art collectors, which, I mean, honestly, sounds liberating to me. She could create designs she wanted and follow her own inspiration without interference. And these days, her pieces are sought after and valuable. Now, people sometimes assume that authenticity means keeping exactly to an old way of doing things, which can be true, but Lewis's work suggests authenticity can be procedural. You honor lineage through method, coil firing, meticulous brush control, while still negotiating new markets and new audiences, honoring your own creativity in the process.
versions.transcriptZh:
请听一段艺术史课上的讲解。
当我给学生看美国原住民陶艺家露西·刘易斯的一只小碗时，他们常说它很现代，几乎像极简主义。露西·刘易斯是二十世纪的美国原住民艺术家，她的陶器看起来很当代，却扎根于传统原住民技艺。怎么讲？刘易斯是从社区里的女性那里学会制陶的。小时候，她做陶器卖给游客，卖给路过的旅行者。她从出版物和书籍中寻找灵感，尤其是一种可追溯到十一世纪的当地绘画风格。她在图书插图里看到传统的黑白几何设计，并复兴了那种风格。刘易斯在盘子、碗等器物上画黑白图案。她用精细线条和均衡对称，以个人化方式诠释古老设计。成年后，她成为获奖艺术家，但住在美国西南部偏远地区。由于位置偏僻，她与博物馆和艺术藏家没有接触。说实话，这在我看来反而令人解放。她可以创作自己想要的图案，追随个人灵感，不受干涉。如今，她的作品备受追捧、价值不菲。人们有时以为，原真性意味着一成不变地沿用旧方法。这当然可以是一种理解，但刘易斯的作品表明，原真性也可以是程序性的。你通过方法传承谱系：盘条烧制、一丝不苟的笔触控制，同时仍在与新市场和新受众协商，并在这一过程中尊重自己的创造力。

versions.mediaTitle: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.
versions.transcript:
Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.
Human societies can be very different from each other. Still, many researchers note that there are certain patterns found worldwide, in one way or another. These are called cultural universals. Generally, cultural universals involve basic needs, like preparing food, and inevitable human experiences, like celebrations for babies being born and rituals related to funerals. An anthropologist named George Murdock first identified cultural universals, like finding food and shelter and using language. This was in the 1940s. One that Murdock identified that I love is actually jokes. They're a worldwide strategy, a way to help people feel unified. Laughter helps ease tense situations, right? Of course, humor varies widely, but still, all societies have jokes of some kind. OK. In 2009, a team of Western researchers traveled to Cameroon, in Africa. There, they asked members of the Mafa people, an indigenous people in Cameroon, to listen to some Western music. The Mafa participants had never heard Western music before. Nevertheless, they identified the emotions that this totally foreign music was intended to convey—happiness, sadness, and fear. So, it seems that another cultural universal was discovered. Now, some theorists focus on understanding a culture based on its own standards, and what makes it unique. This is known as cultural relativism. Cultural relativism can be at odds with the idea of cultural universals. Relativism is less focused on analyzing practices across different cultures, looking for commonalities, more on the specifics of a particular culture.

versions.transcript: How did you wake up this morning? You probably had some kind of alarm. Well, what did people do long ago, in ancient Greece, when people relied on natural indicators like the sun's position for time? One clever solution was the klepsydra, a water clock. This was essentially a container filled with water that drained at a steady rate. The dropping water level marked the passage of time, and at a certain point, it triggered a mechanism to produce sound, effectively serving as an alarm clock. Ingenious, right? Fast forward to the late 19th century, when the industrial age came into full swing. The need for punctuality in factories led to the development of wind up mechanical alarm clocks. These devices, with their recognizable bells, were widely used until the 20th century brought about a significant change: the electric alarm clock. By eliminating the need to wind the clock, these electric models revolutionized how people managed their mornings, offering convenience and accuracy like never before. In the late 20th century, digital technology further transformed our alarm clocks with LED displays and snooze buttons, adding more layers of utility. These devices serve an important function, and our relationship with alarm clocks also reflects cultural evolution. Clocks transitioned from simple timekeepers to indispensable companions in our daily routines, influencing how we perceive time management and punctuality. And if you really want to talk about an indispensable companion in our daily routine, you might have one in your pocket: the mobile phone.

versions.label: Koala 09-13
versions.transcript: We usually think of taste as something that happens only in the mouth, but the dining experience is actually influenced by several senses. What we hear can change how we eat and even how we describe the flavor of food. One factor is tempo. Studies have found that people often eat more quickly when fast music is playing and more slowly when the music has a slower tempo. Eating slowly can give the body more time to register fullness, so slower music may indirectly support healthier eating habits than fast music. Pitch can also influence taste perception. High pitched sounds are often associated with sweetness or lightness, while lower pitched sounds are more often associated with bitterness or heavier flavors. Restaurants and food researchers have experimented with soundtracks designed to emphasize a particular aspect of a food's taste. For example, the food itself might remain exactly the same, but diners may describe it as sweeter when certain high frequency sounds are played. This is sometimes called sonic seasoning. But there is an important criticism of this approach. People do not all respond to music in the same way. Musical preferences, cultural background, previous experiences, and even mood can affect the response. So the same soundtrack may enhance a food for one person and have little effect on another. That makes the results less predictable than a restaurant designer might hope. Still, some experiments have produced interesting effects. In one restaurant study involving seafood, diners heard ocean sounds while eating. The food itself was not changed, but ratings of the dining experience and of some dishes increased. The researchers argued that the ocean sounds created a context that fit the food. The sound encouraged diners to connect what they were eating with the sea. So music and environmental sound do not literally change the chemical composition of food. But they can influence attention, expectations, eating speed, and the way people interpret flavor.

versions.transcript: Cultural diffusion is the transmission of cultural beliefs, practices, and social norms from one group to another. Historically, this phenomenon has unfolded through different channels such as commercial exchange, migratory movements, and, more recently, digital communication. A notable example is the spread of agricultural techniques. Technologies such as irrigation systems from ancient Persia or terrace farming from the Andes gradually spread to neighboring regions. This influenced food production and land use across continents. Similarly, linguistic diffusion has left indelible marks on global communication. The spread of Latin during the Roman Empire laid the foundation for Romance languages. Arabic was carried by traveling traders and scholars to enrich scientific and philosophical vocabularies from Spain to Southeast Asia. Another dimension of cultural diffusion is technological exchange. For example, the wheel was first developed in Mesopotamia, but it revolutionized transportation as it spread across Eurasia. And papermaking, which originated in China, transformed literacy and record keeping after reaching the Islamic world and later Europe. Religious diffusion has also shaped civilizations. Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism have all expanded far beyond their birthplaces through missionary work and trade networks like the Silk Road, though in many cases, religious traditions changed and grew to incorporate local customs. However, cultural diffusion is not always harmonious. The introduction of foreign customs can lead to resistance, especially if it's perceived as a threat to identity or tradition. But despite these kinds of frictions, cultural diffusion is a driving force behind the richness and complexity of human societies.
versions.transcriptZh: 文化扩散是文化信仰、实践和社会规范从一个群体向另一个群体的传播。 从历史上看，这一现象通过不同的渠道展开，如商业交换、迁徙运动，以及最近的数字通信。 一个显著的例子是农业技术的传播。 诸如古波斯的灌溉系统或安第斯山脉的梯田耕作等技术逐渐传播到邻近地区。 这影响了跨大洲的粮食生产和土地利用。 同样，语言扩散也在全球交流中留下了不可磨灭的印记。 罗马帝国时期拉丁语的传播为罗曼语族奠定了基础。 阿拉伯语由旅行商人和学者携带，丰富了从西班牙到东南亚的科学和哲学词汇。 文化扩散的另一个维度是技术交流。 例如，轮子最早在美索不达米亚开发，但随着它在欧亚大陆的传播，它彻底改变了交通运输。 而起源于中国的造纸术，在传入伊斯兰世界及后来的欧洲后，改变了读写能力和记录保存方式。 宗教扩散也塑造了文明。 基督教、伊斯兰教和佛教都通过传教工作和丝绸之路等贸易网络，扩展到远超出其发源地的地区，尽管在许多情况下，宗教传统在演变中融入了当地习俗。 然而，文化扩散并不总是和谐的。 外国习俗的引入可能会导致抵制，特别是如果它被视为对身份或传统的威胁。 但尽管存在这类摩擦，文化扩散仍是人类社会丰富性和复杂性背后的驱动力。

versions.label: Koala 09-05
versions.transcript: One of the most remarkable things about language learning is how much children figure out without anyone explicitly teaching them the rules. A classic demonstration is the Wug Test, developed by psychologist Jean Berko Gleason. In the experiment, young children were shown a picture of an imaginary creature and told, This is a wug. Then they were shown two of the creatures and prompted with a sentence like, Now there are two of them. There are two... Children typically responded, wugs. Why is that important? The children had never heard the word wug before, so they couldn't simply be repeating a memorized plural form. They were applying a grammatical rule to a completely new word. The experiment showed that young children don't learn language only by copying expressions they've already heard. They develop knowledge about the patterns and rules of their language. But learning grammar is only one part of the problem. Babies also have to identify individual words in speech. Written language makes that look easy because spaces separate words. Spoken language doesn't. When adults speak naturally, one word usually flows directly into the next. There are no reliable pauses marking every word boundary. So how do babies begin finding words in this continuous stream of sound? One method researchers use is called the head turn preference procedure. In one set of studies, eight month old babies first heard particular words repeatedly - words they became familiar with. Later, they heard longer passages containing some of those familiar words. Researchers measured how long babies turned their heads toward the sound. The babies listened longer to passages containing the familiar words. That suggests that, by about eight months, infants can recognize at least some recurring word forms even when those forms appear inside continuous speech. Researchers think babies use several kinds of information to do this: sound patterns, stress, and the statistical regularities of which sounds tend to occur together. And this raises a broader question. If infants are tracking patterns, storing sound sequences in memory, and directing attention to useful information, language learning may be closely connected with other developing mental abilities. Next, we'll look at research examining the relationship between language learning and skills such as attention, memory, and pattern recognition.

versions.transcript: Here's a question that sounds simple but actually tells us something important about both chemistry and the environment: why does ice float? Most substances become denser when they change from a liquid to a solid. Their molecules slow down and pack more tightly together. Water is unusual. When liquid water freezes, its molecules arrange themselves into an open crystal structure held together by hydrogen bonds. This structure takes up more space than the same number of molecules occupied in liquid form. In other words, water expands when it freezes. Because the same amount of matter now occupies a larger volume, solid ice is less dense than liquid water. And that's why a piece of ice floats instead of sinking. This unusual property has major consequences in nature. Think about a lake in winter. As temperatures fall, the water at the surface freezes first. Since the ice floats, it forms a layer across the top of the lake. That layer is important for aquatic life. Ice acts as insulation. It slows the loss of heat from the water below, so the entire lake does not freeze solid. Fish and other organisms can continue living in the liquid water beneath the ice. If ice were denser than water and sank, lakes in cold climates could gradually freeze from the bottom upward, making winter survival much more difficult for aquatic organisms. There is another environmental consequence. Ice and snow are relatively bright surfaces, so they reflect a large portion of incoming sunlight. Liquid water is darker and absorbs more solar energy. This difference matters for climate. When large areas of ice melt, darker water or land is exposed. Those surfaces absorb more heat, which can contribute to additional warming and more melting. So a basic molecular property of water has effects that range from the survival of life in a frozen lake to the way Earth's surface absorbs and reflects energy.
versions.transcriptZh: 这里有一个问题，听起来很简单，但实际上它告诉我们一些关于化学和环境的重要信息：为什么冰会浮起来？ 大多数物质从液体变为固体时，密度会变大。 它们的分子减速并更紧密地堆积在一起。 水则不同寻常。 当液态水结冰时，其分子会通过氢键排列成一个开放的晶体结构。 这种结构比相同数量的分子在液态时占据更大的空间。 换句话说，水在结冰时会膨胀。 因为相同量的物质现在占据了更大的体积，所以固态冰的密度比液态水小。 这就是为什么一块冰会浮起来而不是下沉的原因。 这种不寻常的特性在自然界中具有重要的影响。 想想冬天的湖泊。 随着气温下降，湖面上的水首先结冰。 由于冰会浮起来，它在湖面上形成一层。 这一层对水生生物很重要。 冰起到绝缘作用。 它减缓了下方水体热量的散失，因此整个湖泊不会完全冻结。 鱼类和其他生物可以继续生活在冰下的液态水中。 如果冰比水密度大并下沉，那么寒冷气候下的湖泊可能会从底部向上逐渐结冰，这将使水生生物在冬天生存变得更加困难。 还有另一个环境影响。 冰雪是相对明亮的表面，所以它们反射了大部分的入射阳光。 液态水颜色较深，吸收更多的太阳能。 这种差异对气候很重要。 当大面积的冰融化时，会暴露出更深色的水或陆地。 这些表面会吸收更多的热量，这可能导致额外的变暖和更多的融化。 所以，水的一个基本分子特性其影响范围从冰冻湖泊中生命的生存到地球表面吸收和反射能量的方式。

versions.label: Koala 09-02
versions.transcript: Most of us use LED lights every day, but the technology is important for much more than ordinary household lighting. LED stands for light emitting diode, and LEDs have changed the way light can be produced and used. One major advantage of LEDs is energy efficiency. Traditional incandescent bulbs create light by heating a thin wire until it becomes hot enough to glow. A large amount of the electrical energy is therefore lost as heat. LEDs produce light in a different way and require much less electricity to provide the same amount of illumination. They also last much longer, so they don't have to be replaced as often. Another important feature is their size. Individual LEDs can be extremely small. That gives designers much more flexibility than they have with traditional bulbs. LEDs can be arranged in thin displays, placed inside small electronic devices, or combined in large numbers to create lighting systems with very precise shapes and patterns. And researchers are still finding new applications. LEDs are already being used in automobile systems, medical equipment, indoor agriculture, and advanced display technologies. Future designs may allow lighting to respond more precisely to the environment or to be integrated into surfaces and devices in ways that are difficult to achieve today. So the importance of LEDs isn't limited to saving electricity. Their efficiency, small size, long life, and flexibility are continuing to open up new possibilities for how we use light.

versions.label: Koala 09-06
versions.transcript: Renewable energy comes from natural processes that are replenished constantly, such as sunlight, wind, and water. They're an alternative to fossil fuels, which contribute to greenhouse gases and global warming. One of the most widely used forms of renewable energy is solar power. You might have seen solar panels on rooftops of private homes or small buildings that convert sunlight into electricity. These panels can last for decades. Obviously, they wouldn't work in places that are cloudy or rainy most of the year. Even in places with plenty of sunlight, no energy is produced at night. This means that you'll need to store energy for later use. But this requires batteries to be connected to solar panels. And these batteries can be expensive. Wind is another common renewable energy source. Wind turbines are large structures with blades that spin when the wind blows. They're typically installed in open areas like farmland and coastal regions. Why are they rare in residential areas? Well, when the blades of wind turbines slice through the air, they produce a swishing or whooshing sound. The faster the blades, the louder it gets. Imagine living near a wind turbine. Unlike solar panels, wind turbines require lots of maintenance. Oil changes, blade inspections, mechanical repairs. A lot needs to be done on a regular basis. Don't forget that some wind farms are located offshore in the open sea. Think about the extra expenses needed to reach these farms and the harsh conditions that need to be overcome.
versions.transcriptZh: 可再生能源来源于不断补充的自然过程，如阳光、风和水。 它们是化石燃料的替代品，化石燃料会导致温室气体和全球变暖。 最广泛使用的可再生能源之一是太阳能。 你可能在私人住宅或小型建筑的屋顶上看到过太阳能电池板，它们将阳光转化为电能。 这些电池板可以使用几十年。 显然，它们在一年中大部分时间多云或多雨的地方无法工作。 即使在阳光充足的地方，夜间也无法产生能量。 这意味着你需要储存能量以备后用。 但这需要电池连接到太阳能电池板上。 而且这些电池可能很昂贵。 风是另一种常见的可再生能源。 风力涡轮机是带有叶片的大型结构，当风吹时叶片会旋转。 它们通常安装在农田和沿海地区等开阔区域。 为什么它们在居民区很少见呢？ 嗯，当风力涡轮机的叶片划过空气时，它们会产生嗖嗖或呼呼的声音。 叶片转得越快，声音就越大。 想象一下住在风力涡轮机附近。 与太阳能电池板不同，风力涡轮机需要大量维护。 换油、叶片检查、机械维修。 很多事情都需要定期完成。 别忘了有些风力发电场位于开阔海域的近海。 想想到达这些发电场所需的额外费用以及需要克服的恶劣条件。

versions.transcript: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. One of its most recognizable features is its Great Red Spot, which is actually a huge storm. It appears as a large red oval on the planet's surface and has been observed for centuries. This storm is enormous, larger than the planet Earth, and it's been raging for centuries. But did you know that the Great Red Spot is actually shrinking? This topic is interesting not only for astronomers, but also for anyone who studies weather system dynamics, even though this exists on a much larger scale than we're used to for weather we experience on Earth. The shrinkage of the Great Red Spot could give us clues about Jupiter's atmosphere and maybe even our own. Jupiter's atmosphere is primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. It's the trace gases and cloud dynamics that make it fascinating. As the Great Red Spot shrinks, we study changes in wind patterns and atmospheric conditions, hoping for insights into the underlying processes. It could help us understand atmospheric evolution, not only on Jupiter, but potentially on Earth or other planets. Why is it shrinking? The exact reasons remain a mystery. versions.transcript: Today we're going to look at the history of blue pigment and why the color blue has held such a special place in art. This may seem surprising, since blue is everywhere in nature: the sky, the ocean, distant mountains. But for much of human history, a stable and brilliant blue pigment was actually difficult to obtain. Because it was rare and expensive, blue often became associated with wealth, importance, and spiritual value. One of the most famous sources of blue pigment was lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone mined mainly in what is now Afghanistan. To make the pigment known as ultramarine, artists or specialists had to grind the stone and separate the blue mineral from impurities. The process was labor intensive, and the material traveled long distances before reaching European workshops. So ultramarine could cost more than gold. During the Renaissance, patrons sometimes specified in contracts exactly how much ultramarine an artist was required to use, especially in paintings of the Virgin Mary. The blue cloak in such paintings was not just a color choice; it signaled devotion, prestige, and the patron's willingness to pay for the finest materials. But the use of blue changed over time. As new pigments became available, especially synthetic blues, artists no longer had to reserve blue for the most sacred or wealthy subjects. Prussian blue, discovered in the early eighteenth century, was cheaper and easier to produce. Later, other synthetic blues expanded the palette even further. This changed both artistic practice and public access to blue. Blue could appear more freely in landscapes, decorative objects, printed materials, and eventually everyday products. Even so, some artists and collectors continued to prefer lapis lazuli. Why? Partly because of its extraordinary depth and slight variation in tone. Synthetic pigments could be consistent and practical, but lapis had a history and a visual richness that some people felt could not be fully replaced. So the story of blue pigment is not simply a story of technology replacing older materials. It is also about symbolism, economics, and the emotional value people attach to a color.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天我们将探讨蓝色颜料的历史，以及为什么蓝色在艺术中占据如此特殊的地位。 这可能令人惊讶，因为蓝色在大自然中随处可见：天空、海洋、远山。 但在人类历史的大部分时间里，稳定而鲜艳的蓝色颜料实际上很难获得。 因为它稀有而昂贵，蓝色常常与财富、重要性和精神价值联系在一起。 最著名的蓝色颜料来源之一是青金石，一种主要在今天的阿富汗开采的深蓝色石头。 为了制造被称为群青的颜料，艺术家或专家必须研磨石头，并将蓝色矿物质与杂质分离。 这个过程是劳动密集型的，而且这种材料在运到欧洲作坊之前要经过长途跋涉。 所以群青的成本可能比黄金还高。 在文艺复兴时期，资助人有时会在合同中明确规定艺术家需要使用多少群青，尤其是在绘制圣母玛利亚的画作中。 此类画作中的蓝色斗篷不仅仅是一种颜色选择；它象征着虔诚、声望和资助人愿意为最好的材料买单的意愿。 但蓝色的使用随着时间而改变。 随着新颜料的出现，尤其是合成蓝色颜料，艺术家不再需要将蓝色保留给最神圣或最富有的主题。 普鲁士蓝，在18世纪早期被发现，更便宜也更容易生产。 后来，其他合成蓝色颜料进一步拓宽了调色板。 这改变了艺术实践和公众对蓝色的使用。 蓝色可以更自由地出现在风景画、装饰品、印刷材料，并最终出现在日常产品中。 即便如此，一些艺术家和收藏家仍然喜欢青金石。 为什么？ 部分原因在于其非凡的深度和细微的色调变化。 合成颜料可以保持一致和实用，但青金石拥有历史和视觉上的丰富性，有些人觉得这些是无法完全取代的。 因此，蓝色颜料的故事不仅仅是技术取代旧材料的故事。 它也关乎象征意义、经济学以及人们赋予一种颜色的情感价值。

versions.transcript: Today we're going to discuss a fascinating cognitive bias known as the Dunning Kruger effect. This effect describes a situation where people with low ability in a particular domain tend to overestimate their competence. In other words, they're not just unskilled; they're also unaware of how unskilled they are. Why does this happen? The core reason is that the skills needed to perform a task well are often the same skills required to recognize competence in oneself and in others. So, a person who lacks those skills is in a double bind: they perform poorly, and they lack the metacognitive framework to evaluate their performance accurately. For example, think about a novice chess player who has just learned the basic rules. After winning a few games against other beginners, they might believe they have a real talent for the game, not realizing the vast depth of strategy they haven't even encountered. They might even challenge a much more experienced player, completely misjudging the gap in their abilities. Interestingly, the Dunning Kruger effect also has a flip side. Highly competent individuals often underestimate their relative ability. They might assume that tasks they find easy are also easy for others, leading them to be less confident in their expertise than they should be. This highlights the complex relationship between actual performance and self perception.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天我们要讨论一种引人入胜的认知偏差，即邓宁-克鲁格效应（Dunning-Kruger effect）。 这种效应描述的是这样一种情况：在特定领域能力较低的人往往会高估自己的能力。 换句话说，他们不仅缺乏技能，而且还意识不到自己有多么缺乏技能。 为什么会发生这种情况？ 核心原因是，做好一项任务所需的技能，往往与识别自己和他人能力所需的技能是相同的。 因此，缺乏这些技能的人陷入了双重困境：他们表现不佳，且缺乏准确评估自己表现的元认知框架。 例如，想一想一个刚学会基本规则的国际象棋初学者。 在赢了其他几个初学者几局后，他们可能会认为自己在这类游戏中极具天赋，却没有意识到自己甚至还未接触到那些博大精深的策略。 他们甚至可能会挑战经验丰富得多的玩家，完全误判了彼此能力上的差距。 有趣的是，邓宁-克鲁格效应也有另一面。 高能力的人往往会低估自己的相对能力。 他们可能会认为对自己来说容易的任务对其他人也容易，从而导致他们对自己的专业知识不如应有的那么自信。 这凸显了实际表现与自我感知之间复杂的关系。

transcriptSentences.text: Today we're going to discuss a fascinating cognitive bias known as the Dunning Kruger effect.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 今天我们要讨论一种引人入胜的认知偏差，即邓宁-克鲁格效应（Dunning-Kruger effect）。

transcriptSentences.text: This effect describes a situation where people with low ability in a particular domain tend to overestimate their competence.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这种效应描述的是这样一种情况：在特定领域能力较低的人往往会高估自己的能力。

transcriptSentences.text: In other words, they're not just unskilled; they're also unaware of how unskilled they are.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 换句话说，他们不仅缺乏技能，而且还意识不到自己有多么缺乏技能。

transcriptSentences.text: Why does this happen?
transcriptSentences.textZh: 为什么会发生这种情况？

transcriptSentences.text: The core reason is that the skills needed to perform a task well are often the same skills required to recognize competence in oneself and in others.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 核心原因是，做好一项任务所需的技能，往往与识别自己和他人能力所需的技能是相同的。

transcriptSentences.text: So, a person who lacks those skills is in a double bind: they perform poorly, and they lack the metacognitive framework to evaluate their performance accurately.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 因此，缺乏这些技能的人陷入了双重困境：他们表现不佳，且缺乏准确评估自己表现的元认知框架。

transcriptSentences.text: For example, think about a novice chess player who has just learned the basic rules.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 例如，想一想一个刚学会基本规则的国际象棋初学者。

transcriptSentences.text: After winning a few games against other beginners, they might believe they have a real talent for the game, not realizing the vast depth of strategy they haven't even encountered.

transcriptSentences.text: They might even challenge a much more experienced player, completely misjudging the gap in their abilities.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他们甚至可能会挑战经验丰富得多的玩家，完全误判了彼此能力上的差距。

transcriptSentences.text: Interestingly, the Dunning Kruger effect also has a flip side.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 有趣的是，邓宁-克鲁格效应也有另一面。

transcriptSentences.text: Highly competent individuals often underestimate their relative ability.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 高能力的人往往会低估自己的相对能力。

transcriptSentences.text: They might assume that tasks they find easy are also easy for others, leading them to be less confident in their expertise than they should be.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 他们可能会认为对自己来说容易的任务对其他人也容易，从而导致他们对自己的专业知识不如应有的那么自信。

transcriptSentences.text: This highlights the complex relationship between actual performance and self perception.
transcriptSentences.textZh: 这凸显了实际表现与自我感知之间复杂的关系。

versions.transcript: Today, the Mexican visual artist Frida Kahlo is a household name worldwide. But before her death in 1954, she was mainly known as the wife of another famous artist, Diego Rivera, and critics and the public barely heard of her until decades later. Probably not until a Hollywood movie about her life in 2002. These days, Frida Kahlo's best known artworks are her paintings, especially her self portraits, showing her with a serious expression, thick eyebrows and traditional Mexican clothes. Kahlo's drawings, however, are rather obscure, even now. One drawing, a self portrait from 1946, was intended as a gift for a Mexican politician that Kahlo and her husband knew. Similar to her paintings, Kahlo drew herself with a serious facial expression, like she's asking, what's my life's meaning? Also, her eyebrows form the shape of a hummingbird, which seems ready to fly onto her forehead, where some cloud like shapes appear. My favourite part of this drawing is Kahlo's hair. One side is arranged in a modest braid, while the other is loose and wild. I think it shows her inner struggle between two ways of being, reserved versus free.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天，墨西哥视觉艺术家弗里达·卡罗（Frida Kahlo）在全世界都是家喻户晓的名字。 但在1954年她去世之前，她主要作为另一位著名艺术家迭戈·里维拉（Diego Rivera）的妻子为人所知，直到几十年后，评论家和公众才真正听说她的事迹。 可能直到2002年有一部关于她生平的电影在好莱坞上映后才真正成名。 如今，弗里达·卡罗最著名的作品是她的绘画，尤其是她的自画像，画中她神情严肃，眉毛浓密，穿着传统的墨西哥服饰。 然而，卡罗的素描作品直到现在依然鲜为人知。 其中一幅素描是1946年的自画像，原本是打算送给卡罗夫妇认识的一位墨西哥政治家的礼物。 与她的油画作品类似，卡罗画中的自己也带着严肃的面部表情，仿佛在询问：我人生的意义是什么？ 此外，她的眉毛勾勒出一只蜂鸟的形状，它似乎准备飞向她的前额，而那里出现了一些云朵般的形状。 这幅画中我最喜欢的部分是卡罗的头发。 头发的一侧梳成了端庄的辫子，而另一侧则是披散且狂野的。 我认为这展现了她内心在两种生存状态之间的挣扎：克制与自由。

versions.transcript: The Galapagos are a chain of islands roughly 1,000 kilometers off the coast of Ecuador. Throughout the 1800s, people, mostly whalers and explorers, stopped at the islands during long ocean voyages. At that time, long ocean voyages made it hard to keep fresh meat on ships. So sailors released goats on some islands as a living food supply they could hunt later when passing through. They most likely didn't know how much their actions were going to damage the islands. Goats are very adaptable and can survive in harsh environments like the Galapagos. They definitely are not picky eaters. They consume everything from tough shrubs to grasses, so they didn't run out of food easily. With no natural predators, their population exploded. As time went on, the goats' eating habits caused native plants, like one species of cactus, to mostly disappear. And that was a huge problem for native animals like giant tortoises. These tortoises rely on plants like this cactus for food and shade. Without them, many tortoise populations collapsed. So how can we address this problem? Well, in the early 2000s, conservation efforts began to reintroduce tortoises to islands where they had gone extinct. Let's take a look at these efforts and determine how effective they've been.

versions.transcript: Picture a creature that's smaller than a mouse, yet as territorial as a lion. Does it sound like a cartoon character? It's actually the real life Scarlet badis. A freshwater fish. It's only about 2 cm long at most. In the wild, it generally thrives peacefully in the slow moving streams of India. Because of its size and attractive coloring, it's also a popular choice for aquariums and fish tanks. However, in captive environments like aquariums, males are more aggressive. They'll chase and nip at other males if they encroach on their territory. So it's crucial to include lots of vegetation. Plants act as hiding places and borderlines between males' territories. Now, male Scarlet badis are a vivid orangish red scarlet with light bluish stripes. When a male isn't having a confrontation with another male in the aquarium, though, his scarlet is less bright. It can almost but not quite resemble female coloring, which is dull gray. This could make it hard to tell the sexes apart. Except, if you can see any scarlet at all on the fish, it's a male. Plus, unlike in most fish species, males are also usually a bit larger than females. And the other time a male Scarlet baddess shows his brightest coloring is during breeding season. In aquariums, he can be observed doing a sort of dance to impress females, showing himself off. His dance also involves following the female around until she decides whether to mate with him.

versions.label: Koala 04-19
versions.transcript: Today, we're going to explore the fascinating world of street art and its impact on urban environments. Street art, which includes graffiti and mural painting, has evolved from being seen as mere vandalism to being recognized as a legitimate form of artistic expression. Artists use public spaces to showcase their work, often reflecting social and political themes. One of the key benefits of street art is its ability to transform drab and neglected areas into vibrant and visually stimulating environments. Murals can brighten up a dull wall, adding color and life to a community. This transformation can foster a sense of pride among residents. Street art can also serve as a powerful tool for social change. It provides artists with a platform to address important issues such as inequality, environmental concerns, and cultural identity. For example, artists may create pieces that highlight the struggles of marginalized communities. However, street art is not without challenges. The legality of street art is often debated, as many artists work without official permission. This can lead to conflicts with property owners and law enforcement. Additionally, the transient nature of street art means that it can be painted over or removed at any time, making it a potentially impermanent form of expression. Despite these challenges, street art remains an influential aspect of contemporary art. It allows artists to reach a wider audience and engage with the public in meaningful ways, while transforming urban spaces.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天，我们将探讨街头艺术迷人的世界及其对城市环境的影响。 街头艺术包括涂鸦和壁画，它已经从仅仅被视为破坏公物的行为，演变为被认可的一种合法的艺术表达形式。 艺术家利用公共空间展示他们的作品，通常反映社会和政治主题。 街头艺术的主要好处之一是它能够将单调和被忽视的区域转化为充满活力和视觉刺激的环境。 壁画可以照亮沉闷的墙壁，为社区增添色彩和生命力。 这种转变可以培养居民的自豪感。 街头艺术还可以作为社会变革的有力工具。 它为艺术家提供了一个平台来探讨不平等、环境问题和文化身份等重要议题。 例如，艺术家可能会创作凸显边缘化社区挣扎的作品。 然而，街头艺术并非没有挑战。 街头艺术的合法性经常受到争议，因为许多艺术家在没有官方许可的情况下进行创作。 这可能会导致与物业所有者和执法部门的冲突。 此外，街头艺术的瞬时性意味着它可能随时被覆盖或移除，使其成为一种具有潜在临时性的表达形式。 尽管面临这些挑战，街头艺术仍然是当代艺术中具有影响力的一个方面。 它让艺术家能够接触到更广泛的受众，并以有意义的方式与公众互动，同时改造城市空间。

versions.label: Koala 09-05
versions.transcript: When people think about Renaissance art, they usually think first of painting and sculpture - works by artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, or Raphael. Those art forms are certainly important, but today I want to focus on another form of Renaissance art that was highly valued at the time and is sometimes overlooked today: tapestry. A tapestry is a large woven textile, often designed to hang on a wall. During the Renaissance, wealthy rulers, churches, and noble families commissioned enormous tapestries showing religious stories, historical events, hunting scenes, or symbols of political power. One reason tapestries were especially useful was their portability. Compare a tapestry with a fresco. A fresco is painted directly onto wet plaster on a wall, so once it is created, it stays with the building. A tapestry, however, can be removed, rolled up, transported, and hung somewhere else. A ruler who moved between several residences could take valuable tapestries along and use them to decorate different rooms. Of course, being portable did not mean they were easy to move. Large tapestries could be extremely heavy. They had to be rolled or folded carefully and protected from moisture and rough handling. Historical records show that tapestries were sometimes damaged during transportation. Threads could be pulled, edges could tear, or moisture could weaken the fibers. So portability was an advantage, but it came with risks. Another point that's easy to miss is how collaborative tapestry production was. A famous painter might create the original design, sometimes called a cartoon. But that was only the beginning. Other specialists enlarged the design, selected colors, prepared dyed wool or silk, and worked at large looms to weave the image. Highly skilled weavers had to translate painted forms into patterns made entirely from thread. And some luxury tapestries included silk, silver, or gold wrapped threads. That made them extremely expensive. In fact, for some Renaissance courts, tapestries could be more valuable than paintings. So when we talk about Renaissance art, we shouldn't imagine that artistic achievement belonged only to individual painters or sculptors. Tapestries were major works of art too, and their creation depended on teams of specialized artisans working together.
versions.transcriptZh: 当人们想到文艺复兴时期的艺术时，他们通常首先想到绘画和雕塑——例如达·芬奇、米开朗基罗或拉斐尔等艺术家的作品。 这些艺术形式固然重要，但今天我想把重点放在文艺复兴时期另一种当时备受重视而如今有时却被忽视的艺术形式上：挂毯。 挂毯是一种大型编织纺织品，通常设计用于挂在墙上。 在文艺复兴时期，富有的统治者、教堂和贵族家庭委托制作了巨大的挂毯，展示宗教故事、历史事件、狩猎场景或政治权力的象征。 挂毯特别有用的一個原因是它们的便携性。 将挂毯与壁画进行比较。 壁画是直接画在墙壁湿灰泥上的，所以一旦创作完成，它就与建筑物融为一体。 然而，挂毯可以被取下、卷起、运输并挂在其他地方。 一位在多处住所之间迁徙的统治者可以随身携带珍贵的挂毯，用它们来装饰不同的房间。 当然，便携性并不意味着它们易于移动。 大型挂毯可能非常重。 它们必须小心地卷起或折叠，并保护好，避免受潮和粗暴搬运。 历史记录显示，挂毯在运输过程中有时会受损。 线可能会被扯断，边缘可能会撕裂，或者潮湿可能会削弱纤维。 因此，便携性是一个优点，但也伴随着风险。 另一个容易忽略的重点是挂毯生产的协作性。 一位著名的画家可能会创作原始设计，有时被称为“卡通”稿。 但这仅仅是个开始。 其他专家会放大设计、选择颜色、准备染色的羊毛或丝绸，并在大型织机上工作，编织出图像。 技艺高超的织工必须将绘画形式转化为完全由线构成的图案。 一些奢华的挂毯还包括丝绸、银线或金线缠绕的线。 这使得它们极其昂贵。 事实上，对于一些文艺复兴时期的宫廷来说，挂毯可能比绘画更有价值。 因此，当我们谈论文艺复兴艺术时，我们不应该认为艺术成就只属于个体画家或雕塑家。 挂毯也是主要的艺术品，它们的创作依赖于专业工匠团队的共同努力。

versions.transcript: Today we're going to talk about viral marketing. Viral marketing uses social networks to spread brand information through content that users share voluntarily. Because the audience helps distribute the message, the cost can be relatively low while the potential reach can be enormous. A single post, video, or image may spread across regions and social groups within only a few hours. However, viral marketing is not a guaranteed formula. It is difficult to predict what people will find interesting enough to share. Audience tastes are hard to measure, and a campaign that seems clever to a marketing team may simply be ignored. Another risk is controversy. Controversial content may spread quickly, but it can also create backlash and damage the brand. There is also the issue of control. Once content becomes popular, the company may lose control over how it is interpreted. Users may parody it, criticize it, or change its meaning in ways the brand did not intend. Even so, viral marketing can be very valuable, especially for new brands that need attention quickly. For a start up trying to enter the market, it can be a powerful tool, as long as the company understands both its promise and its risks.
versions.transcriptZh: 今天我们要讨论的是病毒式营销。 病毒式营销利用社交网络，通过用户自愿分享的内容来传播品牌信息。 由于受众通过分发信息提供了帮助，因此成本可能相对较低，而潜在的影响范围可能非常巨大。 一个帖子、视频或图像可能在短短几个小时内跨越不同地区和社交群体进行传播。 然而，病毒式营销并不是一个万全之策。 很难预测人们会觉得什么内容足够有趣到愿意去分享。 受众的品味难以衡量，对营销团队来说看似聪明的活动可能就会被忽略。 另一个风险是争议性。 有争议的内容可能传播很快，但也可能引发抵制并损害品牌形象。 还有控制权的问题。 一旦内容变得流行，公司可能会失去对其被如何解读的控制。 用户可能会对其进行恶搞、批评，或者以品牌方并非初衷的方式改变其含义。 即便如此，病毒式营销仍然非常有价值，特别是对于需要快速获得关注的新品牌。 对于试图进入市场的初创企业来说，只要公司了解其机遇与风险，它就是一个非常强大的工具。

versions.label: Koala 09-13
versions.transcript: Bird migration is one of the most remarkable seasonal movements in the animal world. Some species travel thousands of kilometers between breeding and wintering areas, and they have to navigate across landscapes they may see only once or twice a year. Birds use several kinds of information to find their way. Some use the position of the Sun during the day or patterns of stars at night. Others can detect Earth's magnetic field. Researchers think that, in some species, a light sensitive protein in the eye plays a role in this magnetic sense. The protein is thought to respond differently depending on the direction of Earth's magnetic field. That may allow a bird to perceive magnetic information as part of what it sees and use it like a compass. But navigation is only one part of the migration story. Migrating birds face many challenges along the way. They need suitable places to rest and feed, and they are affected by habitat loss, storms, changing seasonal temperatures, and human built environments. A major concern is population decline. Migrating birds are connected to other species in food webs. Some eat insects, some spread seeds, and some are prey for larger animals. If the number of migratory birds drops sharply, those relationships can be disrupted. For example, insect populations may increase in some areas, while predators that depend on birds may lose an important food source. Artificial light is another problem. Many birds migrate at night, and bright buildings can confuse them, pulling them away from normal routes or causing collisions. One simple conservation measure is to turn off unnecessary lights at night, particularly during major migration periods. Some cities already operate lights out programs during spring and fall migration. It's a relatively easy step, but it can make urban areas much safer for birds making these long seasonal journeys.
versions.transcriptZh: 鸟类迁徙是动物界最引人注目的季节性迁徙之一。 有些物种在繁殖地和越冬地之间迁徙数千公里，它们必须在一年中可能只看到一两次的景观中导航。 鸟类利用多种信息来寻找方向。 有些在白天利用太阳的位置，或者在夜晚利用星辰的模式。 另一些则能探测到地球的磁场。 研究人员认为，在某些物种中，眼睛中一种光敏蛋白在这种磁感中起作用。 这种蛋白质被认为会根据地球磁场的方向做出不同的反应。 这可能使鸟类将磁信息视为其所见的一部分，并像指南针一样使用它。 但导航只是迁徙故事的一部分。 迁徙的鸟类在途中面临许多挑战。 它们需要合适的休息和觅食场所，并受到栖息地丧失、风暴、季节温度变化以及人类建造环境的影响。 一个主要问题是种群数量下降。 迁徙的鸟类在食物网中与其他物种相互关联。 有些吃昆虫，有些传播种子，有些则成为大型动物的猎物。 如果候鸟数量急剧下降，这些关系就会被破坏。 例如，某些地区的昆虫种群可能会增加，而依赖鸟类的捕食者可能会失去重要的食物来源。 人造光是另一个问题。 许多鸟类在夜间迁徙，明亮的建筑物会迷惑它们，使它们偏离正常路线或导致碰撞。 一个简单的保护措施是夜间关闭不必要的灯光，尤其是在主要的迁徙时期。 一些城市已经在春季和秋季迁徙期间实施了熄灯计划。 这是一个相对简单的步骤，但它能使城市地区对这些进行长途季节性旅行的鸟类来说更加安全。
